# Harness Patterns — full text for AI agents

Software design patterns mapped onto AI agent harness engineering, in plain English.

---

---
id: game-loop
number: "1.01"
title: Game Loop
chapter: agent-loop
fit: adapted
review_id: rev-game-loop
figure_number: Fig. 1.01
figure_caption: "The run is one cycle, repeated until the model stops asking for tools."
diagram: game-loop.svg
analogy_title: "The ship's navigator taking fixes"
---
## Gist

Run the agent as a loop: build the request, call the model, run any tools it asks for, and repeat until it stops asking.

## Everyday comparison

### The ship's navigator taking fixes

At sea, the navigator does not plan the whole trip once and walk away. Every hour they read the instruments and mark the ship's position on the chart. Then they set a new direction and wait for the next reading. The ship arrives because this small cycle repeats. The trip ends when the harbour is in sight.

## Classic meaning

A main loop that keeps taking input, updating state and producing output. It keeps the pace of the program separate from any single event.

## In the agent system

Every harness has a loop at its centre, wrapped around the call to the model. Each pass sends the system prompt (the standing instructions) and the transcript (the conversation so far). It also sends the tool schemas (descriptions of the tools the model may use). Then the harness looks at the reply. If the reply has tool_use blocks (the model's requests to run a tool), the harness runs those tools. It puts the matching tool_result blocks (the tools' answers) into the next user message and goes round again. If stop_reason (the field that says why the model stopped) is end_turn, the model has finished. The loop ends and the final text goes to the user. Other stop reasons need their own handling. max_tokens means the reply was cut off at the length limit. A cut-off tool_use must never be run. pause_turn means a server-side tool (a tool the provider runs) paused a long turn. The harness should then send the request again to continue. The harness checks its guards at the start of every pass. These are max_turns (a limit on turns), a token budget (a limit on how much text the run may use) and a cancel flag. This is also where it handles compaction (shrinking old context to save space) and user messages waiting in a queue.

## In a large company

In a large company platform, the agent loop usually runs inside a durable execution engine such as Temporal or AWS Step Functions. A durable execution engine saves each step, so the work survives a crash. If a worker (the server running the job) crashes, the run picks up from the last finished model call or tool call. Each pass of the loop is traced with OpenTelemetry, a standard for recording what software does. It uses the GenAI semantic conventions, which are agreed names for model and tool records (called spans). Each pass is also charged against a per-tenant token budget. A tenant is one customer company sharing the platform. The LLM gateway (a central service that all model calls pass through) enforces this budget. The key control is a hard limit per run on turns, tokens and wall-clock time (real elapsed time). Tenant policy sets this limit, not the prompt.

## Step by step

1. Build the request from the system prompt, the transcript and the tool definitions.
1. Call the model and stream the reply to the screen as it arrives.
1. If the reply has tool_use blocks, run them and add the tool_result blocks.
1. Check the stop conditions (end_turn, max_turns, budget, cancel), then loop again or stop.

## Code sketch

```python
while turn < max_turns and not cancelled:
    turn += 1
    resp = model.create(system=sys_prompt,
                        messages=msgs,
                        tools=tools)
    msgs.append(resp.as_message())
    if resp.stop_reason == 'max_tokens':
        raise Truncated(resp)  # never run it
    if resp.stop_reason == 'pause_turn':
        continue  # resend to resume
    calls = resp.tool_use_blocks()
    if not calls:
        break  # end_turn: answer is ready
    msgs.append(run_tools(calls))
```

## Be careful

A loop with no turn limit or budget check can run forever. This happens when the model keeps calling the same failing tool.

## Diagram

![Fig. 1.01: The run is one cycle, repeated until the model stops asking for tools.](/diagrams/game-loop.svg)

id: update-method
number: "1.02"
title: Update Method
chapter: agent-loop
fit: adapted
figure_number: Fig. 1.02
figure_caption: "The loop knows one call, and each subsystem decides what that call does."
diagram: update-method.svg
analogy_title: "The zookeeper's feeding round"
---
## Gist

Give each part of the harness its own update hook, and let the loop call every hook once per turn.

## Everyday comparison

### The zookeeper's feeding round

Every morning the zookeeper walks the same path past every enclosure. The penguins get fish, the giraffes get acacia leaves, and the tortoise gets lettuce and a quick shell check. The keeper does not need to remember each animal's diet. Each enclosure has its own routine posted on the gate. The round simply visits them all in turn.

## Classic meaning

Each object in a simulation has an update method. The main loop calls it on every active object once per frame.

## In the agent system

Between model calls, a harness has many small jobs that must move forward a little each turn. The token meter works out how much text has been used so far. The compactor watches the context window (the text the model can see at one time). It checks whether the window is nearly full and must be shrunk. A todo tracker reminds the model if its task list is out of date. A poller collects background tasks that have finished. The harness does not write all of this into the loop itself. Instead, each subsystem (each separate part of the harness) registers an object with an on_turn(ctx) method. Here ctx is the context object that holds this turn's information. The loop goes through the list of registered objects once per turn. So adding a new behaviour means one new registration, not a change to the loop.

## In a large company

Enterprise harnesses use per-turn update hooks for duties that touch every part of the system. One example is a budget meter. It reports spending to the chargeback ledger (the record used to bill each customer). Another is a policy refresher that picks up changed tenant settings. A tenant is one customer company sharing the platform. A third is a DLP monitor that samples new context. DLP (data loss prevention) means tools that stop sensitive data from leaking. Each hook should send its own OpenTelemetry span. OpenTelemetry is a standard for tracing software, and a span is one timed record of work. This way a slow part shows up against the turn latency SLOs (reliability targets for how fast a turn finishes). The control to enforce is this. The platform registers the hooks that tenants require, and a user or plugin setting cannot remove them or change their order.

## Step by step

1. Subsystems register objects that have an on_turn(ctx) method.
1. At the start of each turn, the loop builds a TurnContext (this turn's shared information).
1. The loop calls on_turn(ctx) on every registered object, in order.
1. Each object reads or changes the context, then the model call goes ahead.

## Code sketch

```python
class Compactor:
    def on_turn(self, ctx):
        if ctx.tokens > 0.8 * ctx.window:
            ctx.msgs = summarise(ctx.msgs)

systems = [BudgetMeter(), Compactor(),
           TaskPoller(), TodoNudger()]

for turn in agent_loop():
    for s in systems:
        s.on_turn(turn.ctx)
```

## Be careful

Sometimes one update needs another update's result. Then the order of registration matters, so write that order down or merge those parts.

## Diagram

![Fig. 1.02: The loop knows one call, and each subsystem decides what that call does.](/diagrams/update-method.svg)

id: state
number: "1.03"
title: State
chapter: agent-loop
fit: direct
figure_number: Fig. 1.03
figure_caption: "Each state owns its own transitions, so a tool cannot run before approval."
diagram: state.svg
analogy_title: The laundromat washing machine
---
## Gist

Make each phase of the loop its own state object, so each state decides how to react to messages, interrupts and tool results.

## Everyday comparison

### The laundromat washing machine

Press the start button on a washing machine, and what happens depends on where it is in the cycle. While it fills with water, the door can still open. During the spin, the door stays locked and the button does nothing. When it finishes, the light turns green and the door opens. It is the same button with a different response, because each stage has its own rules.

## Classic meaning

Let an object change its behaviour when its internal state changes. It does this by handing the work to a separate object for each state.

## In the agent system

An agent session moves through clear phases: Idle, CallingModel, AwaitingApproval, RunningTool and Done. The same event means different things in each phase. A new user message starts a turn when the session is Idle. The same message waits in a queue while a tool is running (RunningTool). Pressing Esc in CallingModel stops the reply that is streaming in. Pressing Esc in AwaitingApproval counts as saying no. Each phase can be written as a state class with methods such as on_message, on_interrupt and on_tool_result. This replaces a tangle of if-statements. It also makes illegal transitions impossible to write by accident. A transition is a move from one state to another. An illegal one is, for example, running a tool without approval.

## In a large company

On an enterprise platform, the harness saves the session state to storage, not just in memory. So a session in AwaitingApproval can wait hours for a human reviewer. It can then continue on another worker (another server). Durable workflow engines such as Temporal or Step Functions model these phases directly. They save each step so the work survives crashes. Every transition is written to an append-only audit log, a record that can be added to but never changed. Each record holds the actor, the tool call and the decision. The important control is in the approval step. It checks the approver's role through RBAC (role-based access control: permissions given by job role) or a policy engine. This way the person who asked cannot approve their own high-risk action.

## Step by step

1. The session keeps a reference to its current state object.
1. Every event (message, interrupt, model reply, approval) goes to that state.
1. The state handles the event and returns the next state.
1. The session switches to the new state, and the screen shows it.

## Code sketch

```python
class AwaitingApproval(State):
    def on_approve(self, s):
        return RunningTool(self.call)
    def on_deny(self, s):
        s.add_result(self.call, 'denied')
        return CallingModel()
    def on_message(self, s, m):
        s.queue.append(m)  # hold it
        return self
```

## Be careful

Do not let tools or hooks set the state field directly. Every change of state should go through the current state's methods.

## Diagram

![Fig. 1.03: Each state owns its own transitions, so a tool cannot run before approval.](/diagrams/state.svg)

id: template-method
number: "1.04"
title: Template Method
chapter: agent-loop
fit: direct
figure_number: Fig. 1.04
figure_caption: "The outline is fixed, and subclasses fill in only the marked slots."
diagram: template-method.svg
analogy_title: "The builder's standard house plan"
---
## Gist

Fix the order of a turn's steps in a base class, and let each agent type change only the hooks it needs.

## Everyday comparison

### The builder's standard house plan

A housing developer builds every home in the same order: foundation, frame, roof, then the inside. Buyers choose the kitchen tiles, the bathroom fittings and the paint. But nobody gets to put the roof on before the walls. The plan is fixed, and the choices are slots inside it.

## Classic meaning

Write the outline of a process in one method of a base class. Subclasses can replace certain steps, but they cannot change the outline.

## In the agent system

A harness base class (shared parent code that other classes build on) defines run_turn(). This method builds the system prompt, trims the context, calls the model, sends out tool calls and records the turn. The method is final. That means subclasses (classes built on the base class) cannot replace it. A coding agent overrides (replaces) system_prompt() to add the repository's rules. It also overrides on_tool_result() to run a linter (a code style checker) after edits. A research subagent overrides only select_tools(), so it can use just search and fetch. The outline never changes. So certain rules hold for every agent type. For example, every turn is logged to the transcript, and the token budget is checked before each call.

## In a large company

Platform teams ship a base agent whose fixed outline enforces rules for every tenant (each customer company on the platform). The outline passes on the user's identity and runs policy checks before each tool call. It removes PII (personal data such as names and emails) before logging. It also records OpenTelemetry spans (timed records of work, in a standard format) and checks each tenant's budget. Product teams build subclasses and override only prompts, tool choice and result handling. The risk is a team skipping the outline by calling the model client directly. To stop this, the LLM gateway (the central service all model calls pass through) should reject such calls. It rejects any call that does not carry the platform's tenant and trace headers, which are labels attached to each request.

## Step by step

1. The base class writes run_turn() as a fixed list of steps.
1. Some steps call hook methods that have a default behaviour.
1. A subclass overrides only the hooks it cares about.
1. Every agent type runs the same outline with its own changes.

## Code sketch

```python
class BaseAgent:
    def run_turn(self, msgs):  # fixed
        sp = self.system_prompt()  # hook
        resp = self.model.create(
            system=sp, messages=msgs)
        for call in resp.tool_calls:
            out = self.tools.run(call)
            self.on_tool_result(call, out)
        self.transcript.record(resp)
class CodingAgent(BaseAgent):
    def system_prompt(self):
        return BASE + REPO_RULES
```

## Be careful

If subclasses start to override run_turn() itself, the guarantees are lost. Mark it final and add a new hook instead.

## Diagram

![Fig. 1.04: The outline is fixed, and subclasses fill in only the marked slots.](/diagrams/template-method.svg)

id: chain-of-responsibility
number: "1.05"
title: Chain of Responsibility
chapter: agent-loop
fit: adapted
review_id: rev-chain-of-responsibility
figure_number: Fig. 1.05
figure_caption: Each hook can stop the call or pass it to the next one.
diagram: chain-of-responsibility.svg
analogy_title: Airport departure checkpoints
---
## Gist

Pass each tool call through an ordered chain of hooks that can block, change or pass it on. Only the chain's end lets it run.

## Everyday comparison

### Airport departure checkpoints

Between the kerb and the plane door, a passenger meets the check-in desk, passport control, the security scanner and the gate agent. Each one checks a single thing. They either wave you on to the next one or stop you there. None of them needs to know what the others check. The airport can add a new checkpoint without retraining the rest.

## Classic meaning

Give more than one object a chance to handle a request. Link the handlers in a chain and pass the request along until one handles it.

## In the agent system

Before a tool call runs, the harness passes it through a chain of PreToolUse hooks. A hook is a small piece of code that runs at a set moment, here just before a tool is used. The chain might start with an allowlist check (a list of allowed tools). Next comes a path guard that blocks writes outside the workspace (the project folder the agent works in). Then a secrets scanner looks for passwords and keys. Last comes a prompt that asks the user to approve. Each hook gets the call and returns deny, modify or pass. A deny stops the chain at once. It becomes an error tool_result (the tool's answer, marked as an error) that the model can read. A pass hands the call to the next hook. Hooks managed by the organisation sit at the front of the chain. User settings cannot remove or override them. So a user hook that says allow can only skip the final approval prompt, never a required guard. Users and plugins add their own hooks after the managed ones, without changing harness code.

## In a large company

In enterprise platforms, the chain usually starts with a call to a central policy engine such as OPA or Cedar. A policy engine is a service that decides what is allowed from written rules. Next comes DLP scanning (data loss prevention: checking for sensitive data that must not leak). Then come allowlists for each tenant (each customer company), and finally a human approval step for high-risk actions. Every decision goes into the audit trail. The record holds the deciding hook, the policy version and the principal (the user or service making the request). Auditors for SOC 2 and ISO 27001, two common security standards, expect to see this. The key risk is ordering. Required guards managed by the organisation must run first and fail closed, which means they block when something goes wrong. That way a plugin hook or a timeout can never turn into a silent allow.

## Step by step

1. The model sends a tool_use block, and the harness wraps it as a request.
1. The first hook checks it and returns deny, modify or pass.
1. On pass, the request goes to the next hook. On deny, the chain stops.
1. If the last hook passes it, the tool runs with the input, which may have been changed.

## Code sketch

```python
class PathGuard(Hook):
    def handle(self, call, nxt):
        p = call.input.get('path')
        if p:
            rp = Path(ROOT, p).resolve()
            if not rp.is_relative_to(ROOT):
                return Deny('outside root')
        return nxt(call)

ROOT = Path(WORKSPACE).resolve()
chain = [Allowlist(), PathGuard(),
         SecretScan(), AskUser()]
result = run_chain(chain, call, execute)
```

## Be careful

In a long chain, it is hard to see which hook made the decision. Log the name of the deciding hook with every allow and every deny.

## Diagram

![Fig. 1.05: Each hook can stop the call or pass it to the next one.](/diagrams/chain-of-responsibility.svg)

id: interpreter
number: "1.06"
title: Interpreter
chapter: agent-loop
fit: direct
review_id: rev-interpreter
figure_number: Fig. 1.06
figure_caption: "Text becomes a tree of nodes, and each node knows how to run itself."
diagram: interpreter.svg
analogy_title: The knitting pattern
---
## Gist

Read the model's structured output as action objects from a small grammar (a set of language rules), then run them on the workspace.

## Everyday comparison

### The knitting pattern

A knitting pattern reads like code: "k2, p2, repeat to end", then "row 3: k all". Here k means knit and p means purl. The knitter does not make things up. They read each short code, turn it into a stitch, and follow the repeats and row instructions as rules. A tiny language with a few words produces a whole jumper.

## Classic meaning

Define the rules (the grammar) of a simple language, and store each sentence as a tree of expression objects. Run the tree by calling interpret on each node.

## In the agent system

Some harnesses let the model answer in a compact action language instead of one tool call per step. Examples are an edit block format, or a plan DSL with steps like edit, run and if_fail. A DSL (domain-specific language) is a small language made for one job. The harness parses (reads and breaks down) that text into a tree of expression nodes: Seq, Edit, Run and OnFail. Each node has an interpret(ctx) method that does its part of the work on the workspace (the project files). It goes through the same permission checks and sandbox as an ordinary tool call. A sandbox is a locked-down area where code runs safely. Sometimes the program arrives inside a tool_use input (the model's request to run a tool). Then parse errors go back as an error tool_result (the tool's answer, marked as an error), so the model can fix its syntax. Other times the program arrives as plain text from the model. Then errors go back in the next user message, because a tool_result needs a matching tool_use id.

## In a large company

Enterprise platforms meet Interpreter in workflow DSLs (small languages for describing workflows) and structured edit formats. They also meet it in policy languages such as Rego and Cedar, which are themselves small interpreted languages for access rules. When the model writes the program, treat that program as untrusted input. Each node must run under the caller's identity, inside the sandbox, and through the same policy checks as a direct tool call. Grammar versions should be pinned (fixed to a known version) and covered by eval suites (sets of automated tests of model behaviour). Then a model upgrade that changes the output syntax fails a regression test gate. It does not break live production traffic.

## Step by step

1. The model returns text in the agreed action syntax.
1. A parser turns the text into a tree of expression objects.
1. The harness calls interpret(ctx) on the root node (the top of the tree).
1. Each node acts on the workspace and passes results to its child or parent nodes.

## Code sketch

```python
class Seq(Expr):
    def interpret(self, ctx):
        return [s.interpret(ctx)
                for s in self.steps]

class Edit(Expr):
    def interpret(self, ctx):
        return ctx.fs.patch(self.path,
                            self.diff)

tree = parse(model_text)  # Seq([Edit, Run])
results = tree.interpret(ctx)
```

## Be careful

Keep the grammar tiny. Once it needs variables and loops, you are building a programming language, and a real language in a sandbox is safer.

## Diagram

![Fig. 1.06: Text becomes a tree of nodes, and each node knows how to run itself.](/diagrams/interpreter.svg)

id: memento
number: "1.07"
title: Memento
chapter: agent-loop
fit: direct
figure_number: Fig. 1.07
figure_caption: "The session makes and reads snapshots, and the store only keeps them."
diagram: memento.svg
analogy_title: The film set continuity photo
---
## Gist

Save a snapshot of the session's messages and file edits before each risky step, so the user can go back to any earlier turn.

## Everyday comparison

### The film set continuity photo

Before the crew breaks for lunch, the continuity supervisor photographs the set. She records the half-full glass, the open book and the actor's loosened tie. She does not need to understand why each prop is where it is. After lunch, the photo lets everyone put the scene back exactly as it was. Then the next take matches the last one.

## Classic meaning

Save an object's inner state in a sealed snapshot, without exposing its internals. Later, the object can be put back into that state.

## In the agent system

Before each turn that edits files, the session makes a checkpoint. A checkpoint is a copy of the message list plus the original contents of every file the turn is about to change. A checkpoint store keeps these snapshots by turn number, without looking inside them. When the user runs a rewind command, the session restores the chosen checkpoint. It rewrites the files and cuts the transcript back to that turn. So both the conversation and the workspace (the project files) return to that point. Long sessions keep only recent checkpoints, or store file diffs (only the changes) to save disk space.

## In a large company

In an enterprise harness, checkpoints hold transcripts and file contents. So they take on the strictest data classification of anything inside them. They need encryption at rest (encrypted while stored). The keys must belong to each tenant (each customer company) and come from a KMS (key management service). They need a retention period (how long data is kept) that matches the tenant's policy. They must be deleted when a GDPR erasure request arrives, which is a person's legal request under EU privacy law to delete their data. Durable execution engines give a similar rewind point at the workflow level. These are systems that save each step of a workflow so it can resume. The control to explain to users is this. Rewinding the workspace never reverses effects outside it. Those effects must be covered by compensating actions (steps that undo an effect) or by approvals instead.

## Step by step

1. Before a turn with edits, the session snapshots the messages and the files it will touch.
1. The checkpoint store saves the snapshot under the turn number.
1. The user asks to go back to an earlier turn.
1. The store hands back that snapshot, and the session restores itself from it.

## Code sketch

```python
class Session:
    def checkpoint(self):
        files = self.fs.copy(self.touched)
        return Snapshot(self.msgs[:], files)
    def restore(self, snap):
        self.msgs = list(snap.msgs)
        self.fs.write_all(snap.files)

store[turn] = session.checkpoint()
session.restore(store[6])  # /rewind 6
```

## Be careful

Snapshots cannot undo actions outside the workspace, such as a sent message or a deployed build. Tell the user this when they rewind.

## Diagram

![Fig. 1.07: The session makes and reads snapshots, and the store only keeps them.](/diagrams/memento.svg)

id: iterator
number: "1.08"
title: Iterator
chapter: agent-loop
fit: direct
review_id: rev-iterator
figure_number: Fig. 1.08
figure_caption: Consumers pull one item at a time and never see the source behind it.
diagram: iterator.svg
analogy_title: The sushi conveyor belt
---
## Gist

Go through stream events, turns or stored messages one at a time with next(), without loading or exposing the whole source.

## Everyday comparison

### The sushi conveyor belt

At a conveyor-belt sushi bar, you never see the kitchen's order list. Plates arrive in front of you one at a time, and you take the next one when you are ready. The chef may be slicing fresh fish or taking plates from the fridge. Either way, your side of the counter works the same.

## Classic meaning

Give a way to go through the items of a collection one by one, without showing how the collection is stored.

## In the agent system

A streaming model reply arrives as server-sent events (SSE: small messages the server pushes one after another). Their names include message_start, content_block_delta and content_block_stop. The SDK (the provider's code library) wraps the raw stream of bytes in an async iterator. An async iterator hands out items one at a time as they arrive, without freezing the program. So the harness can write async for event in stream and show text deltas (new pieces of text) as they come in. The same idea is used in other places. A transcript iterator reads JSONL lines (one JSON record per line) from disk only when needed. A paginated iterator over a long history fetches the next page only when the consumer asks. Consumers never care whether the items come from a network socket, a file or an API.

## In a large company

Enterprise platforms usually stream model output through an LLM gateway, a central service that all model calls pass through. The gateway iterates over the provider's SSE events (server-sent events) and sends them on to clients. While doing so, it counts tokens for chargeback (billing each customer). It also scans each delta (new piece of text) for DLP violations. DLP means data loss prevention, which stops sensitive data from leaking. Long transcripts and audit logs are read with paginated or cursor-based iterators from object storage or a database. A cursor marks where the last read stopped. These records are never loaded into memory all at once. The risk is that inline streaming DLP sees text one delta at a time. So a secret split across two deltas can slip through, unless the scanner keeps a sliding window (a short memory of recent text).

## Step by step

1. The harness wraps the source (a stream, a file or a paged API) in an iterator object.
1. The consumer asks for the next item.
1. The iterator reads just enough of the source to make one item.
1. When the source runs out, the iterator signals the end and the loop stops.

## Code sketch

```python
async for ev in client.stream(req):
    if (ev.type == 'content_block_delta'
        and ev.delta.type == 'text_delta'):
        ui.append(ev.delta.text)
    elif ev.type == 'message_stop':
        break

def turns(path):  # lazy over a JSONL file
    with open(path) as f:
        for line in f:
            yield json.loads(line)
```

## Be careful

An iterator over a live stream can be read only once. If both the screen and the transcript writer need the events, keep a copy of them.

## Diagram

![Fig. 1.08: Consumers pull one item at a time and never see the source behind it.](/diagrams/iterator.svg)

---
id: composite
number: "1.09"
title: Composite
chapter: agent-loop
fit: direct
figure_number: Fig. 1.09
figure_caption: "Containers and leaves answer the same call, so the caller never checks types."
diagram: composite.svg
analogy_title: Freight on a warehouse pallet
---
## Gist

Treat a message, a tool result and a single text block through the same interface, because content blocks sit inside each other.

## Everyday comparison

### Freight on a warehouse pallet

A pallet holds cartons, a carton holds boxes, and a box holds single items. The forklift scale weighs any of them the same way: put it on and read the number. A carton's weight is just the total of what is inside. So nobody needs a special method for each level.

## Classic meaning

Arrange objects in a tree, and let other code treat a single object and a group of objects in the same way.

## In the agent system

A message's content is a list of blocks: text, image, tool_use and tool_result. A tool_result (the answer from a tool) can itself contain text and image blocks. The harness gives every block the same small interface (the same set of methods), such as token_count(), render() and redact(). Leaves (blocks with nothing inside them) answer directly. Containers like Message and ToolResult ask their children and combine the answers. So counting the tokens (the small text units models count) of a whole transcript becomes one call on the root (the top of the tree). It no longer needs nested loops that check each block's type.

## In a large company

In enterprise platforms, DLP, PII redaction and audit export all walk this content tree before anything leaves the trust boundary. DLP (data loss prevention) stops sensitive data from leaking. PII redaction removes personal data such as names and emails. The trust boundary is the edge of the systems the company trusts. A redactor must go down into nested tool_result content, including images and documents. A scanner that checks only top-level text blocks misses most leaked data. Token counts made locally from the tree are only estimates. So chargeback (billing each customer) and budget limits should use the usage numbers reported by the provider. They can also use the numbers from the LLM gateway, the central service all model calls pass through.

## Step by step

1. Define one Block interface with the operations the harness needs.
1. Write leaves (TextBlock, ImageBlock) that answer directly.
1. Write containers (Message, ToolResult) that loop over their children.
1. Callers use the operation on any node, from one block to a full transcript.

## Code sketch

```python
class TextBlock(Block):
    def tokens(self):
        return count(self.text)

class ToolResult(Block):
    def tokens(self):
        return 8 + sum(c.tokens()
                       for c in self.content)

total = sum(m.tokens() for m in transcript)
```

## Be careful

Do not force methods onto the shared interface when they make no sense for every block. A leaf with fifteen methods that do nothing is a warning sign.

## Diagram

![Fig. 1.09: Containers and leaves answer the same call, so the caller never checks types.](/diagrams/composite.svg)

---
id: visitor
number: "1.10"
title: Visitor
chapter: agent-loop
fit: direct
review_id: rev-visitor
figure_number: Fig. 1.10
figure_caption: "Blocks send the call to the right method, and operations live in visitors."
diagram: visitor.svg
analogy_title: The fire safety inspector at the mall
---
## Gist

Keep content block classes stable, and put each operation that runs across them, like token counting or redaction, in its own visitor class.

## Everyday comparison

### The fire safety inspector at the mall

A fire inspector walks through a shopping centre: the bakery, the cinema, the pharmacy. Each shop lets the inspector in and shows what matters for its kind of business. The bakery shows its ovens, the cinema its projection booth, and the pharmacy its chemical store. Next month a different inspector, checking access for disabled visitors, walks the same route with a different checklist. The shops change nothing.

## Classic meaning

Put an operation on a structure's elements into a separate object. Then you can add new operations without changing the element classes.

## In the agent system

Content blocks (the pieces of a message, such as text, images and tool calls) rarely change. But the list of operations run over them keeps growing. The harness counts tokens, redacts (hides) secrets before logging, and renders blocks to the terminal or to HTML. It also converts them to another provider's format. With Visitor, each block has a single accept(v) method. That method calls the matching method on the visitor v, such as v.visit_text(self) or v.visit_tool_use(self). A new operation is a new visitor class with one method per block type. The block classes and the code that walks the transcript stay the same.

## In a large company

Enterprise platforms run several visitors over every transcript. One does PII redaction (removing personal data such as names and emails) before logs and traces are exported. One adds classification tags for data residency, the rules about which country data must stay in. One converts formats for an LLM gateway (a central service all model calls pass through) that sits in front of several providers. One exports records for audit. Keeping each as a separate visitor lets compliance teams own and test the redactor apart from the rendering code. The risk is coverage. A redaction visitor must handle every block type, including nested tool results and documents. Otherwise sensitive data reaches log storage.

## Step by step

1. Each block class writes accept(visitor) so it calls the matching visit method.
1. An operation is a visitor class with one visit method per block type.
1. The harness walks the transcript and calls block.accept(visitor) on each block.
1. The visitor builds up its result, such as a token total or a redacted copy.

## Code sketch

```python
class ToolUseBlock(Block):
    def accept(self, v):
        return v.visit_tool_use(self)

class Redactor(Visitor):
    def visit_text(self, b):
        return scrub(b.text)
    def visit_tool_use(self, b):
        return scrub_json(b.input)  # deep

clean = [b.accept(Redactor()) for b in blocks]
```

## Be careful

Adding a new block type means updating every visitor. If new block types arrive often, use Acyclic Visitor or plain methods on the blocks instead.

## Diagram

![Fig. 1.10: Blocks send the call to the right method, and operations live in visitors.](/diagrams/visitor.svg)

---

---
id: acyclic-visitor
number: "1.11"
title: Acyclic Visitor
chapter: agent-loop
fit: direct
review_id: rev-acyclic-visitor
figure_number: Fig. 1.11
figure_caption: "The block asks the visitor what it handles, so visitors never list every type."
diagram: acyclic-visitor.svg
analogy_title: "The museum's specialist tours"
---
## Gist

Let each visitor handle only the block types it knows, so a new content block type never forces edits elsewhere.

## Everyday comparison

### The museum's specialist tours

A museum runs a sculpture tour, a paintings tour and a textiles tour. Each guide stops only at the exhibits they know and walks past the rest. When the museum opens a new photography wing, it hires a photography guide. Nobody retrains the sculpture guide.

## Classic meaning

A form of Visitor with no single interface that lists every element type. Each visitor uses small interfaces, one per type, and elements check for them while the program runs.

## In the agent system

New content block types keep arriving: thinking blocks, citations, documents and server tool results. In a classic Visitor, every new type means adding a new method to every visitor. In the acyclic version, ImageBlock.accept(v) checks whether v implements ImageVisitor. ImageVisitor is a small interface, meaning a promised set of methods, for image blocks. The block calls visit_image only if v has it. A thumbnail generator implements only ImageVisitor. A new DocumentBlock comes with its own DocumentVisitor interface, and the thumbnail generator does not change. Safety visitors are the exception. A secret redactor must treat any block type it does not handle as an error. So a new DocumentBlock is blocked until the redactor learns to scan it.

## In a large company

Enterprise platforms add block types and provider formats faster than compliance tools get updated. This is where Acyclic Visitor helps and where it hurts. Feature visitors such as thumbnail makers, renderers and analytics can safely skip unknown types. Security visitors such as DLP scanners, PII redactors and audit exporters must fail closed. DLP means data loss prevention, and PII means personal data such as names and emails. Fail closed means they block anything they cannot handle. Add a CI test, an automatic check run on every code change. It fails when any block type has no handler in a required security visitor.

## Step by step

1. Declare one small visitor interface for each block type.
1. Each visitor class implements only the interfaces it needs.
1. A block's accept(v) checks whether v supports its type.
1. If it does, the block calls the visit method. If not, it skips or uses a default.

## Code sketch

```python
@runtime_checkable
class ImageVisitor(Protocol):
    def visit_image(self, b): ...

class ImageBlock(Block):
    def accept(self, v):
        if isinstance(v, ImageVisitor):
            return v.visit_image(self)
        return v.unhandled(self)  # skip/raise

class Thumbnailer(ImageVisitor):
    def visit_image(self, b):
        return shrink(b.data, 256)
```

## Be careful

Skipping unknown types is safe for a thumbnail maker. It is not safe for a redactor or a DLP scanner (a tool that stops sensitive data from leaking). These must fail closed and reject any block type they do not handle.

## Diagram

![Fig. 1.11: The block asks the visitor what it handles, so visitors never list every type.](/diagrams/acyclic-visitor.svg)

---
id: double-dispatch
number: "1.12"
title: Double Dispatch
chapter: agent-loop
fit: direct
figure_number: Fig. 1.12
figure_caption: "The event type picks the method, and the current state picks its behaviour."
diagram: double-dispatch.svg
analogy_title: "The referee's foul call"
---
## Gist

Choose the handler from two runtime types at once: the incoming event's type and the session's current state.

## Everyday comparison

### The referee's foul call

A football referee's decision depends on two things together: what the foul was and where it happened. A trip in midfield gives a free kick. The same trip inside the penalty box gives a penalty. A handball on the goal line may add a red card. The rulebook is a grid of foul type against pitch position, not one list.

## Classic meaning

A way to pick which method to call from the runtime types of two objects (their actual types while the program runs). Usually the first object calls back into the second.

## In the agent system

The harness receives several event types: UserMessage, Interrupt, ToolResult and ApprovalReply. Meanwhile the session can be in several states: Idle, Streaming and RunningTool. The right action depends on both. A UserMessage in Idle starts a turn, but in RunningTool it waits in a queue. An Interrupt in Streaming cancels the request, but in RunningTool it kills the child process (the separate program running the tool). The event's dispatch(state) method calls state.on_user_message(self) or state.on_interrupt(self). So the language's own method lookup picks the right cell in the event-by-state grid. No type switches (long if-else checks on type) are needed.

## In a large company

In practice, enterprise harnesses dispatch on more than two things: event type, session state, and the caller's role or tenant tier. A tenant is one customer company, and its tier is its service level. Once the role axis appears, many teams move the grid into a policy engine such as OPA or Cedar. A policy engine decides what is allowed from written rules. Event-by-state behaviour stays in code, and identity-based decisions go in policy. Then each part can be reviewed by its own owners. The control is a default cell that denies or queues. So an unexpected combination is rejected and logged instead of acted on. An example is an approval reply that arrives while the session is Idle.

## Step by step

1. An event arrives, and the harness calls event.dispatch(current_state).
1. The event calls back the state method named after its own type.
1. That state method runs the behaviour for this event in this state.
1. It returns the next state, which handles the next event.

## Code sketch

```python
class Interrupt(Event):
    def dispatch(self, state):
        return state.on_interrupt(self)

class RunningTool(State):
    def on_interrupt(self, ev):
        self.proc.kill()
        return Idle()
    def on_user_message(self, ev):
        self.pending.append(ev)
        return self
```

## Be careful

The grid grows as types times states. When most cells share a default, a small lookup table is easier to read than many methods.

## Diagram

![Fig. 1.12: The event type picks the method, and the current state picks its behaviour.](/diagrams/double-dispatch.svg)

---

---
id: callback
number: "1.13"
title: Callback
chapter: agent-loop
fit: direct
figure_number: Fig. 1.13
figure_caption: "The client hands over functions, and the loop calls them at the right moments."
diagram: callback.svg
analogy_title: The garage that rings you
---
## Gist

Pass functions into the loop, and the loop calls them when a token streams in, a tool finishes or a turn ends.

## Everyday comparison

### The garage that rings you

You drop your car at the garage and leave a note. It says: call this number when it is ready, and text me if a repair will cost more than two hundred pounds. Then you go about your day. The mechanic does not need to know who you are or what you will do next. They just ring the number at the right moments.

## Classic meaning

Pass a piece of code to other code as an argument. The other code calls it back at the right time.

## In the agent system

Several clients share one agent loop: a terminal UI, a web client, an SDK script and an eval runner. An eval runner is a tool that tests the agent automatically. Each one wants to react at different moments. The loop accepts callbacks (functions it will call later) such as on_text_delta, on_tool_start, on_tool_end and on_turn_complete. It calls each one at its moment. The terminal prints the new pieces of text (deltas). The web client pushes them over a websocket, a live two-way connection to the browser. The eval runner ignores deltas but records every tool call. The loop itself never imports any UI code.

## In a large company

Enterprise platforms attach callbacks for audit records, OpenTelemetry exporters, cost metering and webhooks. OpenTelemetry is a standard for tracing software. A webhook sends a message to another system, such as a ticketing or chat tool. Callbacks that cross a trust boundary (the edge of trusted systems) should get redacted data, with sensitive parts removed. They should be delivered asynchronously, later and separately, through a queue such as Kafka, Pub/Sub or EventBridge. Then a slow receiver cannot hold up a turn. Audit callbacks are the exception to ignoring errors. A tenant is one customer company, and regulated tenants work under strict laws. If the audit record cannot be written, regulated tenants usually require the action to fail. They do not want it to go ahead without a log.

## Step by step

1. The caller passes callback functions when it starts a run.
1. The loop stores them and starts calling the model.
1. At each event (text delta, tool start, tool end), it calls the matching callback.
1. When the turn ends, it calls on_done with the final message.

## Code sketch

```python
def show(delta):
    term.write(delta.text)

def save(msg):
    transcript.append(msg)

agent.run(prompt,
          on_text_delta=show,
          on_tool_end=lambda c, r: log(c, r),
          on_done=save)
```

## Be careful

A slow or failing callback can block or crash the loop. Give callbacks a time limit and catch their errors, so the turn still finishes.

## Diagram

![Fig. 1.13: The client hands over functions, and the loop calls them at the right moments.](/diagrams/callback.svg)

id: context-object
number: "1.14"
title: Context Object
chapter: agent-loop
fit: direct
figure_number: Fig. 1.14
figure_caption: "One object carries the turn's facts to every component that needs them."
diagram: context-object.svg
analogy_title: "The patient's travelling folder"
---
## Gist

Bundle everything one turn needs (ids, budget, working folder, permissions, cancel signal) into one object passed to every component.

## Everyday comparison

### The patient's travelling folder

When a hospital patient moves from admissions to X-ray to surgery, a folder travels on the trolley with them. It holds the wristband number, allergies, consent forms and the doctor's notes. Every department reads what it needs from the same folder. Nobody has to phone the other departments.

## Classic meaning

Put the state and services that many layers need into one object, and pass that object along. This replaces passing many separate parameters.

## In the agent system

Every turn touches many components: the model client, the tool runner, hooks, the tracer and the code that starts subagents. Each one needs some of these facts: the session id, turn number, working directory, permission mode, remaining token budget, abort signal and trace span. A trace span is one timed record of work, used for tracing. The harness builds a TurnContext at the start of the turn. It passes that single object down every call. Say you add a field, such as the active MCP servers. MCP is a standard way to connect tools to an AI model. You change only the context class and the code that reads it. You do not change every function signature in between, meaning the list of inputs each function takes.

## In a large company

In an enterprise harness, the context object carries the tenant id (which customer company this is) and the authenticated principal (the verified user or service). It also carries the principal's OIDC claims, which are identity facts from the login system. It holds the data residency region (where data must stay), the W3C trace context (a standard trace id) and the remaining per-tenant budget. Every tool, policy check and log line reads identity from it. The identity fields should be immutable (unchangeable), so no component can raise its own privileges mid-turn. Raw credentials do not belong in it. Instead, keep a handle, which is a reference. The tool runner swaps it for a short-lived token from Vault or workload identity. Vault is a secrets store, and workload identity gives each service its own login. This way secrets never reach prompts, logs or the model.

## Step by step

1. At the start of a turn, the loop builds a TurnContext.
1. It passes ctx to the model client, the tool runner and the hooks.
1. Each component reads the fields it needs and may record usage back into it.
1. When the turn ends, the context is thrown away or saved with the trace.

## Code sketch

```python
@dataclass
class TurnContext:
    session_id: str
    turn: int
    cwd: Path
    perms: PermissionMode
    budget: TokenBudget
    cancel: AbortSignal

ctx = TurnContext(sid, n, cwd, mode, b, sig)
resp = model.call(msgs, ctx)
out = tools.run(resp.tool_calls, ctx)
```

## Be careful

A context object that collects every global value in the system becomes a hidden bag of dependencies. Keep it for one turn only, and keep it small.

## Diagram

![Fig. 1.14: One object carries the turn's facts to every component that needs them.](/diagrams/context-object.svg)

id: collecting-parameter
number: "1.15"
title: Collecting Parameter
chapter: agent-loop
fit: direct
figure_number: Fig. 1.15
figure_caption: One list travels through every check and fills up along the way.
diagram: collecting-parameter.svg
analogy_title: The wedding guest book
---
## Gist

Pass one collector object through a series of steps, so each step adds its findings instead of returning separate results to merge.

## Everyday comparison

### The wedding guest book

At a wedding, the guest book travels from table to table. Each guest writes a line and passes it on. At the end of the night, the couple has one book with every message. Nobody had to gather loose cards from each table.

## Classic meaning

Pass a collecting object into methods, so each one can add its results. This builds one combined result across many calls.

## In the agent system

A code review subagent (a helper agent started by the main one) runs several checks. It uses grep (a text search tool) to find TODO notes and scans the diff (the code changes) for secrets. It also runs the tests and checks the changelog. Each check gets the same Findings object. It adds issues with the file, line and severity. After the last check, the subagent turns the collected findings into one report message for the orchestrator (the agent in charge). The same shape appears when a harness adds up usage across smaller calls. One UsageCollector is passed into every model call and tool call. The turn total is read from it at the end.

## In a large company

Enterprise platforms use collecting parameters to add up usage and cost across a turn, its subagents and its tool calls. This feeds the per-tenant chargeback ledger, the record used to bill each customer company. They also use them for compliance findings gathered by review agents. Sometimes subagents run in parallel or on other workers (other servers). Then each returns its own partial collection, and the parent merges them. This is because a shared, changeable collector cannot cross process boundaries. Some findings contain pieces of code or data. Redact them (remove the sensitive parts) before writing them to tickets or audit storage.

## Step by step

1. Create an empty collector at the start of the task.
1. Pass it into each step or tool wrapper.
1. Each step adds what it found or what it used.
1. Read the collector once at the end to build the report or the totals.

## Code sketch

```python
findings = Findings()
check_todos(diff, findings)
scan_secrets(diff, findings)
run_tests(repo, findings)

def scan_secrets(diff, out):
    for ln in diff.added_lines():
        if KEY_RE.search(ln.text):
            out.add(ln.path, ln.no, 'high')
report = findings.to_markdown()
```

## Be careful

If steps run in parallel, the collector needs a lock, so only one step writes at a time. Otherwise each step should return its own list to merge afterwards.

## Diagram

![Fig. 1.15: One list travels through every check and fills up along the way.](/diagrams/collecting-parameter.svg)

id: pipeline
number: "1.16"
title: Pipeline
chapter: agent-loop
fit: direct
review_id: rev-pipeline
figure_number: Fig. 1.16
figure_caption: Each stage narrows the data and passes it on.
diagram: pipeline.svg
analogy_title: The water treatment works
---
## Gist

Prepare context in fixed stages: find candidates, rerank them by relevance, shorten the best ones, then insert them into the prompt.

## Everyday comparison

### The water treatment works

River water first passes through screens that catch branches. Then it goes to settling tanks where mud sinks, then through sand filters, and finally to a stage that kills germs. Each stage does one job and hands cleaner water to the next. Engineers can upgrade the filters without touching the screens.

## Classic meaning

Pass data through a series of stages, where each stage's output is the next stage's input. Then each stage can be built, tested and replaced on its own.

## In the agent system

Before calling the model, a retrieval-augmented harness runs a context pipeline. Retrieval-augmented means it looks up documents and adds them to the prompt. The retriever pulls fifty chunks (short pieces of text) from a vector store and a keyword index. A vector store finds text by meaning, and a keyword index finds it by words. A reranker scores the chunks against the query and keeps eight. A compressor trims each one to the sentences that matter. An injector formats them as document blocks in the prompt, with source ids. Each stage takes the query and a list of chunks, and returns a new list. So a team can swap the reranker model without touching the other stages. They can also add a stage, such as one that removes duplicates or one that checks access rights. Evals (automated quality tests) can score each stage on its own.

## In a large company

Enterprise retrieval pipelines add stages that a demo leaves out. These include an access-control filter that drops chunks the user may not read. They include a residency filter, for rules on where data must stay. They also include PII redaction (removing personal data such as names and emails) and provenance tagging, which records where each chunk came from for citations. The access check must use the end user's identity. It must run before reranking and injection. Once a chunk reaches the context window (the text the model can see), the model can repeat it. Each stage is traced with OpenTelemetry, a standard for recording what software does. Each is also scored by offline evals (tests run outside live traffic). So a reranker change can be held back until retrieval quality is proven, before rollout.

## Step by step

1. The user's query enters the first stage.
1. Retrieve returns a broad set of candidate chunks.
1. Rerank and compress narrow down and shorten the set.
1. Inject formats the remaining chunks into the context window for the model call.

## Code sketch

```python
stages = [retrieve(k=50), rerank(top=8),
          compress(max_tokens=2000), inject]

def run(query):
    data = []
    for stage in stages:
        data = stage(query, data)
    return data  # prompt-ready blocks

prompt = run(user_msg)
```

## Be careful

Any stage can drop the one chunk that mattered. Log what each stage removed, so a bad answer can be traced back to its stage.

## Diagram

![Fig. 1.16: Each stage narrows the data and passes it on.](/diagrams/pipeline.svg)

---

---
id: rule-engine
number: "1.17"
title: Rule Engine
chapter: agent-loop
fit: direct
review_id: rev-rule-engine
figure_number: Fig. 1.17
figure_caption: "Facts go in, rules match, and the matching actions come out."
diagram: rule-engine.svg
analogy_title: The insurance claims desk
---
## Gist

Check a set of written rules against each turn's facts to decide routing, approvals and compaction, without hard-coded branches.

## Everyday comparison

### The insurance claims desk

A claims handler works from a rulebook, not from instinct. Claims under five hundred pounds with photos are paid at once. Anything mentioning a flood goes to a specialist. A third claim in one year triggers a fraud check. When the company changes its policy, it edits the rulebook. The handlers apply the new rules the next morning.

## Classic meaning

Keep business rules apart from the program code by writing them as condition-action pairs. An engine checks them against a set of facts.

## In the agent system

Each turn, the harness gathers facts. These include context usage, the requested tool and a risk class for its arguments. They also include the user's plan tier, the working directory and the time of day. A rule engine checks rules loaded from a settings file. One rule says: if the context is over 80 percent full, compact it (shrink it) first. Another says: if a command classifier marks the shell command as destructive, require approval. A command classifier is code that reads a command and labels how risky it is. A third says: if the task is classified as simple, send it to a smaller model. Matching rules produce actions, and the loop applies them in priority order. Operators change behaviour by editing rules as data. The rules can be tested against recorded turns.

## In a large company

Enterprise platforms keep two kinds of rules apart. Operational rules handle routing, compaction and model choice. Authorization rules decide who may do what. A dedicated policy engine checks them, such as OPA with its Rego language, or Cedar. Both kinds are kept as versioned policy-as-code, meaning rules stored and tracked like program code. They are reviewed through change management. They are unit-tested in CI (automatic checks on every change) against recorded turns. Every decision is logged with its policy version for audit. The key risk is fail-open behaviour, where the system allows actions when something breaks. If the engine or its rule bundle is not available, authorization decisions must default to deny.

## Step by step

1. Load the rules from configuration at startup or when they change.
1. At each turn, collect the facts into a dictionary (a set of named values).
1. Check every rule's condition against the facts.
1. Apply the actions of matching rules in priority order.

## Code sketch

```python
RULES = [  # loaded from rules.yaml
  {'if': {'ctx_pct': {'gt': 80}},
   'then': 'compact_first', 'prio': 1},
  {'if': {'cmd_risk': {'eq': 'high'}},
   'then': 'require_approval', 'prio': 0},
  {'if': {'task': {'eq': 'simple'}},
   'then': 'use_small_model', 'prio': 2}]

hits = [r for r in RULES
        if match(r['if'], facts)]
hits.sort(key=lambda r: r['prio'])
for r in hits:
    apply(r['then'])
```

## Be careful

Rules that affect each other are hard to reason about, for example when one rule's action changes another rule's facts. Keep actions independent, or check the rules only once per turn.

## Diagram

![Fig. 1.17: Facts go in, rules match, and the matching actions come out.](/diagrams/rule-engine.svg)

---

---
id: trampoline
number: "1.18"
title: Trampoline
chapter: agent-loop
fit: adapted
review_id: rev-trampoline
figure_number: Fig. 1.18
figure_caption: The driver keeps the call stack flat by running each returned step itself.
diagram: trampoline.svg
analogy_title: The choose-your-own-adventure book
---
## Gist

Run deep recursive planning as a flat loop, where each step returns the next step instead of calling it.

## Everyday comparison

### The choose-your-own-adventure book

When reading a choose-your-own-adventure book, you could keep a finger in every page you passed through. But you would soon run out of fingers. Instead, you read the note at the bottom, "turn to page 84", and flip there. You only ever hold one place in the book, however long the story runs.

## Classic meaning

Run recursive functions in a loop. Each call returns a thunk (a small package describing the next call), and a driver loop runs it until a final value appears.

## In the agent system

Some agents refine a plan one subgoal at a time. This is naturally written as a tail-recursive function, where the function's last act is to call itself. Here, plan(goal, steps) asks the model for the next subgoal and calls itself with the longer list. Python has no tail-call elimination, so it does not reuse memory for such calls. A long plan driven by the model keeps every in-between frame (a record of each unfinished call). It can then hit Python's recursion limit. With a trampoline, plan returns either Bounce(fn, args) for the next step or Done(result). A small driver loop keeps calling the bounces. This also gives the harness a natural place between steps to check the turn budget, save a checkpoint and respect a cancel request. A trampoline only flattens tail calls. A planner that branches into a tree of subgoals needs an explicit work stack instead, which is a list of pending tasks it manages itself.

## In a large company

In enterprise platforms, a durable execution engine such as Temporal or Step Functions usually replaces the trampoline's driver loop. Such an engine saves each step, so work survives crashes. Each step is a recorded activity. After a crash or deploy, the workflow continues from the last finished one. The point between bounces is where the platform enforces budgets for each tenant (each customer company). It also checks whether an operator has cancelled the run, and writes a checkpoint for audit. The risk is depth with no limit, driven by the model. So the driver needs a hard step limit set by tenant policy, not by the model's own judgement.

## Step by step

1. Rewrite the recursive planner so it returns the next call instead of making it.
1. The driver loop calls the first step.
1. While the result is a Bounce, the driver calls the function inside it.
1. When a Done arrives, the driver returns its value.

## Code sketch

```python
def plan(goal, acc):
    sub = model.next_subgoal(goal, acc)
    if sub is None:
        return Done(acc)
    return Bounce(plan, goal, acc + [sub])

def trampoline(r):
    while isinstance(r, Bounce):
        budget.check(); cancel.check()
        r = r.fn(*r.args)
    return r.value
```

## Be careful

Trampolining adds an extra layer to code that rarely goes deep. Use it only when the depth of recursion depends on model output you do not control.

## Diagram

![Fig. 1.18: The driver keeps the call stack flat by running each returned step itself.](/diagrams/trampoline.svg)

id: command
number: "2.01"
title: Command
chapter: tool-system
fit: direct
figure_number: Fig. 2.01
figure_caption: A tool call becomes a command object before anything runs it.
diagram: command.svg
analogy_title: The restaurant order ticket
---
## Gist

Turn every tool call into an object that the harness can queue, log, approve, retry or undo.

## Everyday comparison

### The restaurant order ticket

A waiter does not cook. They write your order on a ticket and clip it to the rail. The ticket can wait in line. Any free cook can pick it up. The head chef can check it. If you change your mind, someone tears it up. The ticket is the order, kept apart from the person who cooks it.

## Classic meaning

A request is wrapped up as an object. Other code can then queue it, log it or undo it without knowing how it runs.

## In the agent system

A tool call is the model's request to run a tool, like reading a file. The model sends it as a tool_use block (a part of its reply that names the tool, its inputs and a call id). The harness wraps that block in a ToolCommand object. The object holds the tool name, the arguments and the call id. It then travels through the permission gate (the step that decides if the call may run), the execution queue and the transcript (the saved record of the conversation). The call is now data, not a function that runs at once. So the harness can pause it for the user to approve. It can replay it in an eval (an automated test of the agent). It can log it for audit. And it can run a compensating undo (an action that reverses the effect) when a later step fails.

## In a large company

Enterprise platforms save each tool call as a durable command record (one stored safely, so it survives crashes). The record is keyed by the tool_use id. That id also works as an idempotency key (a label that makes a repeat safe). So if a worker retries or a workflow replays, the same payment or email is never sent twice. Durable execution engines such as Temporal or AWS Step Functions keep long tasks running through crashes. They run these commands as activities (single steps) with retry rules. The command log feeds an append-only audit store (records can be added but never changed). The store is kept under SOC 2 and ISO 27001 controls, two common security standards. The key rule is this. The platform retries a command automatically only if it is marked idempotent (safe to run twice with the same result) or reversible. Every other command needs a person to approve it, or a compensating action.

## Step by step

1. The model returns a tool_use block with a name, an input and an id.
1. The harness builds a ToolCommand and puts it on the execution queue.
1. A permission check approves, edits or rejects the command.
1. The executor runs it, records the result, and keeps undo data when the tool supports it.

## Code sketch

```python
class ToolCommand:
    def __init__(self, tool, args, cid):
        self.tool, self.args = tool, args
        self.id = cid
    def execute(self):
        return self.tool.run(**self.args)
    def undo(self):
        return self.tool.revert(self.id)

cmd = ToolCommand(tools['write_file'],
                  block.input, block.id)
queue.put(cmd)
```

## Be careful

Some commands change the outside world, like sending an email or paying an invoice. These often cannot be undone. Mark them as irreversible and ask for approval before they run.

## Diagram

![Fig. 2.01: A tool call becomes a command object before anything runs it.](/diagrams/command.svg)

id: strategy
number: "2.02"
title: Strategy
chapter: tool-system
fit: direct
review_id: rev-strategy
figure_number: Fig. 2.02
figure_caption: "The tool's name and schema stay fixed while the backend behind it is swapped."
diagram: strategy.svg
analogy_title: Interchangeable camera lenses
---
## Gist

Keep one tool name and schema, but swap the code behind it, such as which backend a search tool uses.

## Everyday comparison

### Interchangeable camera lenses

A photographer keeps the same camera body all day. They twist on a different lens for a portrait, a landscape or a distant bird. The shutter button, the viewfinder and the memory card never change. Only the glass in front decides how the light comes in.

## Classic meaning

Several ways of doing the same job sit behind one shared interface. The caller picks one while running, without changing its own code.

## In the agent system

The model sees one search tool. Its input schema (the fixed list of inputs it accepts) is query and max_results. Its description does not promise any particular backend (the system that does the real searching). Behind it, the harness holds a SearchStrategy interface with several versions. One uses a hosted web search API. One uses a vector store (a database for search by meaning) over the user's documents. One uses local ripgrep (a fast file search program) when the machine is offline. The config or the workspace type picks the strategy when the session starts. So the tool definition in the request stays byte-identical, exactly the same down to each character. That keeps the prompt cache hitting. The prompt cache is saved work the provider can reuse when a request starts the same way. Evals (automated tests of the agent) plug in a canned strategy that returns fixed results.

## In a large company

Enterprise deployments pick the strategy per tenant (one customer company sharing the platform) from central config. One tenant searches an internal index hosted in its own region, for data residency (keeping data in a set region). Another uses a public web provider through an egress proxy (a gate that controls outgoing traffic). Eval runs use a canned strategy. The platform makes this choice from tenant policy, never from the model or from user input. Every strategy must apply the same document-level access checks. Then a cheaper backend cannot get around permissions. Record the chosen strategy as a span attribute in OpenTelemetry (a standard for tracing requests). Teams can then compare quality and cost for each backend.

## Step by step

1. The harness reads its config and picks a SearchStrategy for this session.
1. The search tool is registered with one schema, whatever the choice.
1. The model sends a tool_use block for search with a query.
1. The tool hands the work to the chosen strategy and formats its hits as one tool_result.

## Code sketch

```python
class SearchStrategy(Protocol):
    def search(self, q, k): ...

class SearchTool:
    name = 'search'
    def __init__(self, strategy):
        self.strategy = strategy
    def run(self, query, max_results=5):
        hits = self.strategy.search(
            query, max_results)
        return format_hits(hits)

tool = SearchTool(STRATEGIES[cfg.search])
```

## Be careful

Strategies may return results of different shape or quality. Then the model cannot learn what the tool does. Convert every strategy's output to one format.

## Diagram

![Fig. 2.02: The tool's name and schema stay fixed while the backend behind it is swapped.](/diagrams/strategy.svg)

id: adapter
number: "2.03"
title: Adapter
chapter: tool-system
fit: direct
review_id: rev-adapter
figure_number: Fig. 2.03
figure_caption: "Each foreign interface gets one adapter, so the loop only ever calls Tool.run()."
diagram: adapter.svg
analogy_title: The travel plug adapter
---
## Gist

Wrap MCP servers and outside APIs so each one looks like a native tool, with the harness's own name, schema and run method.

## Everyday comparison

### The travel plug adapter

You land in London with a laptop charger built for American sockets. You do not rewire the charger or rip out the wall socket. A small plastic block takes two flat pins on one side and offers three square pins on the other. The charger and the socket each keep their own shape. Only the adapter knows both.

## Classic meaning

An adapter changes the interface of an existing piece of code into the one a caller expects. Parts that do not fit together can then work together.

## In the agent system

The agent loop (the cycle of calling the model and running tools) knows one contract. A Tool has a name, a description, an input_schema, and run(args) that returns a ToolResult. MCP is a standard way to connect tools to an AI model. An MCP server speaks JSON-RPC instead, a message format for calling remote functions. It uses tools/list to list its tools and tools/call to run one. A REST API speaks HTTP, with its own auth headers and status codes. The harness writes one adapter for each outside source. An MCP adapter maps tools/call replies into a ToolResult. It turns isError, JSON-RPC errors and timeouts into error results. An HTTP adapter maps 4xx and 5xx responses (the HTTP error codes) the same way. Each adapted tool carries its server name as a prefix, such as mcp__github__create_issue. So two servers cannot clash on the same name. The loop, the permission gate and the transcript never learn where a tool really lives.

## In a large company

Enterprises usually keep adapters in one central MCP or tool gateway. The gateway sits in front of approved internal APIs and third-party MCP servers. So every tool reaches the loop through one path that is audited and rate-limited (capped in how often it can be called). Remote MCP servers over streamable HTTP should sign in with OAuth (a standard for granting access), as the MCP authorization spec describes. The tokens are limited to the user and held by the adapter. They are never placed in the model context (the text the model can see). Treat tool descriptions from third parties as untrusted input. Pin server versions (lock them to a known version) and review any change to a description. An altered description can steer the model.

## Step by step

1. At startup, the harness connects to each MCP server and lists its tools.
1. It wraps every remote tool in an adapter that follows the Tool interface.
1. The model calls the tool by name, exactly like a built-in tool.
1. The adapter turns the call into tools/call or HTTP and maps the reply back into a ToolResult.

## Code sketch

```python
class McpToolAdapter(Tool):
    def __init__(self, client, srv, spec):
        self.client, self.spec = client, spec
        self.name = f'mcp__{srv}__{spec.name}'
    def run(self, args):
        try:
            r = self.client.call_tool(
                self.spec.name, args)
        except McpError as e:
            return ToolResult.error(str(e))
        return ToolResult(
            content=r.content,
            is_error=r.isError)
```

## Be careful

Some adapters turn remote failures into empty successes. This misleads the model. Pass errors and timeouts through as is_error results (results marked as failures).

## Diagram

![Fig. 2.03: Each foreign interface gets one adapter, so the loop only ever calls Tool.run().](/diagrams/adapter.svg)

id: converter
number: "2.04"
title: Converter
chapter: tool-system
fit: direct
review_id: rev-converter
figure_number: Fig. 2.04
figure_caption: "One converter owns every mapping between internal types and the wire, both ways."
diagram: converter.svg
analogy_title: The interpreter at a summit
---
## Gist

Translate tool specs, calls and results between the harness's own types and each provider's wire format, in both directions.

## Everyday comparison

### The interpreter at a summit

An interpreter sits in a glass booth at the back of the hall. A minister speaks French, and the interpreter says the same words in English into the delegates' headsets. When the reply comes, they do the reverse. Neither minister learns the other's language. The meaning stays the same. Only the form changes, and it changes both ways.

## Classic meaning

A converter is a separate object that changes data from one form to another. It usually has one function for each direction.

## In the agent system

Inside the harness, a tool is a ToolSpec, a call is a ToolCall and an output is a ToolResult. Each model provider wants something else on the wire, meaning in the exact format it sends and receives. One expects input_schema at the top level. Another puts parameters under a function key. Results go back as tool_result blocks with text or image content and an is_error flag. A provider converter owns all of these mappings in both directions. It turns a spec into the wire format. It turns a tool_use block into a ToolCall, and back again when the history is sent again. It turns a ToolResult into content blocks. Adding a provider then touches only one class. Round-trip tests (converting out and back again) can prove that nothing is lost.

## In a large company

Some platforms send traffic to several providers through an LLM gateway (a central service that routes all model traffic). They keep one standard internal message format and one converter per provider. The converter is a natural place to pull out OpenTelemetry GenAI attributes, such as the model name and token use. OpenTelemetry is a standard for tracing requests. Round-trip tests and golden-file tests (comparisons against saved, known-good provider messages) should run in CI as a regression gate. CI is the automatic checks that run on every code change, and a regression gate blocks changes that break old behaviour. This matters because a quiet mapping change can drop tool errors or image content. PII redaction (removing personal data such as names and emails) can also happen here. It runs just before content leaves the platform's trust boundary for an outside provider.

## Step by step

1. Before a request, the converter turns each ToolSpec into the provider's tool format.
1. When the response arrives, it reads each tool_use block into a ToolCall.
1. After the tool runs, it turns each ToolResult into a tool_result block that points to the call id.
1. On the next turn, it turns stored ToolCalls back into tool_use blocks, so the history replays exactly.
1. Round-trip tests check that converting out and back gives an equal object.

## Code sketch

```python
class MessagesConverter:
    # spec_out(): ToolSpec -> tools[] entry
    def call_in(self, b):
        return ToolCall(b.id, b.name, b.input)
    def call_out(self, c):  # history replay
        return dict(type='tool_use', id=c.id,
            name=c.name, input=c.args)
    def result_out(self, r):
        return dict(type='tool_result',
            tool_use_id=r.call_id,
            content=r.blocks,
            is_error=r.is_error)
```

## Be careful

Converters break quietly when a provider adds a new block type. Fail loudly on unknown types instead of dropping them.

## Diagram

![Fig. 2.04: One converter owns every mapping between internal types and the wire, both ways.](/diagrams/converter.svg)
