---
id: parameter-object
number: "2.28"
title: Parameter Object
chapter: tool-system
fit: direct
review_id: rev-parameter-object
figure_number: Fig. 2.28
figure_caption: Loose JSON is parsed once into a typed request that travels whole
diagram: parameter-object.svg
analogy_title: The photo lab order envelope
---
## Gist

Bundle a tool's many arguments into one typed request object. Check it once and pass it along whole.

## Everyday comparison

### The photo lab order envelope

At a photo lab you do not shout instructions across the counter. You fill in one envelope with print size, gloss or matte, number of copies, crop, and your name and phone. You drop the film inside. The envelope travels with the job from counter to machine to pickup shelf. Everyone who handles it reads the same fields.

## Classic meaning

Some parameters always travel together. You replace them with one object that gives the group a name, checks and default values.

## In the agent system

A run_command tool can take a command, a working folder, environment variables, a timeout, stdin (input fed to the command), a sandbox profile and an output limit. Passing seven loose arguments through the permission gate, the sandbox and the executor invites mix-ups. So the harness parses the tool_use input once into a typed ShellRequest. This is a dataclass or Pydantic model (a Python class that checks data types), built from the same JSON schema the model sees. Checks and defaults happen in one place. The gate checks req.command and req.cwd. The transcript stores the request whole. Adding a field later changes the request class, not every function along the way.

## In a large company

In a company harness, the policy engine checks the typed request, and the audit trail stores it. So it needs a stable, versioned schema shared by the gate, the sandbox and the log pipeline. Some fields the model can set change how secure the call is, such as env, cwd and timeout. These must have limits or an allowlist (a list of approved values). A PATH or LD_PRELOAD value from the model can break out of a sandbox. (These environment variables control which programs and libraries load.) Secrets never appear in the request. The executor adds them from a secrets manager after the gate has approved the call.

## Step by step

1. The model sends tool_use input as a JSON object.
1. The harness parses it into a typed request, fills in defaults and rejects bad fields.
1. The gate, sandbox and executor each get the one request object.
1. The harness logs the same object with the result, so the call can be replayed exactly.

## Code sketch

```python
class ShellRequest(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(
        frozen=True, extra='forbid')
    command: str
    cwd: Path = Path('.')
    timeout_s: int = Field(60, le=600)
    env: dict[str, str] = {}
    max_output: int = 30_000

req = ShellRequest.model_validate(block.input)
gate.check(req)    # command, cwd, env keys
result = sandbox.run(req)
```

## Be careful

Do not let one request class turn into a grab bag shared by unrelated tools. One request type per tool keeps the schema the model sees honest.

## Diagram

![Fig. 2.28: Loose JSON is parsed once into a typed request that travels whole](/diagrams/parameter-object.svg)

---
id: execute-around
number: "2.29"
title: Execute Around
chapter: tool-system
fit: direct
review_id: rev-execute-around
figure_number: Fig. 2.29
figure_caption: "Setup and cleanup belong to the wrapper, so no tool can skip them"
diagram: execute-around.svg
analogy_title: The cleanroom airlock
---
## Gist

Run every tool inside a function that sets up the sandbox first and always cleans it up afterwards, even on failure.

## Everyday comparison

### The cleanroom airlock

In a chip factory, an engineer cannot simply walk onto the floor. The airlock dresses them in a gown and runs an air shower, then lets them work. On the way out it takes the gown back and logs the time. The routine is the same whatever job they came to do. Nobody skips the exit half.

## Classic meaning

A method does the setup and the cleanup around a block of code the caller passes in. So callers cannot forget either half.

## In the agent system

Running a code tool needs setup. It needs a scratch folder and a container or a slice of a VM (an isolated mini computer). It needs the workspace files mounted (made available inside), a network policy, and limits on CPU and clock time. Afterwards, the container must be stopped, temporary files deleted and logs collected. The harness offers one context manager, sandbox(profile), that does all of this. (A context manager is a Python block that runs setup at the start and cleanup at the end.) It runs the tool's body in the middle. Tool authors write only the body. A crash, a timeout or the user pressing stop still reaches the finally block (the cleanup code that always runs). So leftover containers do not pile up between turns.

## In a large company

Company platforms wrap every sandboxed action this way. First they get a short-lived workload identity credential (a temporary login for the job). They open an audit span (a timed audit record). They start an isolated container or microVM (a very small virtual machine) with an egress policy (rules for outgoing network traffic). Afterwards they revoke the credential, collect logs and destroy the sandbox. But if the harness process itself crashes, its finally block never runs. So production systems pair the wrapper with an outside reaper (a process that finds and removes leftovers). Or they use a durable execution engine such as Temporal, which keeps running cleanup steps even after crashes. Platforms track sandbox lifetimes and cleanup failures as metrics. Leftover sandboxes cost money. They can also break data-residency rules (rules about where data may be stored).

## Step by step

1. The executor enters sandbox(profile) and passes control to the tool body.
1. The wrapper starts the container, mounts files and applies limits.
1. The body runs its command inside the sandbox and either returns or raises an error.
1. Either way, the finally block collects logs, stops the container and deletes temporary files.

## Code sketch

```python
@contextmanager
def sandbox(profile):
    box = containers.start(profile)
    try:
        box.mount(workspace, ro=profile.ro)
        yield box
    finally:
        box.collect_logs(transcript)
        box.kill(); box.cleanup()

with sandbox(DEFAULT) as box:
    out = box.exec(req.command, timeout=60)
```

## Be careful

Cleanup cannot depend on the body behaving well. Enforce time limits from a watchdog (a separate timer process) outside the sandbox. A body that hangs never hands control back to the finally block.

## Diagram

![Fig. 2.29: Setup and cleanup belong to the wrapper, so no tool can skip them](/diagrams/execute-around.svg)

id: fluent-interface
number: "2.30"
title: Fluent Interface
chapter: tool-system
fit: direct
figure_number: Fig. 2.30
figure_caption: Every call returns the same builder until build() checks and freezes it
diagram: fluent-interface.svg
analogy_title: The sandwich counter in one breath
---
## Gist

Set up an agent with chained method calls that read like a sentence. Each call returns the builder for the next.

## Everyday comparison

### The sandwich counter in one breath

'Rye, turkey, swiss, toasted, cut in half, to go.' Each word passes the same half-made sandwich down the counter to the next station. 'To go' is the moment it gets wrapped and handed over. Leave out a word and you get the house default. Ask for something impossible and the counter tells you before wrapping.

## Classic meaning

An API built on method chaining. Each call returns an object for the next call, so the code reads like a small sentence in the problem's own language.

## In the agent system

Agent SDKs (software kits for building agents) often offer a fluent setup API: Agent('reviewer').model(...).system(...).tools(read, grep).max_turns(20).on_tool_use(audit).build(). Each method records one setting and returns the builder. So a whole agent definition fits in one readable expression. It is easy to review in a pull request (a proposed code change). The final build() checks that the settings fit together. For example, a shell tool must have a sandbox, and the token budget must fit the model's context window (the text the model can see at one time). Then build() returns an AgentConfig that cannot be changed. Subagent definitions start from a shared base chain and add a few calls.

## In a large company

Company teams use fluent builders to define agents in code. But the code usually turns into a declarative, versioned config file (one that states the settings, not the steps). That file goes through review, eval gates (automatic tests that must pass) and staged rollout, like any other change. The build step is a good place to enforce platform policy. For example, it can reject a shell tool with no sandbox profile. It can reject a model that is not approved for the tenant's data residency region (where the customer's data must stay). It can reject a token budget above the tenant's limit. Only the built, unchangeable config is deployed. So what was reviewed is exactly what runs.

## Step by step

1. Start a builder with the agent's name.
1. Chain calls for model, system prompt, tools, limits and hooks. Each returns the builder.
1. Call build() to check the whole setup at once.
1. Hand the unchangeable config to the harness to start runs.

## Code sketch

```python
class Agent:
    def model(self, m):
        self.cfg['model'] = m
        return self          # enables chaining

cfg = (Agent('reviewer')
       .model('large')
       .system(load('review.md'))
       .tools(read_file, grep, git_diff)
       .max_turns(20)
       .build())           # validates once
```

## Be careful

Chains hide the in-between state. A setting given twice, or in a conflicting order, can silently win. Make build() reject contradictions instead of keeping the last call.

## Diagram

![Fig. 2.30: Every call returns the same builder until build() checks and freezes it](/diagrams/fluent-interface.svg)

id: gateway
number: "3.01"
title: Gateway
chapter: llm-layer
fit: adapted
review_id: rev-gateway
figure_number: Fig. 3.01
figure_caption: "Callers see one client. Routing, keys and failover live behind it."
diagram: gateway.svg
analogy_title: The alliance check-in desk
---
## Gist

Send every model call through one client that holds the keys, picks a provider and switches over when one is down.

## Everyday comparison

### The alliance check-in desk

At a big airport, partner airlines share one check-in desk. You show your passport once. The agent books you onto whichever partner has a seat on your route. If one airline cancels, the same desk rebooks you on another, and you do not queue again. You never deal with the airlines one by one.

## Classic meaning

A gateway is one object that wraps access to an outside system. Callers use its simple interface and never deal with the system directly.

## In the agent system

The agent loop (the code that runs the model turn after turn) never imports a provider SDK (the provider's own code library). It calls gateway.complete(request). The gateway adds API keys (secret passwords for the provider) from the secret store. It turns the request into the provider's wire format (the exact shape that provider expects). It then routes the request by model alias, region or tenant policy. A model alias is a short name, like 'large', that points to real models. A tenant is one customer company sharing the platform. The gateway also records usage and latency (how long each call takes) for every call in one place. Sometimes a provider returns errors or is marked unhealthy. Then the gateway sends the same request to the next configured route. It returns a response in one standard shape. So subagents (helper agents started by the main agent) and scheduled tasks all get the same behaviour.

## In a large company

In an enterprise platform, this is the LLM gateway (the central entry point for all model calls). Every agent, subagent and batch job must use it. It often runs as a central service, such as LiteLLM, Envoy AI Gateway or a cloud API gateway. Traffic to model providers is blocked everywhere else. The gateway enforces several rules in one place. It uses workload identity (each service proves who it is) instead of fixed keys. It keeps a list of allowed providers for each tenant. It enforces data residency (keeping data in an approved country or region). It tracks token budgets and chargeback tags for each tenant (labels for billing costs back to each team). It also keeps an audit record of which model served each call. The main risk is that failover (switching to a backup route) crosses a residency or contract boundary. So policy must decide which routes are allowed, not provider health alone.

## Step by step

1. An agent or subagent calls gateway.complete with messages, tools and a model alias.
1. The gateway looks up the alias, gets a list of provider routes and adds the keys.
1. It writes the request in that provider's format and sends it.
1. If the provider is down, the gateway marks it unhealthy and tries the next route.
1. It returns one response in a standard shape, with usage attached.

## Code sketch

```python
class ModelGateway:
    def complete(self, req, tenant):
        routes = self.policy.allowed(
            tenant, self.routes[req.model])
        for p in routes:  # residency, vendor
            if not p.healthy():
                continue
            try:
                r = p.send(req, self.keys)
            except ProviderDown:
                p.mark_down(); continue
            self.meter.record(tenant, r.usage)
            return p.decode(r)
        raise NoProviderAvailable(req.model)
```

## Be careful

A gateway might quietly switch to a weaker model. That can change how the agent behaves in the middle of a task. So log every reroute and record which model actually answered.

## Diagram

![Fig. 3.01: Callers see one client. Routing, keys and failover live behind it.](/diagrams/gateway.svg)

---

---
id: ambassador
number: "3.02"
title: Ambassador
chapter: llm-layer
fit: direct
review_id: rev-ambassador
figure_number: Fig. 3.02
figure_caption: The agent speaks plain HTTP locally. The sidecar deals with the outside world.
diagram: ambassador.svg
analogy_title: "The reporter's local fixer"
---
## Gist

Run a sidecar, a helper beside the harness, that owns the model connection: keys, TLS encryption, retries, timeouts and telemetry.

## Everyday comparison

### The reporter's local fixer

A foreign reporter arrives in a new city and hires a fixer who goes everywhere with them. The reporter says who they want to interview. The fixer handles permits, translation, phone lines that drop, and checkpoints that want paperwork. The reporter's notebook holds only the story. A fixer who knows a different city can replace this one, and the reporter's job does not change.

## Classic meaning

An ambassador is a helper service that runs next to a client. It sends network requests for the client and adds features such as retries, monitoring and security.

## In the agent system

The harness does not call the provider directly. It sends plain HTTP requests to a sidecar on localhost (the same machine). The sidecar runs in the same pod or container group (a set of containers deployed together). It holds the API key and handles TLS (the encryption on the connection to the provider). It adds retries with backoff (waiting longer before each new try) and enforces timeouts. It also sends out metrics and traces (records of each call's path and timing) for every model call. The sidecar does not care what language the caller uses. So a Python agent worker and a TypeScript UI server share one connection policy. To rotate keys or change egress rules (rules about which outside addresses traffic may reach), you redeploy the sidecar, not the agent code.

## In a large company

In an enterprise platform, the ambassador is usually a service-mesh or egress sidecar. A service mesh is a network layer that manages traffic between services. Examples are Envoy, a mesh proxy, or a small LLM-proxy container. It gets short-lived credentials through workload identity (each service proves who it is) or Vault (a secrets store). It never shows them to the agent process. The sidecar applies the same rules for every language. These include mTLS (both sides prove who they are with certificates) and egress allowlists (approved outside addresses). They also include timeouts and OpenTelemetry spans (standard trace records) with GenAI attributes (fields that describe model calls). The sidecar also removes PII (personal data such as names and emails) from outgoing prompts. Platform teams change its settings through change management (a formal review and approval process). So the docs must say that the sidecar owns retry and timeout policy, and that these are turned off in the SDK.

## Step by step

1. The harness sends a model request to the sidecar on localhost.
1. The sidecar checks who the caller is. It adds the key, a timeout and a trace id (a tag that follows the request).
1. It forwards the request to the provider over TLS. It retries only failures that happen before any response bytes arrive.
1. It streams the response back and passes mid-stream errors through to the harness. It also records latency and token metrics.

## Code sketch

```python
# harness: no keys, no retry logic
client = ModelClient(
    base_url='http://localhost:8787')
resp = client.messages.create(**req)

# ambassador sidecar, same pod
@app.post('/v1/messages')
async def relay(req):
    req.headers['x-api-key'] = vault.key()
    return await retry(upstream.post, req,
                       timeout=60)
```

## Be careful

If both the harness and the ambassador retry, one failure turns into many calls. Decide which side owns retries, and turn them off on the other side.

## Diagram

![Fig. 3.02: The agent speaks plain HTTP locally. The sidecar deals with the outside world.](/diagrams/ambassador.svg)

id: bridge
number: "3.03"
title: Bridge
chapter: llm-layer
fit: direct
figure_number: Fig. 3.03
figure_caption: "Two families grow on their own, joined by one reference."
diagram: bridge.svg
analogy_title: The universal remote
---
## Gist

Keep the family of agent types apart from the family of model backends, so each side can grow without a class for every pair.

## Everyday comparison

### The universal remote

A universal remote comes in a basic model with volume and channel buttons. A deluxe model can also record and pause. Separately, every TV brand uses its own infrared codes. Any remote can drive any brand, because it holds the code set for the TV it is paired with. Nobody makes a 'deluxe remote for brand X'.

## Classic meaning

A bridge separates an abstraction (what something does) from its implementation (how it does it). One reference joins the two families, so each can change on its own.

## In the agent system

The agent side has its own family of classes. ChatAgent, CodingAgent and ResearchAgent differ in system prompt, tools and loop policy. The backend side has another family. A backend is the code that actually talks to a model. There is a hosted API backend, a cloud-platform backend and a local inference backend (running the model on your own machines). Each backend knows its own request format, streaming quirks and login method. Each agent holds a reference to a ModelBackend. It calls only that backend's narrow interface: generate, stream and count_tokens. Three agents and three backends need six classes, not nine combinations. A new backend works with every agent from day one.

## In a large company

In an enterprise platform, the backend side often covers three options. One is a direct provider API. Another is the same models through a cloud platform such as Bedrock, Vertex AI or Azure. The third is a self-hosted model for sensitive work. Policy picks the backend for each tenant (one customer company sharing the platform). The implementor interface (the backend's side of the bridge) stays narrow. So the platform can move a regulated tenant to an in-region or private backend without touching agent classes. Add a conformance and eval suite (automated tests of behaviour and quality) and run it against every backend. Streaming, tool calling and token counting differ in small ways between deployments of the same model.

## Step by step

1. Define a narrow ModelBackend interface with generate, stream and count_tokens.
1. Write one backend class per provider or deployment.
1. Write agent classes against that interface, and pass in a backend when you create each agent.
1. Choose the pairing in config. For example, use CodingAgent with a local backend in tests.

## Code sketch

```python
class Agent:                 # abstraction
    def __init__(self, backend):
        self.backend = backend

class CodingAgent(Agent):
    def step(self, msgs):
        return self.backend.generate(
            CODE_PROMPT, msgs, TOOLS)

class LocalBackend(ModelBackend): ...
class HostedBackend(ModelBackend): ...

agent = CodingAgent(LocalBackend())
```

## Be careful

Keep the backend interface to what every provider can support. If one provider's special feature leaks into it, the bridge quietly becomes an adapter for just one provider.

## Diagram

![Fig. 3.03: Two families grow on their own, joined by one reference.](/diagrams/bridge.svg)

---
id: retry
number: "3.04"
title: Retry
chapter: llm-layer
fit: direct
review_id: rev-retry
figure_number: Fig. 3.04
figure_caption: "Each failure earns a longer, jittered wait before the same request goes again."
diagram: retry.svg
analogy_title: The radio phone-in competition
---
## Gist

Re-send a model call that failed for a short-lived reason, waiting longer each time, and give up after a fixed limit.

## Everyday comparison

### The radio phone-in competition

When a radio station opens its prize line, thousands of people call at once. Most hear the busy tone. If everyone calls back straight away, the line stays jammed. Callers who wait a few seconds, then a bit longer, each at a slightly different moment, get through. After ten tries, sensible people stop and listen to the rest of the show.

## Classic meaning

Retry repeats an operation that failed because of a short-lived fault. It usually waits longer each time, until the operation succeeds or a limit is reached.

## In the agent system

Model APIs return transient errors (short-lived errors that may pass if you try again). A 429 rate_limit_error means you hit a usage limit. A 529 overloaded_error means the service is busy. There are also occasional 500 or 504 errors, and connections that drop mid-stream. A streaming call can also fail after a 200 (success) status, with an error event inside the stream. The client treats that error the same way as the matching HTTP error. If the response has a retry-after header (the provider's advice on how long to wait), the client follows it. Otherwise it waits using capped exponential backoff plus jitter. That means the wait doubles each time up to a maximum, plus a small random extra. Then it sends the identical request again. This is safe because a model call has no side effects (it changes nothing outside itself). Some errors will never succeed on a resend. Examples are 400 invalid_request_error, 401, 403, or a 429 caused by a used-up spending cap. These fail at once. The retry budget is limited by the number of attempts and by the turn's deadline. So a user in the chat never waits forever.

## In a large company

In an enterprise platform, retries live in exactly one layer, usually the LLM gateway (the central entry point for model calls). SDK retries behind it are set to zero. Each tenant (customer company) gets its own retry budget. So one tenant's storm of retries does not use up the shared quota. Every retry is logged as a span event in OpenTelemetry (a standard tracing system), with the status and the wait. So SLO dashboards (charts of reliability targets) can tell provider overload (529) apart from self-caused rate limiting (429). Retrying a model call is safe because it has no side effects. But a turn may have already run tools. That turn must resume from its checkpoint (a saved point), not replay the tools. A durable execution engine such as Temporal (a system that saves each step so work can resume) usually does this.

## Step by step

1. The client sends the request and gets a 529 overloaded error.
1. It marks the error as transient. It works out a delay: a base time doubled for each attempt, plus jitter.
1. If the response has retry-after, it waits at least that long.
1. It sends the same request again, up to the maximum number of attempts.
1. It returns the first success, or passes the last error up to the agent loop.

## Code sketch

```python
RETRYABLE = {408, 429, 500, 503, 504, 529}
for attempt in range(MAX_TRIES):
    try:
        return api.create(**req)
    except APIError as e:  # incl. SSE error
        if e.status not in RETRYABLE:
            raise
        if attempt == MAX_TRIES - 1:
            raise GaveUp(req) from e
        wait = min(CAP, BASE * 2 ** attempt)
        wait = random.uniform(wait / 2, wait)
        sleep(max(wait, e.retry_after or 0))
```

## Be careful

Retries can be stacked at several layers, such as the SDK, the gateway and the agent loop. During an outage they multiply into dozens of calls. Retry in exactly one place.

## Diagram

![Fig. 3.04: Each failure earns a longer, jittered wait before the same request goes again.](/diagrams/retry.svg)

---

---
id: fallback
number: "3.05"
title: Fallback
chapter: llm-layer
fit: direct
review_id: rev-fallback
figure_number: Fig. 3.05
figure_caption: The same request walks down a fixed chain until something answers.
diagram: fallback.svg
analogy_title: The understudy in the wings
---
## Gist

When the preferred model cannot answer, give the same request to a substitute, so the turn still finishes, maybe at lower quality.

## Everyday comparison

### The understudy in the wings

Every lead role in a theatre show has an understudy who knows the lines. If the star loses their voice an hour before the show, a note goes into the programme and the understudy goes on. The audience still sees the show, a little differently. Nobody cancels the night because one actor is out.

## Classic meaning

Fallback gives an alternative action or result when the main operation fails. The system then works less well instead of showing an error.

## In the agent system

Sometimes retries run out, or a circuit breaker is open (a switch that blocks calls to a failing provider). Then the model client walks a fallback chain, which is an ordered list of substitutes. The chain is first filtered by the tenant's policy (the rules for that customer company). It might try the same model in another allowed region, then a smaller model. Last, it returns a typed 'busy, try again' status. Each step gets the same messages and tool definitions. They change only where the substitute needs it. Examples are a smaller max_tokens (output limit), no extended thinking, or dropping earlier thinking blocks. The substitute starts with a cold prompt cache. The prompt cache is saved work the provider can reuse when a request starts the same way, and cold means it is empty. So the substitute's first call pays the full input price. The harness tags the response with the model that actually served it. This keeps the transcript, cost records and evals (quality tests) honest. Some callers must use the strongest model, such as a review subagent. They opt out and fail loudly instead.

## In a large company

In an enterprise platform, the platform team owns the fallback chain as configuration. It is limited for each tenant. A tenant pinned to EU data residency (keeping data inside the EU), or to one approved vendor, may only fall back inside that boundary, or not at all. Each fallback is logged with served_by in the audit trail and the trace. Cost reports show the shift, because the substitute starts with a cold prompt cache. Change management (the formal review process for changes) treats adding a model to the chain like a release. The same eval suite as the primary model must pass first.

## Step by step

1. Call the primary model with the request.
1. If retries run out or the breaker is open, pick the next entry in the fallback chain.
1. Adjust the request to the substitute's limits and send it.
1. Tag the response with served_by and return it to the agent loop.

## Code sketch

```python
CHAIN = ['large', 'large-eu', 'small']

def complete(req, tenant):
    for model in tenant.allowed(CHAIN):
        try:
            r = call(model, fit(req, model))
            r.served_by = model
            return r
        except (Overloaded, BreakerOpen):
            continue
    return Degraded('busy, try later')
```

## Be careful

A fallback model may not support the same tools, context length or output format. So run the agent's evals against every model in the chain.

## Diagram

![Fig. 3.05: The same request walks down a fixed chain until something answers.](/diagrams/fallback.svg)

---

---
id: circuit-breaker
number: "3.06"
title: Circuit Breaker
chapter: llm-layer
fit: direct
review_id: rev-circuit-breaker
figure_number: Fig. 3.06
figure_caption: "Three states: pass calls, refuse them fast, or test with one probe."
diagram: circuit-breaker.svg
analogy_title: "The harbour master's storm flag"
---
## Gist

Stop calling a provider that keeps failing, refuse calls quickly for a cool-down period, then let one test call decide whether to resume.

## Everyday comparison

### The harbour master's storm flag

Three ferries in a row turn back in a storm. The harbour master raises the storm flag and stops all sailings. Passengers hear the news at the gate, not halfway out to sea. After a few hours she sends one boat out to test the water. If it crosses safely, the timetable starts again. If not, the flag goes back up.

## Classic meaning

A circuit breaker wraps calls to a remote service in a state machine (a thing with a few fixed states). It opens after repeated failures and refuses calls while open. Then it tries one test call before it closes again.

## In the agent system

The model client keeps one breaker per provider, or per model and region. While the breaker is closed, calls flow normally. It counts 5xx (server error), 529 and timeout failures over a rolling window of recent time. It leaves 429s to rate limiting and retry-after. When failures cross a threshold, the breaker opens. For the next 30 seconds, every call fails at once with BreakerOpen. The fallback layer turns that into a switch to another model. So no agent wastes its retry budget on a dead endpoint. After the cool-down, the breaker goes half-open. It lets exactly one probe (test request) through. Success closes the breaker. Failure opens it again with a longer timer.

## In a large company

In an enterprise platform, breakers usually sit in the LLM gateway (the central entry point for model calls) or the service mesh (the network layer between services). Examples are Envoy outlier detection and Resilience4j-style libraries. They are keyed by provider, model and region. Each state change is sent out as an event. These events page on-call staff and mark SLO dashboards (charts of reliability targets). Breaker state usually lives separately in each gateway replica (copy), and that is acceptable. But tune the thresholds so one tenant's (customer's) badly formed traffic cannot trip a shared breaker. Pair the breaker with the fallback chain and a status page entry. Then users see a degraded mode instead of silent errors.

## Step by step

1. Closed: requests pass through, and the breaker counts recent failures.
1. Open: once failures cross the threshold, calls fail at once for a cool-down period.
1. Half-open: when the timer ends, one test request may go through.
1. The test result closes the breaker or opens it again.

## Code sketch

```python
def call(self, req):
    with self.lock:          # one probe only
        if self.state == 'open' and \
           now() >= self.retry_at:
            self.state = 'half_open'
        elif self.state != 'closed':
            raise BreakerOpen(self.name)
    try:
        r = self.provider.send(req)  # 4xx ok
    except (ServerError, Timeout):
        self.fail()   # half_open -> open
        raise
    self.reset()      # closed, fails = 0
    return r
```

## Be careful

Count only failures on the provider's side. A 400 error caused by a badly formed prompt is not the provider's fault. If those errors trip the breaker, a healthy provider goes offline for every agent.

## Diagram

![Fig. 3.06: Three states: pass calls, refuse them fast, or test with one probe.](/diagrams/circuit-breaker.svg)

---
id: rate-limiting
number: "3.07"
title: Rate Limiting
chapter: llm-layer
fit: direct
review_id: rev-rate-limiting
figure_number: Fig. 3.07
figure_caption: Each tenant spends from its own bucket. Overdrafts are refused with a wait time.
diagram: rate-limiting.svg
analogy_title: Timed tickets at the museum
---
## Gist

Cap how many requests and tokens each caller may use per time window, and refuse the extra with a clear time to retry.

## Everyday comparison

### Timed tickets at the museum

A popular exhibition sells entry in half-hour slots of fifty people. When the 2:00 slot is full, the fifty-first visitor hears that the next free slot is 2:30. Everyone inside gets a calm look at the paintings. The people turned away know exactly when to come back.

## Classic meaning

Rate limiting limits how many operations a client may do in a time window. Requests over the limit are refused or delayed.

## In the agent system

Providers already limit requests per minute, and input and output tokens per minute. Tokens are the small chunks of text that models read and write. When you go over, the provider answers 429 with a retry-after header (how long to wait). A multi-tenant harness serves many customer companies, called tenants. It adds its own limiter in front. This is usually a token bucket per organisation or per user. A token bucket is a counter that refills at a steady rate, and each call spends from it. The buckets live in a shared store. So one user's runaway agent loop cannot use up the shared provider quota. Before each call, the limiter charges the estimated input tokens plus the full max_tokens reservation (the most output the call may produce). This is on purpose, and it is stricter than the provider. The provider counts output as it is generated, and for most models it ignores cache reads. After the call, the limiter settles the real usage. A request that would overdraw the bucket is refused at once, with the time until enough tokens refill. A request that can never fit is refused outright.

## In a large company

In an enterprise platform, per-tenant limits are enforced in the LLM gateway or the API gateway (the central entry points for calls). Examples are Kong, the Envoy rate-limit service, or a token bucket stored in Redis (a fast shared data store). The limit is keyed by the tenant and user taken from the OIDC token (the signed login token). It never comes from a header that the client sets. Limits come in tiers set by contract. They are reported back as rate-limit headers. They are tied to budgets and chargeback (billing costs back to each team), so finance sees the same numbers as the limiter. Every refusal is logged with the tenant and principal (the user or service that made the call). So noisy-neighbour incidents, where one tenant hurts others, can be traced.

## Step by step

1. Estimate the request's input tokens and add the max_tokens reservation.
1. Refill the caller's bucket for the time that has passed, and check its balance.
1. If there is room, take the tokens and forward the call. If not, return 429 with retry_after.
1. After the response, refund or charge the difference against actual usage.

## Code sketch

```python
class TokenBucket:
    def take(self, n):
        if n > self.capacity:
            raise TooLarge(n)   # never fits
        self.refill(now())
        if self.tokens < n:
            need = n - self.tokens
            raise RateLimited(need/self.rate)
        self.tokens -= n

# shared store, so all replicas agree
bucket = buckets.get(req.org_id)
bucket.take(estimate(req) + req.max_tokens)
```

## Be careful

Bad token estimates make the limiter useless or unfair. So compare against the usage the provider reports after every call.

## Diagram

![Fig. 3.07: Each tenant spends from its own bucket. Overdrafts are refused with a wait time.](/diagrams/rate-limiting.svg)

---

---
id: throttling
number: "3.08"
title: Throttling
chapter: llm-layer
fit: adapted
review_id: rev-throttling
figure_number: Fig. 3.08
figure_caption: A burst queues on the ramp and leaves at an even pace set by the headers.
diagram: throttling.svg
analogy_title: Ramp meters on the motorway
---
## Gist

Keep the harness's own agents within a safe share of the provider quota by pacing, capping, degrading or delaying their calls.

## Everyday comparison

### Ramp meters on the motorway

At rush hour, a traffic light on the motorway entry ramp lets one car on every few seconds. Every car gets on in the end. The queue on the ramp soaks up the surge, so the main road keeps moving. When traffic thins, the light turns green and stays green.

## Classic meaning

Throttling controls how many resources an app instance, a tenant (customer) or a whole service may use. Once use crosses a threshold, it rejects work, degrades it (does a cheaper version) or defers it (does it later). This keeps the system meeting its SLOs (reliability targets) under heavy load.

## In the agent system

Every agent, subagent and scheduled job in the harness shares one provider quota. So the harness slows its own users before the provider starts returning 429 errors. A controller reads the rate-limit headers after each call. These headers say how many tokens remain and when the limit resets. As the remaining tokens shrink, it takes graded steps, one after another. First, a shared pacer spaces out calls. Next, fewer subagents may run at once. Then background work is degraded: shorter max_tokens, a smaller model, or no extended thinking. Last, the lowest-priority jobs are deferred (put off until later). Interactive turns, where a person is waiting, still go through, a little later. As headroom (spare quota) comes back, the harness lifts the steps in reverse order.

## In a large company

In an enterprise platform, throttling is how the platform shares a fixed provider commitment among many tenants and workloads. That commitment might be provisioned throughput (capacity bought in advance) or a negotiated rate limit. Throttling caps how many agent runs each tenant may have at once. It degrades background work to a smaller model. It defers batch jobs before interactive users feel anything. Policies are set per tier in the gateway. Tenants can see them through headers and status pages, so a slowed job can be explained. Each throttling action is recorded as a metric and an audit event. This matters when an SLA credit (a refund for missing a service promise) or a chargeback dispute depends on whether a tenant was degraded.

## Step by step

1. Read the rate-limit headers after each model call.
1. Work out a minimum gap between calls from the remaining tokens and the reset time. The reset header is a timestamp, so subtract the current time.
1. Before each call, reserve the next slot, then wait for it.
1. As headroom shrinks further, cap how many subagents run at once. Degrade or defer background work.
1. Lift the limits in reverse order as headroom returns.

## Code sketch

```python
class Pacer:
    def adjust(self, h):
        left = int(h['tokens-remaining'])
        # reset is an RFC 3339 timestamp
        ts = parse_rfc3339(h['tokens-reset'])
        until = max(ts - now(), 0)
        self.gap = until / max(left / AVG, 1)

    async def wait_turn(self):
        slot = max(now(), self.next)
        self.next = slot + self.gap  # reserve
        await sleep(slot - now())
```

## Be careful

Throttling only hides overload up to a point. If the ramp queue grows without end, you also need load shedding (dropping low-priority work) or backpressure (making the sender wait).

## Diagram

![Fig. 3.08: A burst queues on the ramp and leaves at an even pace set by the headers.](/diagrams/throttling.svg)

---

---
id: load-shedding
number: "3.09"
title: Load Shedding
chapter: llm-layer
fit: direct
review_id: rev-load-shedding
figure_number: Fig. 3.09
figure_caption: "Under load, low-priority calls are put off so the chat stays fast."
diagram: load-shedding.svg
analogy_title: Rolling cuts on a heatwave grid
---
## Gist

When demand is more than capacity, drop or delay the least important model work, so interactive turns keep getting answers.

## Everyday comparison

### Rolling cuts on a heatwave grid

On the hottest afternoon of the year, people want more power than the power stations can make. The operator does not let the whole grid collapse. Instead, it cuts power to a few industrial areas for an hour. Hospitals, homes and traffic lights stay on. The cut is announced in advance and reversed when demand falls.

## Classic meaning

Load shedding means refusing some incoming requests on purpose when a system is overloaded. It chooses them by priority, to protect the system's main job.

## In the agent system

Each model request carries a priority. It inherits that priority from the root of its run (the request that started the work). A user waiting in the chat UI is high priority, and so is any subagent working for that turn. A subagent on a background task is medium. Scheduled digests, eval runs and memory consolidation (tidying stored memories) are low. Sometimes provider errors rise, or the queue gets long. Or p95 latency (the time within which 95% of calls finish) crosses a threshold. Or the organisation's token budget is nearly gone. Then the admission check (the gate before each call) refuses calls below the current cut-off. It gives them a 'shed' status and moves them to a later scheduled task. Interactive turns stay fast. Shed work is recorded so it can run when load drops.

## In a large company

In an enterprise platform, the gateway decides what to shed using server-side context. The priority class comes from the logged-in workload and its run lineage (the chain of runs that led to this call). It never comes from a field the client sets, or every caller will claim to be interactive. Shed and deferred work is visible per tenant (customer company) in job status and metrics. The deferred queue has a size limit and is drained slowly, so recovery does not cause a second spike. Contracts and SLOs (reliability targets) should say which tiers of work can be shed. Then an eval or batch customer is not surprised.

## Step by step

1. Tag every model request with a priority class.
1. Measure load: queue depth, latency, provider errors and remaining budget.
1. Above a threshold, refuse or defer requests below the current cut-off priority.
1. Record shed work, and lower the cut-off as load recovers.

## Code sketch

```python
PRIORITY = {'chat': 3, 'subagent': 2,
            'eval': 1, 'digest': 0}

def admit(req):
    cutoff = 0
    if load.p95_ms > 8000: cutoff = 2
    elif load.queue > 200: cutoff = 1
    if PRIORITY[req.kind] < cutoff:
        deferred.put(req)   # run later
        raise Shed(req.kind)
    return dispatch(req)
```

## Be careful

Shedding must be visible. A background job that quietly gets dropped every afternoon looks like a bug. So show deferrals in logs and in job status.

## Diagram

![Fig. 3.09: Under load, low-priority calls are put off so the chat stays fast.](/diagrams/load-shedding.svg)

---

---
id: backpressure
number: "3.10"
title: Backpressure
chapter: llm-layer
fit: direct
review_id: rev-backpressure
figure_number: Fig. 3.10
figure_caption: A full buffer makes the producer wait instead of piling up work.
diagram: backpressure.svg
analogy_title: The sushi conveyor belt
---
## Gist

Let a slow consumer push back on its producer, so work waits at the source instead of piling up in memory.

## Everyday comparison

### The sushi conveyor belt

At a conveyor-belt sushi bar, the chef puts a plate only where the belt has a gap. When diners are slow and the belt is full, there is nowhere for the next plate. So the chef pauses and waits. As diners take plates off, gaps appear and the chef starts again. The belt never spills onto the floor.

## Classic meaning

Backpressure is a way to control flow. The downstream part (the consumer) tells the upstream part (the producer) how much it can take. Producers slow down or pause when buffers fill up.

## In the agent system

An orchestrator (the agent that hands out work) may fan out many subagents. It puts each task into a bounded queue, which has a fixed maximum size. Suppose every model-call slot in the dispatcher is busy. Then queue.put waits, and the orchestrator stops starting new subagents. So memory stays flat, however many tasks the model plans. Streaming to the chat UI works differently. If the harness pauses reading from the provider, the model does not slow down. A long pause may also make the provider close the stream. So the harness reads the provider stream at full speed. It writes into the transcript and into a bounded buffer for each client. When a slow mobile client falls behind, the harness coalesces (merges) the queued text pieces instead of holding up the provider. Wherever the producer can truly wait, the slowest stage sets the pace.

## In a large company

In an enterprise platform, backpressure shows up as bounded queues and concurrency limits (caps on how many run at once). These sit between the orchestrator, the dispatcher and the gateway. It also shows up as consumer lag on event streams such as Kafka (a system for streams of messages), where consumers pull at their own pace. Backpressure is a key part of cost control. A planner that can queue unlimited subtasks is also a tenant (customer) that can spend unlimited tokens. Queue depth and wait time per tenant are sent out as metrics. So capacity planning and alerts can follow the slowest stage.

## Step by step

1. Connect the producer and consumer with a bounded buffer.
1. The consumer empties the buffer at its own pace.
1. When the buffer is full, the producer's put or write waits.
1. Freed space releases the producer, and work flows again.

## Code sketch

```python
q = asyncio.Queue(maxsize=8)

async def orchestrator(plan):
    for task in plan.subtasks:
        await q.put(task)   # waits when full

async def dispatcher():   # start 4 of these
    while True:
        task = await q.get()
        try:
            await run_subagent(task)
        finally:
            q.task_done()
```

## Be careful

An unbounded queue anywhere in the chain breaks backpressure. The producer never feels the push, and memory grows until the process dies.

## Diagram

![Fig. 3.10: A full buffer makes the producer wait instead of piling up work.](/diagrams/backpressure.svg)

---

---
id: queue-based-load-leveling
number: "3.11"
title: Queue-Based Load Leveling
chapter: llm-layer
fit: direct
review_id: rev-queue-based-load-leveling
figure_number: Fig. 3.11
figure_caption: Bursts fill the queue. Workers empty it at the rate the model can take.
diagram: queue-based-load-leveling.svg
analogy_title: The reservoir behind the dam
---
## Gist

Put model jobs in a durable queue that a fixed pool of workers empties, so bursts become a steady, affordable call rate.

## Everyday comparison

### The reservoir behind the dam

A storm drops a week of rain on the hills in one night. The river below would flood, but the reservoir fills instead. The gates release water at a steady rate that the town's channels can carry, day after day, until the level falls.

## Classic meaning

A queue sits as a buffer between tasks and a service. It smooths out sudden heavy loads. The service then handles work at its own steady rate.

## In the agent system

At 9am, hundreds of scheduled tasks start at once. A CI webhook (an automatic message from the build system) can launch fifty review agents in a minute. These do not each call the model right away. Instead, the harness writes a job record to a durable queue, one that keeps jobs safe if machines restart. It returns a run id. A pool of workers pulls jobs and runs the agent loop. The pool is sized to the provider's sustained rate limit (the steady rate it allows). So the provider sees a flat line of traffic, and the 429 errors stop. Callers watch the run status or get a notice when it is done. Nothing is lost if a worker restarts.

## In a large company

In an enterprise platform, the queue is a managed, durable service such as SQS, Pub/Sub or Kafka. It may also be a durable execution engine like Temporal (a system that saves each step so work can resume). The worker pool is sized to the provisioned model throughput (capacity bought in advance) of the tenant or platform. Delivery is at least once, so a job may arrive more than once. So every job carries an idempotency key (an id that makes repeats safe). Before any outside side effect, such as a PR comment or a ticket update, the worker checks that key. Separate queues or priorities per tenant (customer company) and for interactive work stop one tenant's burst from slowing everyone.

## Step by step

1. Producers (schedules, webhooks, users) add a job to the queue and get a run id.
1. The queue stores jobs safely and soaks up the burst.
1. A fixed pool of workers pulls jobs at a rate that fits the model budget.
1. Each worker runs the agent and posts the result and a notice.

## Code sketch

```python
def on_webhook(event):
    run_id = f'pr-{event.pr}-{event.sha}'
    jobs.enqueue({'run': run_id,  # dedupe
                  'agent': 'pr_review',
                  'pr': event.pr})
    return {'run_id': run_id}   # at once

def worker():                    # N of these
    while job := jobs.receive(lease=900):
        if not runs.done(job['run']):
            result = run_agent(job)
            notify(job['run'], result)
        jobs.ack(job)  # redelivered if we die
```

## Be careful

Load leveling trades speed for stability. A user waiting in the chat should not sit behind a thousand batch jobs. So give interactive work its own lane.

## Diagram

![Fig. 3.11: Bursts fill the queue. Workers empty it at the rate the model can take.](/diagrams/queue-based-load-leveling.svg)

---
id: caching
number: "3.12"
title: Caching
chapter: llm-layer
fit: direct
review_id: rev-caching
figure_number: Fig. 3.12
figure_caption: A hit skips the expensive work. A miss pays once and fills the cache.
diagram: caching.svg
analogy_title: "The library's reserve shelf"
---
## Gist

Reuse work already paid for: cache the stable start of the prompt with the provider, and save repeatable tool results locally.

## Everyday comparison

### The library's reserve shelf

In exam season, students ask for the same twenty textbooks all day. The librarian does not send a porter to the basement every time. She keeps copies on a reserve shelf behind the desk. Those requests are answered in seconds. Anything else still comes from the basement. The shelf is refreshed when the reading list changes.

## Classic meaning

Caching stores the results of expensive operations. When the same request comes again, the answer comes from fast storage instead of being worked out again.

## In the agent system

Every turn sends the tool definitions, system prompt and earlier conversation again. This stable part at the start is the prefix. The harness marks the end of the prefix with a cache_control breakpoint. The provider can then reuse its processed work when a later request starts with exactly the same prefix. The first call pays a cache-write premium, an extra charge above the normal input price. Later calls report cache_read_input_tokens. These cost a fraction of the normal input price, and the reply comes faster. The cache entry expires after about five minutes without a hit. A longer TTL (time to live) costs more to write. Prefixes shorter than a minimum length, which depends on the model, are not cached at all. The harness also has its own local cache. It memoises (saves the result of) read-only tool calls, such as fetching the same URL or reading an unchanged file. The cache key includes the tenant (customer company), the user, the tool name and the arguments. It also includes a content hash (a fingerprint of the content) or a short TTL. Anything with side effects or time-sensitive data skips the cache.

## In a large company

In an enterprise platform, the provider's prompt caches are kept separate per organisation or workspace. But the harness's own caches must be keyed by tenant and principal (the user or service). These include tool results, retrieval results and rendered prompts. They must also respect data classification, retention rules and right-to-erasure (a person's legal right to have their data deleted). Teams track cache hit rate and cache-write spend per agent as cost metrics. A template change that breaks the prefix shows up as a sudden jump in the bill. Shared caches such as Redis (a fast shared data store) should be encrypted and split by tenant. They should not hold regulated data unless retention policy allows it.

## Step by step

1. Order the prompt so tools and system text come first and rarely change.
1. Put a cache breakpoint after the stable prefix.
1. On the next call, the provider matches the prefix and bills cached reads.
1. For tool calls, check the local cache before running the tool, and store the result after.

## Code sketch

```python
system = [{'type': 'text', 'text': RULES,
           'cache_control':
               {'type': 'ephemeral'}}]

@memo(key=lambda ctx, a: (ctx.tenant,
      ctx.user, a['url'], day()))
def fetch_page(ctx, a):
    return http.get(a['url']).text

r = client.messages.create(model=M,
    system=system, tools=TOOLS, messages=h)
log(r.usage.cache_read_input_tokens,
    r.usage.cache_creation_input_tokens)
```

## Be careful

A timestamp or random id near the top of the system prompt changes the prefix on every call. Then every call pays the cache-write premium, and none ever gets a cheap read.

## Diagram

![Fig. 3.12: A hit skips the expensive work. A miss pays once and fills the cache.](/diagrams/caching.svg)

---
id: object-pool
number: "3.13"
title: Object Pool
chapter: llm-layer
fit: direct
figure_number: Fig. 3.13
figure_caption: "Borrow, use, reset, return: nothing expensive is built for each call."
diagram: object-pool.svg
analogy_title: Bowling shoes at the lanes
---
## Gist

Keep costly resources such as sandboxes, browsers and connections ready, lend them to agents, and reset them when returned.

## Everyday comparison

### Bowling shoes at the lanes

A bowling alley does not make new shoes for every customer. You give your size, borrow a pair from the rack, bowl, and hand them back. Staff spray and dry each pair before it goes back on the shelf. If the rack is empty, you wait a few minutes for a pair to come back.

## Classic meaning

An object pool keeps a set of ready, reusable objects. Clients borrow one and give it back. This avoids the cost of creating and destroying them again and again.

## In the agent system

Starting a code sandbox container (a sealed space for running code) or a headless browser (a browser with no screen) takes seconds. Opening a fresh TLS connection (an encrypted network link) to the model API on every call also adds delay. So the harness keeps pools. There are a few warm (already started) sandboxes, a browser pool for web tools, and the HTTP client's keep-alive connection pool. An agent checks out a sandbox for a bash or code-execution tool call. When the sandbox comes back, the pool wipes the working folder, kills leftover processes and resets environment variables. Only then does it lend it again. When every instance is busy, callers wait with a timeout, or the pool grows up to a hard limit.

## In a large company

In an enterprise platform, the sandbox pool is often a pool of fresh, never-used microVMs (tiny virtual machines) or gVisor containers (containers with an extra security layer). They start in advance and are destroyed after one session instead of being reset. A reset that misses one file or credential is a data leak between tenants (customer companies). Where reuse is allowed, it stays inside one tenant, and the reset is verified. Every lease (each loan of an instance) is logged with tenant, session and instance id for the audit trail. Pool size is a cost and capacity setting per region. Teams watch it for wait time and running out, like any other SLO (reliability target).

## Step by step

1. At startup, create N warm instances and put them on the idle list.
1. A tool call takes an instance, and waits if none is free.
1. The tool runs inside the borrowed instance.
1. On return, the pool resets it and puts it back on the idle list. If the reset fails, the pool destroys it.

## Code sketch

```python
class SandboxPool:
    def acquire(self, timeout=30):
        sb = self.idle.get(timeout=timeout)
        return Lease(sb, self.release)
    def release(self, sb):
        try:
            sb.reset()  # wipe fs, procs, env
            self.idle.put(sb)
        except ResetFailed:
            sb.destroy(); self.spawn_one()

with pool.acquire() as sb:
    out = sb.run(tool_input['command'])
```

## Be careful

A resource returned dirty can leak one session's files or cookies into another user's agent. So treat the reset as critical for security, and destroy anything that fails it.

## Diagram

![Fig. 3.13: Borrow, use, reset, return: nothing expensive is built for each call.](/diagrams/object-pool.svg)

---
id: multiton
number: "3.14"
title: Multiton
chapter: llm-layer
fit: direct
figure_number: Fig. 3.14
figure_caption: "Same key, same instance. A new key creates exactly one more."
diagram: multiton.svg
analogy_title: Embassy row in the capital
---
## Gist

Keep exactly one client per key, such as provider and model or tenant, created on first use and shared after that.

## Everyday comparison

### Embassy row in the capital

A capital city has one embassy per country. Ask a taxi for the French embassy, and you always arrive at the same building. When a new country is recognised, its embassy opens, and from then on that is the one. There is never a second French embassy across town giving out different visas.

## Classic meaning

A multiton is like a Singleton (a class with only one instance), but it keeps a map of named instances. It guarantees one instance for each key.

## In the agent system

Each provider and model pair needs its own client. Each client has its own base URL, credentials, connection pool and rate-limit tracker. ModelClient.get(provider, model) returns the existing client for that key. On first use, it builds one. It does this under a lock (a guard that lets only one task in at a time). So two subagents running at the same time do not both build it. Every agent that asks for the same key shares one connection pool and one view of remaining quota. Another tenant's key (another customer company) gets a separate client with its own API key.

## In a large company

In an enterprise platform, a multiton keyed by tenant (customer company) holds a model client for each tenant. Each client has its own credentials, base URLs for in-region endpoints, and budgets. So tenant isolation is built into the structure, not a parameter on each call. With thousands of tenants, the map needs a size limit and eviction (removing old entries). Evicted clients must be closed cleanly to release their connections. Keys must come from the logged-in tenant context, never from request input. Otherwise one tenant could get another tenant's client.

## Step by step

1. A caller asks for the client keyed by provider and model, or by tenant.
1. The class looks up the key in its map of instances.
1. If the key is missing, it builds the client under a lock and stores it.
1. Every later caller with that key gets the same instance.

## Code sketch

```python
class ModelClient:
    _all = {}
    _lock = threading.Lock()

    @classmethod
    def get(cls, provider, model):
        key = (provider, model)
        with cls._lock:
            if key not in cls._all:
                cls._all[key] = cls(*key)
            return cls._all[key]
```

## Be careful

A key might include a value that changes often, such as a per-request timeout. Then each call creates a new instance, and the multiton quietly becomes a memory leak.

## Diagram

![Fig. 3.14: Same key, same instance. A new key creates exactly one more.](/diagrams/multiton.svg)

---
id: singleton
number: "3.15"
title: Singleton
chapter: llm-layer
fit: direct
figure_number: Fig. 3.15
figure_caption: "Every caller reaches the one client, which owns the only connection pool."
diagram: singleton.svg
analogy_title: One conductor for the orchestra
---
## Gist

Share one model client and settings object across the whole process, so every agent uses the same connection pool, credentials and limits.

## Everyday comparison

### One conductor for the orchestra

Eighty musicians watch the same baton. Suppose a second conductor stood up and beat a slightly different tempo. Half the strings would follow one, and half the other. There is one podium and one person on it, and everyone knows where to look.

## Classic meaning

A singleton makes sure a class has only one instance. It also gives one global way to reach that instance.

## In the agent system

A harness process usually creates one SDK client (the provider's code library) at startup. It shares that client across the agent loop, subagents and background workers. That one instance owns the HTTP connection pool (open network links kept for reuse). It also owns the API key, default timeouts and the retry policy. If each subagent built its own client, the process would open extra connections. Each copy would also track rate limits on its own. Settings loaded from environment variables and config files work the same way. get_settings() returns one cached object.

## In a large company

In an enterprise platform, one client per process is fine for shared plumbing. Examples are the HTTP connection pool and telemetry exporters (code that sends out metrics and traces). But credentials and limits are usually per tenant (customer company). So in a multi-tenant worker, the singleton should not hold a single API key. Settings come from a config service or the environment. Secrets come from Vault or a cloud KMS (key management service). Key rotation must refresh the cached client without a restart. Dependency injection (handing the object in, instead of grabbing it globally) keeps tests and per-tenant overrides possible.

## Step by step

1. On first use, build the client from settings and keep it at module level.
1. Every later call returns that same instance.
1. All agents and workers share its connection pool and retry policy.
1. Tests replace it through an explicit override hook.

## Code sketch

```python
from functools import cache

@cache
def get_settings():
    return Settings.from_env()

@cache
def get_client():
    s = get_settings()
    return ModelClient(api_key=s.api_key,
                       max_retries=s.retries,
                       timeout=s.timeout)
```

## Be careful

A singleton is global mutable state (shared data anyone can change) in disguise. Pass it into agents instead of calling get_client() deep inside tools. Otherwise tests cannot swap in a fake.

## Diagram

![Fig. 3.15: Every caller reaches the one client, which owns the only connection pool.](/diagrams/singleton.svg)

id: tolerant-reader
number: "3.16"
title: Tolerant Reader
chapter: llm-layer
fit: adapted
figure_number: Fig. 3.16
figure_caption: "Messy text goes in, a strict typed object comes out, and the model is asked again only when it truly matters."
diagram: tolerant-reader.svg
analogy_title: The examiner marking messy scripts
---
## Gist

Read model output by taking what you need and ignoring the rest, fixing small mistakes instead of crashing on them.

## Everyday comparison

### The examiner marking messy scripts

An experienced examiner marking a maths paper looks for the answer and the key steps. Crossed-out working, arrows in the margin and a doodle in the corner do not lose marks. She only stops and flags a paper when the answer itself is missing or cannot be read.

## Classic meaning

A tolerant reader reads only the parts of a message it needs. It accepts unknown fields, a different order and small variations. So it keeps working when the sender changes its output.

## In the agent system

A model asked for JSON (a common text format for structured data) does not always return clean JSON. It may wrap it in a markdown fence ( marks) or add a sentence before it. It may leave a trailing comma, return numbers as strings or invent an extra field. A tolerant reader in the harness removes fences and pulls out the first balanced object (from the first { to its matching }). It applies a gentle repair. Then it reads only the required fields, converts simple types and ignores unknown keys. The harness reads verdicts from grader models (models that score answers) and plans from planner subagents this way. Only when a required field is truly missing does the harness send a short correction request back to the model.

## In a large company

In an enterprise platform, the first defence is to avoid parsing free text at all. Teams use tool calls or structured outputs with a JSON schema (a formal description of the expected shape). The tolerant reader stays for the remaining edges, such as grader verdicts and output from third-party models. Parse failures and repairs are counted per prompt version and model. So a regression (something that gets worse) after a model upgrade shows up in evals (quality tests) before users see it. Anything parsed from model output that drives a privileged action still gets strict checking. It also passes a policy check before it runs, for example with OPA or Cedar (policy engines that decide what is allowed).

## Step by step

1. Remove code fences and any text before the JSON.
1. Pull out the first balanced JSON object and fix small syntax errors.
1. Read the required fields, convert simple types and ignore extra keys.
1. If a required field is missing, ask the model for a corrected answer.

## Code sketch

```python
def read_verdict(text):
    raw = strip_fences(text)
    obj = repair_json(first_obj(raw))
    # take what we need, ignore the rest
    return Verdict(
        score=int(obj['score']),   # '7' ok
        reason=obj.get('reason', ''))

try:
    v = read_verdict(reply.text)
except (KeyError, ValueError):
    ask_model_to_fix(reply)
```

## Be careful

Tolerance belongs only at the edge where text is parsed. Pass strict, typed objects inward. Never 'repair' input that authorises a destructive tool action (one that deletes or changes things).

## Diagram

![Fig. 3.16: Messy text goes in, a strict typed object comes out, and the model is asked again only when it truly matters.](/diagrams/tolerant-reader.svg)

id: partial-response
number: "3.17"
title: Partial Response
chapter: llm-layer
fit: direct
review_id: rev-partial-response
figure_number: Fig. 3.17
figure_caption: Text reaches the user as it arrives. Tools run only once the message is complete.
diagram: partial-response.svg
analogy_title: "Election night, seat by seat"
---
## Gist

Deliver a model's answer piece by piece as it is written, or send only the fields a caller asked for.

## Everyday comparison

### Election night, seat by seat

On election night, the TV studio does not wait until dawn to read out every result at once. Each area's result is announced the moment its count finishes. Viewers watch the map fill in through the night and can go to bed early. Anyone who only wants the headline watches the strip at the bottom of the screen. It shows the seat totals and nothing else.

## Classic meaning

A partial response lets a client get part of a resource. This can be a subset of fields, or a stream of the result as it is produced. It saves bandwidth and waiting time.

## In the agent system

With streaming on, the model API sends server-sent events (SSE: a stream of small messages over one connection). First comes message_start. Then each content block gets a content_block_start event. Next comes a run of content_block_delta events. These carry text_delta or input_json_delta pieces. Each block ends with content_block_stop. Then a message_delta event carries the stop_reason (why the model stopped) and usage. Last comes message_stop. The harness sends text pieces to the chat UI at once. It holds input_json_delta pieces until a tool_use block (the model's request to run a tool) is complete. It runs tools only after the stream ends with stop_reason tool_use. It can cancel the stream when the user presses stop. Field selection is the same idea for reads. The UI polls a status endpoint. That endpoint returns only the run's state and token count, never the whole transcript.

## In a large company

In an enterprise platform, streaming passes through the LLM gateway (the central entry point for model calls). The gateway must stream from end to end. Proxies and load balancers must not hold back the response. The gateway still applies output DLP (data loss prevention: stopping sensitive data from leaving) or redaction. It often does this on a small rolling window, so users still see text quickly. Time to first token and stream completion are SLO metrics (measures tied to reliability targets). Cancelled streams are recorded, so partial output and its cost appear in the audit trail. Field selection on status and transcript endpoints also serves as data minimisation (sharing only the data needed). This supports GDPR (the EU data protection law) and least-privilege access to transcripts (giving each person only the access they need).

## Step by step

1. Open a streaming request to the model API.
1. Send each text piece to the UI and add it to the turn buffer.
1. Collect tool input pieces until each block stops. Ignore ping events and unknown events.
1. On message_delta, record stop_reason and usage. Close the turn on message_stop.
1. Run the buffered tool calls only if stop_reason is tool_use.

## Code sketch

```python
with client.messages.stream(**req) as s:
    for ev in s:
        if ev.type == 'content_block_delta' \
           and ev.delta.type == 'text_delta':
            ui.send(ev.delta.text)
        # input_json_delta: SDK buffers it
        # ping and unknown events: ignore
    msg = s.get_final_message()
if msg.stop_reason == 'tool_use':
    run_tools(msg.content)  # whole inputs
elif msg.stop_reason == 'max_tokens':
    continue_or_fail(msg)   # may be cut off
```

## Be careful

Never act on a partial tool input. A half-streamed path such as '/home/user/pro' is a valid start of the real path, and it points to the wrong file.

## Diagram

![Fig. 3.17: Text reaches the user as it arrives. Tools run only once the message is complete.](/diagrams/partial-response.svg)

id: money
number: "3.18"
title: Money
chapter: llm-layer
fit: direct
review_id: rev-money
figure_number: Fig. 3.18
figure_caption: "Counts become typed tokens, then typed money, before anything is added up."
diagram: money.svg
analogy_title: The bureau de change counter
---
## Gist

Store tokens and cost as typed amounts with a unit or currency, so sums, budgets and reports cannot mix numbers that do not match.

## Everyday comparison

### The bureau de change counter

At a currency exchange desk, nobody writes down just '100'. It is always 100 euros or 100 yen. The clerk will not add the two without looking up today's rate first. Rounding happens once, at the end, to the smallest coin of the currency being paid out.

## Classic meaning

The Money pattern models an amount of money as a value object (a small object defined only by its values). It combines a quantity and a currency. Its arithmetic enforces currency rules and correct rounding.

## In the agent system

Each response has a usage block with four counts. input_tokens is only the uncached part of the prompt. cache_creation_input_tokens counts tokens written to the prompt cache. cache_read_input_tokens counts tokens read from it. output_tokens counts what the model wrote. Each kind has its own price for each model, and cache writes are priced by TTL (how long the cache entry lives). Cached tokens are billed separately, so the cost ledger must include all four counts. As bare integers, these counts invite bugs. Code might treat input_tokens as the whole prompt, or add output tokens to input tokens. It might add a large model's tokens to a small model's as if they cost the same. So the harness uses value objects: Tokens(n, kind, model) and Money(pico, 'USD'). It converts between them through an explicit, versioned price table. It does arithmetic in whole-number units small enough to price one cached token exactly. These are pico-dollars (millionths of a millionth of a dollar). With streaming, it takes usage from the final message_delta. Those counts are cumulative (running totals), so it does not add up every event. Budgets for a session, a subagent tree or a tenant (customer company) are Money too. So a check like spent + estimate > budget is type-safe (the types stop mistakes).

## In a large company

In an enterprise platform, the Money value object supports per-tenant budgets, chargeback to cost centres (billing costs back to each team) and invoices. So the price table is versioned and has effective dates. Every ledger entry records the model, the usage fields, the price version and the tenant. A daily job reconciles (compares and matches) the ledger against the provider's usage and cost reports. The gateway enforces budget alerts and hard stops before a call, not only in reports after it. Currency conversion, where needed, happens once at billing with a recorded rate. It never happens inside per-call arithmetic.

## Step by step

1. Read the usage block from each model response.
1. Wrap each count as Tokens with its kind and model.
1. Convert to Money using the price table for that model and kind.
1. Add it to the session ledger and compare against the Money budget.

## Code sketch

```python
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Money:
    pico: int; cur: str = 'USD'  # 1e-12
    def __add__(s, o):
        assert o.cur == s.cur
        return Money(s.pico + o.pico, s.cur)
def cost(u, model):
    p = PRICES[model]   # pico-USD per token
    n = (u.input_tokens * p.inp
       + u.cache_creation_input_tokens * p.wr
       + u.cache_read_input_tokens * p.rd
       + u.output_tokens * p.out)
    return Money(n)     # exact, round later
```

## Be careful

Floating-point dollars (decimals that computers store inexactly) drift after millions of tiny per-call charges. Store whole-number units smaller than a millionth of a dollar, and round only when displaying or invoicing.

## Diagram

![Fig. 3.18: Counts become typed tokens, then typed money, before anything is added up.](/diagrams/money.svg)

id: repository
number: "4.01"
title: Repository
chapter: memory
fit: direct
review_id: rev-repository
figure_number: Fig. 4.01
figure_caption: "The loop asks one collection, and the repository decides which store answers"
diagram: repository.svg
analogy_title: The library circulation desk
---
## Gist

Give the agent's memory a simple list-like interface (add, search, remove), so loop code never talks to the database directly.

## Everyday comparison

### The library circulation desk

You ask the librarian for books on tide pools. She might get them from the open shelves, the basement or another library. You just get a pile of books at the desk. You return them to the same desk, and she decides where each one goes.

## Classic meaning

A repository sits between your main program and the storage code. It lets the program treat stored objects like an ordinary collection.

## In the agent system

The agent loop (the code that runs the model turn after turn) asks a MemoryRepository for what matters to this turn: repo.search(query, k=5). Here k is the number of results. Behind the repository there might be a vector store (a database that finds text by meaning). It uses embeddings, which are lists of numbers that stand for meaning. It could also be a SQL table of past chats or a folder of markdown memory files. The repository speaks in the harness's own objects, such as Memory and Turn. It applies scope, such as the user id and how recent a memory is. It also hides the embedding call. You can swap the vector store, or use a simple in-memory repository in evals (automated test runs), without changing any loop code.

## In a large company

In an enterprise platform, the memory repository is the one checkpoint where tenant and user scope get fixed. A tenant is one customer company sharing the platform. The scope comes from the logged-in identity, so neither loop code nor the model can widen a search. The repository is also where right-to-erasure requests land (a person's legal right to have their data deleted). remove() and a forget_user() call must delete the memory text, its embedding and any cached copies. Some vector stores offer separate namespaces or indexes per tenant. Postgres with pgvector (a vector search add-on) and row-level security (database rules that limit which rows each user can see) can also do this. These enforce scope below the repository as a second line of defence.

## Step by step

1. The loop builds a search query from the latest user message.
1. It calls repo.search(query, k), limited to the current user.
1. The repository embeds the query, searches its store and turns each hit into a Memory object.
1. The loop puts those memories into the context window and saves new facts with repo.add().

## Code sketch

```python
class MemoryRepo(Protocol):
    def add(self, m: Memory): ...
    def search(self, q, k=5) -> list: ...
    def remove(self, mem_id): ...

class VectorMemoryRepo(MemoryRepo):
    def __init__(self, index, tenant, user):
        self.index = index
        self.ns = f'{tenant}/{user}'  # scope
    def search(self, q, k=5):
        hits = self.index.query(embed(q),
            top_k=k, namespace=self.ns)
        return [Memory.from_hit(h)
                for h in hits]
```

## Be careful

Do not let store-specific query syntax, such as filter dicts or bits of SQL, leak out through the repository. Once callers depend on it, the abstraction is gone.

## Diagram

![Fig. 4.01: The loop asks one collection, and the repository decides which store answers](/diagrams/repository.svg)
