---
id: actor-model
number: "5.01"
title: Actor Model
chapter: multi-agent
fit: adapted
review_id: rev-actor-model
figure_number: Fig. 5.01
figure_caption: Subagents share nothing. Work and results move only as messages between mailboxes.
diagram: actor-model.svg
analogy_title: Lighthouse keepers and the mail boat
---
## Gist

Run each subagent as a sealed-off actor that keeps its own context and only reacts to messages in its mailbox.

## Everyday comparison

### Lighthouse keepers and the mail boat

Each keeper lives alone on a rock with a private logbook that nobody else reads. The only contact is the mail boat. It drops letters in a box on the jetty. The keeper opens them one at a time, acts on each, and sends replies back on the next boat. No keeper ever rows across to adjust another keeper's lamp.

## Classic meaning

Actors are units of work that run at the same time. Each one keeps its own private state, talks to others only by sending messages without waiting, and handles one message at a time from its mailbox.

## In the agent system

Each subagent (a helper agent started by the main agent) has its own context window (the text the model can see at one time). It also has its own system prompt and its own set of tools. The orchestrator (the agent that hands out and tracks the work) cannot reach into that context. Work arrives as a message, a task brief, placed in the subagent's inbox. The subagent's loop takes one message at a time. So its transcript never mixes two tasks together. Results travel back the same way, as a message to the orchestrator's own inbox. Nothing is shared, so a supervisor can restart a crashed subagent without damaging anyone else's state. But the message it was working on survives only if the mailbox is durable (saved so it survives a crash). The mailbox must also remove the message only after the reply has been sent.

## In a large company

Large companies run long-lived agents as actors on a durable runtime, so mailboxes survive restarts. Examples are Temporal workflows (a system that saves each step so work can resume after a crash), Akka or Orleans. Another option is to give each agent its own Kafka or SQS queue (message services that store messages until they are read). Each actor carries its own tenant id (which customer company it works for). It also carries scoped credentials from workload identity (login details issued to the program itself, limited to what it needs) and its own token budget. This makes isolation and chargeback (billing each team for its own use) easy. The control to add is supervision. A parent watches its child actors and restarts, escalates or stops the ones that fail. It records each decision in the audit trail.

## Step by step

1. The orchestrator sends a task message to the subagent's mailbox.
1. The subagent takes one message and runs its loop inside its private context.
1. It may send messages to other actors, including subagents it starts.
1. It posts a result message to the orchestrator's mailbox and takes the next message.

## Code sketch

```python
class SubagentActor:
    def __init__(self, prompt):
        self.inbox = asyncio.Queue()
        self.ctx = [system(prompt)]  # private
    async def run(self):
        while True:
            m = await self.inbox.get()
            out = await turn(self.ctx, m.body)
            await m.reply_to.put(out)

coder.inbox.put_nowait(Msg(task, orc.inbox))
```

## Be careful

Actors that stop and wait for each other's replies can deadlock (get stuck forever, each waiting on the other). So give every request a timeout, and avoid requests that go round in a circle between subagents.

## Diagram

![Fig. 5.01: Subagents share nothing. Work and results move only as messages between mailboxes.](/diagrams/actor-model.svg)

---
id: mediator
number: "5.02"
title: Mediator
chapter: multi-agent
fit: direct
figure_number: Fig. 5.02
figure_caption: "Every subagent talks to the orchestrator, and none of them talk to each other."
diagram: mediator.svg
analogy_title: The control tower
---
## Gist

Send all subagent coordination through one orchestrator, so specialists never need to know about or message each other.

## Everyday comparison

### The control tower

Pilots coming into a busy airport do not argue over runway slots with each other on the radio. Each pilot talks only to the tower. The tower sees every aircraft and tells each pilot when to land, wait or taxi. When a tenth plane arrives, nobody else's instructions change. The tower simply fits one more plane into the order.

## Classic meaning

A mediator is one object that holds the rules for how a group of objects work together. Each object talks to the mediator instead of talking to the others directly.

## In the agent system

In an orchestrator and subagent design, there is a researcher, a coder, a tester and a reviewer. Each is a subagent (a helper agent with its own job). Each one reports only to the orchestrator (the agent in charge of the plan). The orchestrator holds the plan and decides who runs next. It turns one subagent's output into the next one's task brief. It trims the brief down to what that subagent needs in its context (the text the model can see). If subagents chatted directly, the number of message paths would grow fast. Context would repeat in every exchange, and the run would be hard to follow. To add a new specialist, you teach the orchestrator one more route. The existing subagents stay the same.

## In a large company

In a company platform the orchestrator is the natural mediator. It is also the natural place to enforce rules. It checks each hand-off with the policy engine, such as OPA or Cedar (tools that answer 'is this allowed?'). It removes data that the next subagent is not cleared to see. It writes every routing decision to the audit trail. Subagents get only scoped, short-lived credentials (login details limited to their own tools that expire soon). The risk is that the mediator holds a lot of power and is a single point of failure. So give it its own SLO (a reliability target) and keep its state in a durable store (one that survives crashes). Treat changes to its routing rules as reviewed releases that must pass evals (automated quality tests) first.

## Step by step

1. A subagent finishes and returns its result to the orchestrator.
1. The orchestrator records the result in the shared plan.
1. It decides which specialist acts next and writes a focused brief for it.
1. That subagent runs with only the brief and reports back the same way.

## Code sketch

```python
class Orchestrator:
    def __init__(self, agents, plan):
        self.agents, self.plan = agents, plan
    def notify(self, sender, result):
        self.plan.record(sender, result)
        nxt = self.plan.next_step()
        if nxt:
            brief = self.brief_for(nxt, result)
            self.agents[nxt.role].send(brief)
```

## Be careful

A mediator that keeps every subagent's full output in its own context becomes a token bottleneck (it fills up and slows everything down). Store the raw output in files and keep only short summaries in the plan.

## Diagram

![Fig. 5.02: Every subagent talks to the orchestrator, and none of them talk to each other.](/diagrams/mediator.svg)

---

---
id: master-worker
number: "5.03"
title: Master-Worker
chapter: multi-agent
fit: direct
review_id: rev-master-worker
figure_number: Fig. 5.03
figure_caption: "The master owns the task table, so a lost task simply goes back to pending."
diagram: master-worker.svg
analogy_title: The orchard picking boss
---
## Gist

A master agent splits a big job into separate tasks, gives them to worker subagents, and collects or reassigns the results.

## Everyday comparison

### The orchard picking boss

At harvest the boss chalks a row number on each picker's bucket. She keeps a clipboard showing who has which row. Full crates come back to her trailer. When a picker goes home sick at noon, the boss crosses out that name. She gives the unfinished row to whoever is free next.

## Classic meaning

A master process splits work into tasks and hands them to a pool of workers. It gathers their results and gives a failed worker's task to another worker.

## In the agent system

Picture a migration agent that must update 300 files. It acts as master. It lists the files and groups them into batches. It starts one worker subagent (a helper agent) per batch, each with a brief and a token budget (a limit on how much text it may use). The master tracks each task's state (pending, running or done) in a task table. Workers send back a short result message, not their full transcripts. This keeps the master's context (the text its model can see) small. Sometimes a worker runs out of time, or its result fails a check. Then the master marks the batch pending again and gives it to the next free worker.

## In a large company

Company teams usually run the master as a durable workflow, using Temporal or AWS Step Functions (systems that save each step so work survives a crash). Workers run as activities (single steps of that workflow). So the task table survives a crash. Retries, timeouts and heartbeats (regular 'I am still alive' signals) are set in configuration instead of written by hand. Limits on how many workers run at once are set per tenant (per customer company). The LLM gateway (one shared front door to all AI models) enforces them again. So one large job cannot use up shared rate limits. Each worker run is tagged with the job id and cost centre for chargeback (billing each team for its use). Batches that still fail after their retry limit go to a review queue instead of looping forever.

## Step by step

1. The master splits the job into separate tasks and records them as pending.
1. It starts workers up to a limit on how many run at once, one task each.
1. Each worker runs in its own context and returns a short result.
1. The master marks tasks done, puts failed or timed-out ones back, and stops when the table is complete.

## Code sketch

```python
state = {b.id: 'pending' for b in batches}
tries = Counter()
while not finished_all(state):
    free = MAX_WORKERS - running(state)
    for b in pending(state)[:free]:
        state[b.id] = 'running'
        spawn('migrator', b, timeout=600)
    for r in await next_results():  # incl.
        tries[r.id] += 1           # timeouts
        if r.ok and verify(r):
            state[r.id] = 'done'
        elif tries[r.id] >= 3:
            state[r.id] = 'failed'
        else: state[r.id] = 'pending'
```

## Be careful

Master-worker suits tasks that are truly independent and safe to run again. So run each worker in its own git branch or worktree (a separate copy of the files). Then a batch that is handed out again starts clean, and two workers never edit the same files.

## Diagram

![Fig. 5.03: The master owns the task table, so a lost task simply goes back to pending.](/diagrams/master-worker.svg)

---
id: fork-join
number: "5.04"
title: Fork/Join
chapter: multi-agent
fit: direct
figure_number: Fig. 5.04
figure_caption: Each parent forks its children and continues only after joining all of them.
diagram: fork-join.svg
analogy_title: The pit stop
---
## Gist

Split a task into parts for parallel subagents, maybe splitting again, and continue only when every child has finished.

## Everyday comparison

### The pit stop

The car stops. Four crews jump at the four wheels at once while another crew refuels. Nobody waves the car out when the first wheel is on. The crew chief lifts the board only when every crew has raised a hand. Then the car leaves as one.

## Classic meaning

You split a task into smaller parts that run at the same time (fork). Each part may split again. Then you wait for all of them and combine their results (join).

## In the agent system

Say an agent is asked to audit a monorepo (one large code repository holding many packages). It forks one subagent (helper agent) per top-level package. A subagent facing a large package may fork again, one per directory. Each parent then waits at the join. It waits for all its children before summarising their findings and returning to its own parent. The harness sets a maximum depth and a total budget of subagents. This matters because forking again and again multiplies token spend quickly. The join is a barrier (a point that everyone must reach before anyone moves on). So the slowest child sets the pace for its parent.

## In a large company

In production, platform policy limits the forking. It sets a maximum depth, a maximum number of children per parent, and a token budget per run. The harness and the LLM gateway (one shared front door to all AI models) enforce these limits. When a limit is passed, the run stops cleanly. Durable execution engines such as Temporal (systems that save each step so work survives a crash) treat the join as child workflows. So a crashed parent can resume without forking finished children again. In OpenTelemetry (a standard for recording what software does), each child span (a timed record of one piece of work) is linked to its parent. This shows the cost and time of every branch. That supports chargeback (billing each team for its use) and SLO reports (reports on reliability targets).

## Step by step

1. The parent agent checks whether the task is small enough to do directly.
1. If not, it splits the task and forks a child subagent for each part.
1. Children run in parallel and may fork further, within the depth limit.
1. Each parent joins all its children, merges their results and returns upward.

## Code sketch

```python
async def audit(path, depth=0):
    parts = split(path)
    if depth >= MAX_DEPTH or len(parts) < 2:
        return await run_agent('auditor', path)
    kids = [spawn(audit, p, depth + 1)
            for p in parts]  # fork
    res = await asyncio.gather(*kids)  # join
    return merge(res)
```

## Be careful

One stuck child holds up its whole branch at the join. So give every forked subagent a timeout. Decide in advance whether partial results are acceptable.

## Diagram

![Fig. 5.04: Each parent forks its children and continues only after joining all of them.](/diagrams/fork-join.svg)

---

---
id: fan-out-fan-in
number: "5.05"
title: Fan-Out/Fan-In
chapter: multi-agent
fit: direct
review_id: rev-fan-out-fan-in
figure_number: Fig. 5.05
figure_caption: One question goes out to many. One bundle comes back when all reply or the clock runs out.
diagram: fan-out-fan-in.svg
analogy_title: The exam bell
---
## Gist

Send the same question to several subagents at once, then gather their answers in one place, usually by a deadline.

## Everyday comparison

### The exam bell

The examiner hands the same paper to every student at the same moment. Each student works alone, all at the same time. When the bell rings, the papers are collected into one pile, even if the last student has not finished. Only then does marking begin.

## Classic meaning

A sender sends one request to many workers at the same time (fan-out). A collector then combines their answers into one result (fan-in).

## In the agent system

Take a research question. The orchestrator (the agent in charge) sends the same query to three subagents (helper agents) in one turn. One searches the web, one searches code, and one reads docs through an MCP server (MCP is a standard way to connect tools to an AI model). Fan-in happens at a collector. It waits for every reply or for a deadline, whichever comes first. Late or failed replies are marked as missing. So the orchestrator knows its answer rests on partial evidence. The collected replies then enter the orchestrator's context as one tool_result (the block that carries a tool's output back to the model). This is better than three separate interruptions.

## In a large company

This is the Scatter-Gather pattern from the book Enterprise Integration Patterns. Companies use it for research and search across sources that are governed separately. Examples are a document store, a ticketing system and the code host. Each branch must run with the requesting user's own permissions. These pass along through OIDC token exchange (a standard way to swap a user's login token for one that a downstream service accepts). So the gathered bundle never holds documents that the user could not open. Deadlines are tied to the SLO (reliability target) that the user sees. Token and time measurements for each branch feed cost dashboards. Then low-value branches can be dropped.

## Step by step

1. The orchestrator sends the same request to several subagents at once.
1. Each subagent works on its own with its own tools.
1. A collector gathers replies until all arrive or the deadline passes.
1. The orchestrator receives one combined bundle, with missing replies marked.

## Code sketch

```python
jobs = {a: create_task(spawn(a, task=q))
        for a in ('web', 'code', 'docs')}
done, late = await asyncio.wait(
    jobs.values(), timeout=60)
for j in late:
    j.cancel()
ok = {a: j.result() for a, j in jobs.items()
      if j in done and not j.exception()}
bundle = {'answers': ok, 'missing':
          sorted(set(jobs) - set(ok))}
```

## Be careful

Fanning out multiplies the cost of every question. So fan out only when the sources are different enough to add new evidence.

## Diagram

![Fig. 5.05: One question goes out to many. One bundle comes back when all reply or the clock runs out.](/diagrams/fan-out-fan-in.svg)

---
id: mapreduce
number: "5.06"
title: MapReduce
chapter: multi-agent
fit: adapted
figure_number: Fig. 5.06
figure_caption: "No call ever sees all the documents. Maps shrink them, the shuffle groups, and reducers combine."
diagram: mapreduce.svg
analogy_title: Election night count
---
## Gist

Turn each document into short notes with its own subagent, group the notes by theme, then combine each group into one summary.

## Everyday comparison

### Election night count

Every polling station counts its own ballot box and phones in one sheet of totals. At the regional centre, staff sort the sheets by constituency and add up each pile. The national result is built from those few sums. Nobody at the centre ever handles a paper ballot.

## Classic meaning

To process a large set of data, you run a map function on each record at the same time. You group the results by a key. Then a reduce function combines each group.

## In the agent system

Forty PDFs will not fit in one context window (the text the model can see at one time). So the harness runs a map step. It starts one subagent (helper agent) per document or chunk. All use the same summary prompt. Each one returns structured notes tagged with themes. The harness then groups the notes by theme. This is the shuffle step. Next, one reduce subagent per theme writes a summary from that theme's notes alone. A final call merges the theme sections into the report. Every model call sees a limited amount of text. So the job grows with the number of documents, not with the size of the context window.

## In a large company

Companies run map steps through a provider's batch API (a cheaper way to send many requests to be done later). Or they use a queue of workers behind the LLM gateway (one shared front door to all AI models). This gives lower cost, rate limits per tenant (per customer company) and chargeback (billing) per job. PII redaction (removing personal data such as names and emails) and DLP (data loss prevention checks) run before the map step. Source document ids travel with every note, so the final report can cite and audit its evidence. Data residency matters here (keeping data inside a set country or region). Map workers must run in the region where the documents live. The notes made along the way are stored and deleted under the same retention policy (rules on how long data is kept) as the sources.

## Step by step

1. Split the documents into pieces that each fit in one context.
1. Map: one subagent per piece runs the same prompt and returns notes tagged by theme.
1. Shuffle: the harness groups all notes by theme.
1. Reduce: one call per theme combines its notes, and a final call merges the sections.

## Code sketch

```python
notes = await gather(*[
    run('summarise', d) for d in docs])
by_theme = defaultdict(list)
for n in chain(*notes):
    by_theme[n.theme].append(n)
parts = await gather(*[
    run('synthesise', t, ns)
    for t, ns in by_theme.items()])
report = await run('merge', parts)
```

## Be careful

Map summaries lose detail. When the answer needs exact quotes or figures, carry source ids through the map step. Then the reducers can look up the originals.

## Diagram

![Fig. 5.06: No call ever sees all the documents. Maps shrink them, the shuffle groups, and reducers combine.](/diagrams/mapreduce.svg)

---
id: leader-followers
number: "5.07"
title: Leader-Followers
chapter: multi-agent
fit: adapted
review_id: rev-leader-followers
figure_number: Fig. 5.07
figure_caption: "Leadership rotates. The leader claims a task, promotes a follower, and rejoins the line when done."
diagram: leader-followers.svg
analogy_title: The taxi rank
---
## Gist

Worker agents take turns. One leader watches the task queue, claims the next task, then makes a follower the new leader.

## Everyday comparison

### The taxi rank

Cabs queue nose to tail outside the station. Only the cab at the front picks up the next passenger. As it pulls away, the cab behind rolls forward and becomes the one to take the next fare. When the first driver drops off the passenger, they rejoin the back of the line.

## Classic meaning

A pool of threads (units of work inside one program) shares a set of event sources. One leader waits for an event. When one comes, it makes a follower the new leader, then handles the event itself.

## In the agent system

A group of identical worker agents serves a shared queue of tasks, such as new tickets or scheduled code reviews. Only the current leader checks the queue. So idle workers do not all hit it at once, and two workers never claim the same task. When the leader claims a task, it first hands leadership to the next idle worker. Only then does it start its long model and tool calls. So someone is always watching the queue. When the worker finishes, it writes the result and rejoins the followers.

## In a large company

Inside one harness process, a leader-followers pool stops a thundering herd (many idle workers rushing the queue at once). But across machines, companies almost always use competing consumers. They use SQS, Pub/Sub or Kafka consumer groups (message services where workers share one queue). Visibility timeouts or leases take the place of the leader token. Either way, a claimed task needs a lease and a dead-letter path (a place where failing tasks go to be looked at). Worker counts are capped per tenant (per customer company), so one customer cannot take over the whole pool. Alert on queue length and on how long tasks wait to be claimed. These are the SLO measures (measures for the reliability target).

## Step by step

1. One idle worker holds the leader token and waits on the task queue.
1. A task arrives and the leader claims it.
1. The leader passes the token to the next follower, who starts waiting on the queue.
1. The former leader does the task, writes the result and rejoins the followers.

## Code sketch

```python
async def worker(me, pool, queue):
    while True:
        await pool.wait_until_leader(me)
        task = await queue.claim()
        pool.promote_next()   # hand off lead
        out = await run_agent('review', task)
        results.write(task.id, out)
        pool.rejoin(me)
```

## Be careful

Leader-followers works inside one process (one running program). If the leader crashes after claiming a task but before passing the token, nobody watches the queue. So give the token a lease (a hold that expires unless renewed). For workers on several machines, use competing consumers instead. That means all workers read from one queue that hides a claimed message for a set time (a visibility timeout).

## Diagram

![Fig. 5.07: Leadership rotates. The leader claims a task, promotes a follower, and rejoins the line when done.](/diagrams/leader-followers.svg)

---

---
id: leader-election
number: "5.08"
title: Leader Election
chapter: multi-agent
fit: direct
review_id: rev-leader-election
figure_number: Fig. 5.08
figure_caption: "An atomic lease picks one leader. When it expires, the next one takes over with a higher term."
diagram: leader-election.svg
analogy_title: The conclave and the white smoke
---
## Gist

Let a group of identical agents agree on exactly one coordinator, and pick a new one automatically when it disappears.

## Everyday comparison

### The conclave and the white smoke

The cardinals lock themselves in the chapel and vote until one name has the required majority. They burn the ballots after each round. Black smoke means no decision yet. White smoke tells the crowd there is one leader. When that leader dies, the same steps run again, and nobody acts as leader in between.

## Classic meaning

A group of machines (nodes) runs a shared method to choose one node to coordinate them. When that node fails, they choose a replacement.

## In the agent system

Several copies of the harness may share a task queue or run the same scheduled task. Exactly one of them should coordinate. It splits the work, sends reminders and writes the daily summary. Each copy tries to get a lease in a shared store. A lease is a database row or key-value lock with a TTL (a time limit after which it expires). The winner becomes leader and renews the lease while it is healthy. A term number goes up with each new leader. Workers reject commands from an older term. This stops a former leader that was paused from acting on old authority. If the leader's process crashes, its lease expires and another copy wins the next try.

## In a large company

Company harnesses get leases from a store with linearizable compare-and-set. That means a write happens only if the value is still what you expect, and every reader sees the same order of changes. Examples are etcd, ZooKeeper, Consul or a Kubernetes Lease object. Teams use these instead of writing their own consensus (agreement) system. The systems the leader writes to must check the fencing term (the term number used as a guard). One way is a conditional write in the database. Without that check, a paused old leader can still cause duplicate side effects. Log and alert on changes of leader. Frequent changes, called flapping, usually mean an unhealthy node or a network partition (part of the network cut off from the rest).

## Step by step

1. Each agent copy tries to get the coordinator lease with a TTL.
1. One succeeds, gets a new term number and starts coordinating.
1. The leader renews the lease while healthy. The others keep retrying quietly.
1. If renewals stop, the lease expires and the next copy to get it leads with a higher term.

## Code sketch

```python
while running:
    lease = store.try_acquire('coord', me,
                              ttl=30)
    while lease and lease.valid():
        # work in slices shorter than the TTL
        coordinate_step(fence=lease.term)
        lease = store.renew(lease)  # or None
    await sleep(10)
```

## Be careful

Never choose a leader by comparing clocks or by asking the model to pick one. Use an atomic lease (one that is taken in a single step that cannot be split) in a store that gives every copy the same answer.

## Diagram

![Fig. 5.08: An atomic lease picks one leader. When it expires, the next one takes over with a higher term.](/diagrams/leader-election.svg)

---

---
id: observer
number: "5.09"
title: Observer
chapter: multi-agent
fit: direct
figure_number: Fig. 5.09
figure_caption: The task list itself calls every attached observer when an item changes.
diagram: observer.svg
analogy_title: "The coach's text list"
---
## Gist

Let the UI, the orchestrator and loggers watch a shared task list and react when a subagent changes an item.

## Everyday comparison

### The coach's text list

The football coach keeps the parents' numbers in a list on her phone. When rain cancels Saturday's match, she updates the fixture and texts everyone on the list herself. Parents who join mid-season ask to be added. Nobody has to keep ringing the coach to ask whether the match is on.

## Classic meaning

A subject (the thing being watched) keeps a list of observers. When its state changes, it tells each of them automatically.

## In the agent system

The task list behind a todo tool is the subject. Three observers attach when the run starts: the chat UI's checklist panel, the orchestrator (the agent in charge) and the progress logger. Say a subagent (helper agent) calls the tool to mark task 3 done. The task list updates itself. Then it calls update on every attached observer. The panel redraws, the orchestrator thinks about what comes next, and the logger adds a line. Observers detach when the run ends. So finished sessions stop getting updates.

## In a large company

In a company harness, the observers on a task list are usually the UI, the audit writer and a metrics exporter. The audit observer must never be skipped. So teams make audit writes synchronous (finished before the call returns). Or they back them with a durable outbox (a saved list of messages that will be sent even after a crash). UI and metrics observers run in the background, so they cannot slow the agent. Some observers sit in another process or belong to another tenant (customer company). These should use a proper event stream with access control instead of direct calls.

## Step by step

1. The UI panel, orchestrator and logger call attach() on the task list.
1. A subagent changes a task through a tool call.
1. The task list saves the change and calls update() on each observer in its list.
1. Each observer reads the new state and reacts in its own way.

## Code sketch

```python
class TaskList:
    def __init__(self):
        self.items, self.observers = {}, []
    def attach(self, obs):
        self.observers.append(obs)
    def set_status(self, tid, status):
        self.items[tid] = status
        for o in self.observers:
            o.update(self, tid, status)

tasks.attach(checklist_panel)
```

## Be careful

Observers run inside the subject's call. So one slow observer, such as a remote logger, delays the subagent's tool result. Hand slow work off to run in the background.

## Diagram

![Fig. 5.09: The task list itself calls every attached observer when an item changes.](/diagrams/observer.svg)

---
id: publish-subscribe
number: "5.10"
title: Publish-Subscribe
chapter: multi-agent
fit: direct
figure_number: Fig. 5.10
figure_caption: "Publishers name a topic, never a receiver. The broker sends each event on to all its subscribers."
diagram: publish-subscribe.svg
analogy_title: Tuning in to a radio frequency
---
## Gist

Agents publish events such as file.changed or task.done to named topics, and every agent subscribed to a topic gets them.

## Everyday comparison

### Tuning in to a radio frequency

A station broadcasts traffic news on one frequency and music on another. It has no idea who is listening, or how many. A taxi driver tunes to traffic. A hairdresser tunes to music. A new listener can switch on at any moment, and the station changes nothing.

## Classic meaning

Publishers send messages to topics without knowing who will receive them. A broker (a go-between service) delivers each message to every subscriber of that topic.

## In the agent system

In a coding run with several agents, the coder agent publishes file.changed with the file path and a diff hash (a short fingerprint of the change). The test agent publishes task.done with its verdict. A broker keeps a list of subscribers for each topic. The broker can live inside the harness or be an outside message service. The lint agent (a code style checker) and the index refresher both subscribe to file.changed. The orchestrator (the agent in charge) subscribes to task.done. Publishers never address subscribers. So a new watcher, such as a docs-updater agent, joins just by subscribing to an existing topic.

## In a large company

At company scale, the broker is Kafka, Google Pub/Sub, Amazon SNS with SQS, or EventBridge. Teams own topics. Message formats (schemas) are registered and versioned. Tenant isolation (keeping each customer company's data apart) uses separate topics per tenant, or ACLs (access lists) on who may subscribe. This matters because a subscriber added to a shared topic quietly receives every tenant's events. Keep events small. They carry ids rather than raw prompts or PII (personal data such as names and emails). Set the broker's retention (how long it keeps messages) to match the data retention policy.

## Step by step

1. Subscribers tell the broker which topics they want.
1. An agent publishes an event to a topic and carries on.
1. The broker looks up the topic's subscribers.
1. It delivers a copy to each one, and each handles it on its own.

## Code sketch

```python
bus.subscribe('file.changed', lint_agent)
bus.subscribe('file.changed', reindex)
bus.subscribe('task.done', orchestrator)

# inside the coder agent's write tool
bus.publish('file.changed',
            {'path': p, 'sha': sha})
```

## Be careful

Events that wake agents can cause more events. So guard against loops. For example, a formatter agent's own edits can publish file.changed again and wake itself.

## Diagram

![Fig. 5.10: Publishers name a topic, never a receiver. The broker sends each event on to all its subscribers.](/diagrams/publish-subscribe.svg)

---

---
id: event-aggregator
number: "5.11"
title: Event Aggregator
chapter: multi-agent
fit: direct
figure_number: Fig. 5.11
figure_caption: "Sources and listeners each know one object, the hub, instead of each other."
diagram: event-aggregator.svg
analogy_title: The newsroom wire desk
---
## Gist

Collect events from every harness part in one hub, so listeners sign up once instead of connecting to each source.

## Everyday comparison

### The newsroom wire desk

Reports pour in from news agencies, freelance reporters and police scanners. No editor watches every feed. Everything lands at the wire desk. The sports editor asks the desk for anything about football. The business editor asks for markets. A new feed plugs into the desk, and no editor even notices.

## Classic meaning

One object receives events from many sources. Subscribers sign up with that one object instead of with each source.

## In the agent system

A harness has many event sources. They include the tool runner, the subagent pool, the file watcher, the permission gate and the model client's stream. Without a hub, the status bar, the transcript writer and the cost meter would each connect to every source. An event aggregator is the one object they all share. Sources call hub.emit to send an event. Listeners call hub.on with an event type to sign up. The hub usually lives inside the same program. It runs handlers right away, one after another. This is unlike a pub-sub broker (a separate message service) on a network. It also gives one place to add filtering, ordering or recording.

## In a large company

Company harnesses use an in-process event hub as the one place to attach three things. These are audit logging, OpenTelemetry span events (records in a standard format for tracing what software does) and cost metering. So every tool call and approval is recorded without changing each part. A forwarder on the hub sends chosen events to the platform's central stream, such as Kafka or EventBridge. From there they feed the SIEM (the security team's log monitoring system) and analytics. Keep handlers isolated, so an error in one listener cannot stop the emit or block the audit handler. Redact event data (remove secrets and personal data) before it leaves the process.

## Step by step

1. At startup, listeners sign up handlers with the hub by event type.
1. Parts of the harness send events to the hub as things happen.
1. The hub looks up the handlers for that event type.
1. It calls each handler in the order they signed up.

## Code sketch

```python
class EventHub:
    def __init__(self):
        self.handlers = defaultdict(list)
    def on(self, kind, fn):
        self.handlers[kind].append(fn)
    def emit(self, kind, **data):
        for fn in self.handlers[kind]:
            fn(**data)

hub.on('tool.done', cost_meter.add)
tool_runner.hub = subagents.hub = hub
```

## Be careful

When everything talks only to the hub, it gets hard to see who reacts to what. So keep an automatically generated list of event types and their handlers.

## Diagram

![Fig. 5.11: Sources and listeners each know one object, the hub, instead of each other.](/diagrams/event-aggregator.svg)

---

---
id: data-bus
number: "5.12"
title: Data Bus
chapter: multi-agent
fit: direct
figure_number: Fig. 5.12
figure_caption: "Every message reaches every member, and each member does its own filtering."
diagram: data-bus.svg
analogy_title: The site radio channel
---
## Gist

Connect every agent to one shared bus that carries all messages, and let each member decide which messages to act on.

## Everyday comparison

### The site radio channel

On a building site everyone carries a walkie-talkie tuned to one channel. The crane driver says a load is swinging over the east side. The scaffolders hear it, the electricians hear it, and so does the tea van. Each person decides whether the message concerns them. Nobody keeps a list of who should be told.

## Classic meaning

Parts of a system attach to a shared bus (a common channel) and post messages onto it. Every attached member sees every message and filters for itself.

## In the agent system

A small team of agents can share one bus inside the program. The planner, coder, tester, a UI panel and the transcript writer all attach to it. Every message (plan.updated, file.saved, tests.failed) goes onto the bus and reaches all members. Each member checks the message type and ignores what it does not handle. There is no routing table. That keeps things simple while the team is small and there are few messages. The bus is also one single place to record every message into the transcript for replay.

## In a large company

The main company objection is that a broadcast bus breaks least privilege (giving each part only the access it needs). Every member sees every message and any tenant data in it, including UI panels and third-party plugins. A tenant is one customer company sharing the platform. So platforms limit a data bus to one session in one process. Traffic between sessions or between tenants moves to topic-based brokers with ACLs (access lists). When a bus is used, recording every message to the transcript gives a full audit and replay log. But that log must follow the same retention rules (how long data is kept) and redaction rules (removing secrets and personal data).

## Step by step

1. Each agent attaches to the bus when it starts.
1. An agent posts a typed message onto the bus.
1. The bus hands the message to every attached member.
1. Each member filters by message type and acts only on the ones it handles.

## Code sketch

```python
class DataBus:
    def __init__(self):
        self.members = []
    def attach(self, m):
        self.members.append(m)
    def post(self, msg):
        for m in self.members:
            m.receive(msg)

class Tester(Member):
    def receive(self, msg):
        if msg.type == 'file.saved':
            self.queue_tests(msg.path)
```

## Be careful

Every member receives every message, so the bus copes badly with growth. Once members ignore most of the traffic, move to topics or an event aggregator.

## Diagram

![Fig. 5.12: Every message reaches every member, and each member does its own filtering.](/diagrams/data-bus.svg)

---

---
id: polling-pub-sub
number: "5.13"
title: Polling Pub/Sub
chapter: multi-agent
fit: direct
review_id: rev-polling-pub-sub
figure_number: Fig. 5.13
figure_caption: Events wait in the store. The subscriber pulls whatever is newer than its cursor.
diagram: polling-pub-sub.svg
analogy_title: The post office box
---
## Gist

Publishers add events to a shared store, and each subscriber agent checks it on its own schedule using a saved cursor.

## Everyday comparison

### The post office box

Letters for you go into a numbered box at the post office. The postman never knocks on your door. You call in when it suits you, on the way to work or once a week. You take everything that arrived since your last visit. If you are away for two weeks, the letters simply wait.

## Classic meaning

Publishers write messages to a durable topic (one that is saved and survives crashes). Subscribers check from time to time and pull the messages that arrived after the last one they read.

## In the agent system

Some agents run as scheduled tasks or short sessions. They cannot keep a connection open for pushed messages. So the harness writes events to an append-only table or file (one where new items are only added at the end), with ids that keep going up. Each subscriber keeps a cursor, which is the id of the last event it handled. Each time it wakes up, it asks for events after that cursor. A subagent may have been asleep, crashed, or paused while waiting for user approval. It catches up on its next check. The cost is delay, up to the time between checks. There are also wasted calls when nothing has changed.

## In a large company

This is how many company agents read change feeds. A scheduled agent may read a transactional outbox table (a table of messages written in the same database step as the change). Or it may read a Kafka topic by consumer offset (its saved position). Or it may read a SaaS API's changes endpoint with a saved cursor. Cursors are stored per subscriber and per tenant (customer company) in a durable store. Handlers are idempotent, because at-least-once replay is normal. That means the same event may arrive more than once. How often to check is a cost decision. So platforms set it per tenant. They alert on consumer lag (how far behind a reader is) rather than on single failures.

## Step by step

1. A publisher adds an event with the next id in the sequence.
1. A subscriber wakes on its schedule and asks for events after its cursor.
1. It handles the returned events in order.
1. It saves the new cursor, so a restart picks up from the right place.

## Code sketch

```python
cursor = state.get('cursor', 0)
while True:
    events = store.read(topic='repo',
                        after=cursor)
    for ev in events:
        handle(ev)
        cursor = ev.id
    state.save('cursor', cursor)
    await sleep(POLL_SECONDS)
```

## Be careful

Save the cursor only after the events are handled successfully. Make handlers idempotent (safe to run twice with the same result), because a crash replays events. Do not trust raw database sequence ids as cursors. Transactions running at the same time can commit them out of order, so a reader may skip one.

## Diagram

![Fig. 5.13: Events wait in the store. The subscriber pulls whatever is newer than its cursor.](/diagrams/polling-pub-sub.svg)

---

---
id: microservices-messaging
number: "5.14"
title: Microservices Messaging
chapter: multi-agent
fit: direct
figure_number: Fig. 5.14
figure_caption: The sender only needs the channel to be up. Acknowledgements and the dead-letter queue stop messages from vanishing.
diagram: microservices-messaging.svg
analogy_title: "The department store's pneumatic tubes"
---
## Gist

Agent services talk through message channels, so a sender posts work and moves on without waiting for the receiver.

## Everyday comparison

### The department store's pneumatic tubes

A shop assistant rolls the cash and the receipt into a canister. She drops it into a tube and turns to the next customer. The canister shoots off to the counting house, which deals with it when it can. If the counting house is busy, canisters pile up in its basket. None are lost, and the shop floor never waits.

## Classic meaning

Services talk by sending messages over channels such as queues or streams, without waiting for a reply. So neither side needs the other to be running at the same moment.

## In the agent system

A research service and a writing service each run as their own agent deployment. A durable queue (one that saves messages so they survive a crash) called research.results connects them. The research agent sends a message with its findings and a correlation id (a tag that links related messages). Then it picks up its next job without waiting. The writer reads messages at its own pace. It acknowledges each one (confirms it is done) only after it has saved its draft. Messages that are not acknowledged are delivered again. A message that keeps failing moves to a dead-letter queue (a holding place for problem messages). A person or a repair agent can look at it there.

## In a large company

In company agent platforms, the channels are Kafka, RabbitMQ, SQS or Pub/Sub. The producer uses a transactional outbox (it writes the message in the same database step as its own change). So a message is sent only if its database write succeeds. Messages carry a correlation id, a tenant id (which customer company) and W3C trace context in headers. W3C trace context is a standard tag that links all the work in one request. Consumers drop duplicates using an idempotency key (a unique id that marks a repeat). Dead-letter queues have alerts and an owner. Messages are encrypted with keys managed by KMS (a key management service). They are kept no longer than the retention policy allows.

## Step by step

1. The producer agent sends a message with a correlation id to the channel.
1. The channel saves it durably, and the producer moves on.
1. The consumer receives the message, does the work and acknowledges it.
1. Unacknowledged messages are delivered again, and repeated failures go to a dead-letter queue.

## Code sketch

```python
# research service
chan.send('research.results',
    {'cid': job.id, 'findings': notes})

# writer service
for msg in chan.consume('research.results'):
    try:
        draft = write(msg.body['findings'])
        drafts.save(msg.body['cid'], draft)
        msg.ack()
    except Exception:
        msg.nack()   # redeliver, then DLQ
```

## Be careful

Channels deliver at least once, so a message may arrive twice. Consumers must cope with duplicates. For example, save each draft under its correlation id.

## Diagram

![Fig. 5.14: The sender only needs the channel to be up. Acknowledgements and the dead-letter queue stop messages from vanishing.](/diagrams/microservices-messaging.svg)

---

---
id: microservices-aggregator
number: "5.15"
title: Microservices Aggregator
chapter: multi-agent
fit: adapted
review_id: rev-microservices-aggregator
figure_number: Fig. 5.15
figure_caption: The user asks once and gets one answer. The aggregator hides the specialists and names any gaps.
diagram: microservices-aggregator.svg
analogy_title: "The travel agent's holiday folder"
---
## Gist

One aggregator calls several specialist subagents, then merges their partial outputs into a single answer for the user.

## Everyday comparison

### The travel agent's holiday folder

You ask for a week in Crete. The agent rings the airline for flights, the hotel for a room and the hire firm for a car. Then she hands you one folder with a single plan and a single price. You never hear the three phone calls. If no car was free, the folder says so on one line.

## Classic meaning

A service receives a request, calls several backend services and combines their replies into one answer. This is called API Composition, and it all happens inside one request. It is different from the message Aggregator in Enterprise Integration Patterns. That one collects related messages that arrive over time and sends one combined message when the set is complete.

## In the agent system

A user asks for a release readiness report. The aggregator agent sends focused requests to three subagents (helper agents). One reports test results, one writes the changelog and one runs a security scan. Each returns structured output that follows a schema (a fixed format) the aggregator set. The aggregator checks the parts against each other and removes duplicates. It flags conflicts, such as two subagents disagreeing about a version number. Then it writes one reply or artifact. The user and the chat UI talk to one endpoint. They never need to know how many subagents produced the answer.

## In a large company

In a company platform, this is the API Composition layer behind an API gateway (the single front door for requests). One endpoint signs the user in with SSO (single sign-on). It calls specialist agents or services using that user's delegated identity (acting on the user's behalf with the user's permissions). Then it returns one response. Each branch has its own timeout and circuit breaker (a switch that stops calling a failing service for a while). The reply marks missing sections clearly. So a report that matters for compliance is never quietly incomplete. The aggregator is also where the cost of each request is added up and charged to the tenant (customer company).

## Step by step

1. The user's request reaches the aggregator.
1. It sends a focused request to each specialist subagent.
1. Each subagent returns its part as structured output.
1. The aggregator merges and checks the parts and returns one answer, naming any missing part.

## Code sketch

```python
async def readiness(release):
    asks = {'tests': ask('tests', release),
            'log': ask('changelog', release),
            'scan': ask('security', release)}
    timed = [wait_for(a, 120)
             for a in asks.values()]
    res = await gather(*timed,
                       return_exceptions=True)
    parts = dict(zip(asks, res))
    missing = [k for k, v in parts.items()
               if isinstance(v, Exception)]
    ok = {k: v for k, v in parts.items()
          if k not in missing}
    return report(merge(ok), missing)
```

## Be careful

The aggregator is the only place where a partial failure is visible. So it must say which section is missing instead of hiding the gap.

## Diagram

![Fig. 5.15: The user asks once and gets one answer. The aggregator hides the specialists and names any gaps.](/diagrams/microservices-aggregator.svg)

---
id: saga
number: "5.16"
title: Saga
chapter: multi-agent
fit: adapted
review_id: rev-saga
figure_number: Fig. 5.16
figure_caption: Forward steps commit one by one. A failure runs the recorded compensations backwards.
diagram: saga.svg
analogy_title: Booking a wedding
---
## Gist

Run a multi-step job across agents as a chain of steps, each paired with an action that undoes it.

## Everyday comparison

### Booking a wedding

The couple books the venue, then the caterer, and pays a deposit each time. Then they try to book a band. No band is free that weekend, and there is no single undo button. So they ring the caterer to cancel, then the venue. Each one has its own cancellation terms. They work back through the bookings in reverse order.

## Classic meaning

A saga handles a business task that spans several services. It runs as a series of local steps, and each step commits (is made final) on its own. If one step fails, compensating steps undo the steps already done. There are two styles. In choreography, each service reacts to the event from the step before. In orchestration, a central orchestrator tells each service what to do.

## In the agent system

A release job uses three agents. A coder agent creates a branch. A database agent runs a migration (a change to the database structure) on staging. A deploy agent ships to staging. No single transaction can cover git, a database and a deploy tool at once. So each step commits on its own and registers a compensation, an action that undoes it. Here that means delete the branch, or run the down-migration. This is an orchestrated saga. One coordinator tells each agent what to do. It writes every finished step to a durable saga log (a record saved so it survives a crash). In a choreographed saga, by contrast, each agent reacts to the previous agent's event, and there is no central coordinator. When the deploy fails, the coordinator reads the log. A restarted copy of the coordinator can do this too. It runs each compensation in reverse order and retries each one until it succeeds. Then it reports the state the system was left in. Between steps, other users can see the half-finished state, because a saga gives no isolation.

## In a large company

Company teams build agent sagas on a durable orchestrator such as Temporal or AWS Step Functions (systems that save each step so work survives a crash). Or they use choreography over Kafka or EventBridge events, when separate teams own the participants. Every step and compensation carries an idempotency key (a unique id that makes a repeat safe). The saga log is the audit record of what changed and what was undone. Some compensations cannot run automatically. These go to a human approval queue. Change-management policy often requires one more rule. Any agent step that touches production must have a tested compensation before it is allowed into the job.

## Step by step

1. The coordinator runs step 1 and records it, with its compensation, in the saga log.
1. It continues step by step, recording each success.
1. A step fails, and the coordinator stops moving forward.
1. It runs the compensations of the finished steps in reverse order and logs the outcome.

## Code sketch

```python
steps = [(create_branch, delete_branch),
         (migrate_db, migrate_down),
         (deploy, None)]  # last: no undo
for i, (act, undo) in enumerate(steps):
    try:
        act(ctx, key=f'{sid}:{i}')
        log.mark(sid, i, 'done')  # durable
    except StepFailed:
        for j in reversed(log.done(sid)):
            comp = steps[j][1]
            if comp:  # idempotent, retried
                retry_until_ok(comp, ctx)
        raise
```

## Be careful

A compensation is a new forward action. It cannot unsend an email. So plan a correction step for any effect that cannot be reversed.

## Diagram

![Fig. 5.16: Forward steps commit one by one. A failure runs the recorded compensations backwards.](/diagrams/saga.svg)

---

---
id: commander
number: "5.17"
title: Commander
chapter: multi-agent
fit: adapted
review_id: rev-commander
figure_number: Fig. 5.17
figure_caption: "The commander keeps retrying and logging until every step is done, without rolling back."
diagram: commander.svg
analogy_title: "The stage manager's cue calls"
---
## Gist

A commander agent pushes a multi-service job through to the end, retrying failed steps from a saved log until all succeed.

## Everyday comparison

### The stage manager's cue calls

During the show, the stage manager calls each cue over the headset: 'lights twelve, go'. Then she waits to hear 'lights done'. If the sound desk does not answer, she calls again, and keeps calling until it does. She ticks every confirmed cue in the prompt book. So if she is replaced at the interval, her deputy knows exactly where the show is.

## Classic meaning

A coordinator manages a job that spans several services. It tracks the state of each step and retries failures, waiting longer each time (backoff). It records progress so it can pick up again after a crash.

## In the agent system

Publishing a release takes three steps. Push a tag to the repository service, upload a package to a registry, and post release notes through a messaging connector. Unlike a saga, the commander aims to finish rather than undo. Say the registry returns a 503 (a 'service unavailable' error). The commander schedules that step to try again later with backoff, and it keeps the tag. It writes each step's state to a durable transaction log (a record saved so it survives a crash). So if the harness restarts, it picks up the half-finished job. A step that uses up its retries goes to a person through the approval UI.

## In a large company

In company platforms, the commander is usually a durable workflow engine such as Temporal or Step Functions. Its retry rules, timeouts and saved history act as the transaction log directly. Every call carries an idempotency key. So retries after a 429 (too many requests), a 503 or a timeout cannot publish twice. Errors that retrying cannot fix go straight to a human approval or incident queue. Runbooks (written procedures for operators) say who owns a job that has been sent to a person. The saved log also serves as audit evidence for change management.

## Step by step

1. The commander records a new job and its steps as pending.
1. It calls each service in turn and records every success.
1. A failed step is tried again later with backoff.
1. Retries go on until every step succeeds, or a step goes to a person after its retry limit.

## Code sketch

```python
txn = log.resume_or_begin(tid, STEPS)
for step in txn.pending():
    key = f'{tid}:{step}'  # idempotency
    for n in range(MAX_TRIES):
        r = call(step, txn.data, key=key)
        if r.ok:
            log.mark(txn, step, 'done')
            break
        if not r.retryable:  # e.g. 400
            break
        await sleep(r.retry_after
                    or backoff(n))
    if not txn.is_done(step):
        return escalate(txn, step)
```

## Be careful

Retrying until success is safe only for idempotent steps (safe to run twice with the same result). So give every call an idempotency key (a unique id that marks a repeat). Otherwise a retry may publish the package twice.

## Diagram

![Fig. 5.17: The commander keeps retrying and logging until every step is done, without rolling back.](/diagrams/commander.svg)

---

---
id: distributed-tracing
number: "5.18"
title: Distributed Tracing
chapter: multi-agent
fit: direct
review_id: rev-distributed-tracing
figure_number: Fig. 5.18
figure_caption: "The same trace id rides along every hop, so every span lands in one tree."
diagram: distributed-tracing.svg
analogy_title: The parcel tracking number
---
## Gist

Carry one trace id through the orchestrator, subagents, tool calls and model calls, so a whole run reads as one tree.

## Everyday comparison

### The parcel tracking number

Your parcel gets one number at the counter. Every depot, van and sorting belt that touches it scans the number and adds a line with a time and a place. When the parcel is late, you type the number in once. You see the whole journey, including the six hours it sat in a depot nobody suspected.

## Classic meaning

Every request carries a trace context (a shared id and a parent link) from service to service. Each piece of work records a span, a timed record that names its parent. The spans join up into one end-to-end trace.

## In the agent system

When a user message starts a run, the harness creates a trace id. It also opens a root span (the top record in the tree) for the orchestrator's turn. The orchestrator is the agent in charge. When it starts a subagent (helper agent), it passes the trace id and parent span id in the task envelope. Inside the subagent, every model call and tool call opens a child span. Each records timing, token counts and status. MCP requests carry the same context in their metadata (MCP is a standard way to connect tools to an AI model). So remote servers can add their spans too. A collector joins the spans into a tree. The tree shows which subagent spent the tokens, or which tool call held up the run.

## In a large company

Company platforms measure agents with OpenTelemetry (a standard for recording what software does) and its GenAI semantic conventions (agreed names for AI-related data). They pass the W3C traceparent header (the standard trace tag) through task envelopes, HTTP headers and MCP _meta fields. Spans go through an OpenTelemetry Collector to the tracing backend. Spans carry tenant (customer company), user and cost details. So traces support chargeback (billing each team for its use) and SLOs (reliability targets) per tenant. Prompt and reply content stays off by default. When it is turned on, it is redacted (secrets and personal data removed) and kept for a shorter time. Sampling keeps every error and slow trace but only some routine runs, to control storage cost.

## Step by step

1. The harness creates a trace id and a root span when the run starts.
1. Every subagent start, model call and tool call opens a child span with the trace id and its parent's span id.
1. Each span records timing, tokens and status when it closes.
1. A collector joins all spans with the same trace id into one tree.

## Code sketch

```python
with tracer.span('invoke_agent orch') as root:
    sub = spawn('researcher', task,
                trace=root.context)

# inside the subagent's harness
with tracer.span('invoke_agent researcher',
                 parent=task.trace) as s:
    with tracer.span('chat', parent=s):
        r = client.messages.create(**req)
    with tracer.span('execute_tool search',
                     parent=s):
        run_tool(block)
```

## Be careful

Spans that store full prompts and tool outputs copy secrets into the monitoring store. So by default, record only sizes and hashes (short fingerprints). Record full content only when someone turns it on.

## Diagram

![Fig. 5.18: The same trace id rides along every hop, so every span lands in one tree.](/diagrams/distributed-tracing.svg)

---
id: log-aggregation
number: "5.19"
title: Log Aggregation
chapter: multi-agent
fit: direct
figure_number: Fig. 5.19
figure_caption: Scattered logs on each machine become one searchable record keyed by run id.
diagram: log-aggregation.svg
analogy_title: The hospital records office
---
## Gist

Send logs from every agent run, subagent and MCP server to one central store, indexed by run id, for search and alerts.

## Everyday comparison

### The hospital records office

Every department writes its own notes on the patient: the emergency room, the X-ray suite, the surgical ward. When the patient goes home, all those sheets go to the records office. They are filed under one hospital number. Months later, a doctor asks for that number and reads the whole stay in date order.

## Classic meaning

Services send their logs to a central logging service. It stores and indexes them, so operators can search all of them in one place.

## In the agent system

A busy harness runs hundreds of agent sessions across many worker machines. Each session's subagents, sandboxes (sealed-off places to run code) and MCP servers write their own logs. MCP is a standard way to connect tools to an AI model. A shipper on each machine forwards structured JSON log lines to a central log store. It adds the run id, agent name, machine name and time. Operators search one place for every error from a given tool. Evals (automated quality tests) and alert rules query the same data. For example, they can watch for a rising rate of permission denials. Without aggregation, debugging a failed run starts with working out which machine each subagent happened to run on.

## In a large company

Companies send structured agent logs through OpenTelemetry Collector, Fluent Bit or Vector (tools that collect and forward logs). The logs go into Elasticsearch or OpenSearch, Splunk, Loki or a cloud logging service. Every line carries a trace_id and span_id, so logs can be joined to traces (records of one request's full path). Indexes or access rules are split by tenant (customer company). Security events such as approvals, permission denials and tool calls also go to the SIEM (the security team's log monitoring system). There they are kept longer, in a tamper-evident way (any change can be detected). Secrets and PII (personal data such as names and emails) are removed at the shipper, before data leaves the machine or region.

## Step by step

1. Every part writes structured log lines tagged with the run id.
1. A shipper on each machine forwards the lines to the central store.
1. The store indexes them by run id, part, level and time.
1. People and alert rules search across all runs from one place.

## Code sketch

```python
log = logger.bind(run_id=run.id,
                  agent='researcher')
log.info('tool.start', tool='web_search')
log.warn('permission.denied', path=p)

# central query across all runs
store.query('level:warn AND'
            ' event:permission.denied'
            ' | count by agent')
```

## Be careful

Agent logs grow quickly and often hold user data. So set limits on how long logs are kept, and remove secrets before the lines leave the machine.

## Diagram

![Fig. 5.19: Scattered logs on each machine become one searchable record keyed by run id.](/diagrams/log-aggregation.svg)

id: self-registration
number: "5.20"
title: Self-Registration
chapter: multi-agent
fit: direct
review_id: rev-self-registration
figure_number: Fig. 5.20
figure_caption: The service announces itself and keeps its entry alive. Silence gets it removed.
diagram: self-registration.svg
analogy_title: Signing in with the market warden
---
## Gist

Each agent service or MCP server tells a registry its name, address and tools at startup, and keeps renewing that entry.

## Everyday comparison

### Signing in with the market warden

Stallholders at a street market arrive at dawn and sign the warden's book with their pitch number, name and what they sell. Shoppers ask the warden where to find cheese. Traders wave at the warden's hut every few hours. Anyone not seen by noon is crossed off, so shoppers are never sent to an empty pitch.

## Classic meaning

A running copy of a service signs itself up with the service registry (a directory of live services) when it starts. It renews its entry with heartbeats (regular 'still alive' signals) and removes itself when it shuts down.

## In the agent system

An MCP server (MCP is a standard way to connect tools to an AI model) or a specialist agent service starts up. It calls the harness registry with its name, endpoint (address) and tool list, such as search_issues and create_issue. It also gives a TTL (a time limit after which the entry expires). It sends a heartbeat before the TTL runs out. On a clean shutdown it removes its entry. Orchestrators (the agents in charge) ask the registry which tools or agents to offer the model on the next turn. The registry removes entries whose heartbeats stop. So a crashed server drops out of the tool list instead of causing failed tool calls.

## In a large company

Self-registration suits internal agent services that hold a workload identity (login details issued to the program itself). Examples are a SPIFFE ID or a cloud service account. The registry checks that identity on every registration and heartbeat. Many companies prefer third-party registration instead. In that setup, the platform registers the running copies. This can be Kubernetes with its service endpoints, or a registrar that watches deployments. Then a hacked or badly set up service cannot advertise itself. Either way, the tool catalog shown to models is filtered by an allowlist and by RBAC (role-based access control: permissions given by job role) for each tenant (customer company). Every change to a registration is audited.

## Step by step

1. The service starts and registers its name, endpoint and tool list with a TTL.
1. It sends heartbeats to renew the entry.
1. Orchestrators ask the registry what is live and available.
1. If heartbeats stop, the registry removes the entry.

## Code sketch

```python
async def main():
    srv = McpServer('issues', tools)
    await registry.register(
        name='issues', url=srv.url,
        tools=[t.name for t in tools], ttl=30)
    try:
        async with every(10, registry.renew,
                         'issues'):
            await srv.serve()
    finally:
        await registry.deregister('issues')
```

## Be careful

A registry entry is only a claim. So the registry must authenticate (check the identity of) every service that registers. Accept only servers on an allowlist. Then check that the server's live tool schemas (the formats of its tools) match what it registered, before showing them to the model.

## Diagram

![Fig. 5.20: The service announces itself and keeps its entry alive. Silence gets it removed.](/diagrams/self-registration.svg)

---

---
id: service-locator
number: "5.21"
title: Service Locator
chapter: multi-agent
fit: direct
figure_number: Fig. 5.21
figure_caption: Callers know only a name. The locator decides which live connector answers to it.
diagram: service-locator.svg
analogy_title: Ringing directory enquiries
---
## Gist

Code asks a central locator for a connector or agent by name while running, instead of having each one handed in.

## Everyday comparison

### Ringing directory enquiries

You need a plumber in a town you have never visited. You ring directory enquiries and give a name, and the operator reads you a number. You do not need every phone book in the country. If the plumber moves, the operator gives you the new number next time.

## Classic meaning

A service locator is a central registry object. Code calls it to get a service by name. It hides how the service is made or found.

## In the agent system

Skills and subagent code often need a connector they did not create. Examples are the web search MCP client, the issue tracker or a reviewer subagent. MCP is a standard way to connect tools to an AI model. The code calls locator.get('issues'). The locator returns a live client from its cache. If there is none, it builds one using the factory (a function that makes the client) registered under that name. So a skill written once can run in harnesses with different connectors installed, as long as the names match. The cost is hidden dependencies. You cannot tell which connectors a piece of code needs until it runs.

## In a large company

In a harness shared by many tenants (customer companies), the locator must find clients per tenant and per user. It looks them up by name plus identity. It fetches credentials from Vault or a cloud secrets manager (safe stores for passwords and keys) when it builds the client. Otherwise a cached client built with one tenant's token could serve another tenant. The name table usually comes from a connector catalog that an admin has approved. So a skill can only get connectors that policy allows for that tenant. Lookups are logged. This gives auditors a record of which connectors each skill actually used.

## Step by step

1. At startup the harness registers a factory for each name in the locator.
1. Code calls get(name) when it needs a connector or agent.
1. The locator returns a cached client or builds one from the factory.
1. An unknown name raises a clear error that the harness reports back to the model.

## Code sketch

```python
class Locator:
    def __init__(self, table):
        self.table, self.live = table, {}
    def get(self, name):
        if name not in self.live:
            make = self.table[name]
            self.live[name] = make()
        return self.live[name]

issues = locator.get('issues')
```

## Be careful

A locator hides what code depends on. So in the harness core, prefer explicit injection (passing each dependency in directly). Keep the locator for plugins and skills that load while the harness runs.

## Diagram

![Fig. 5.21: Callers know only a name. The locator decides which live connector answers to it.](/diagrams/service-locator.svg)
