---
id: promise
number: "6.01"
title: Promise
chapter: async
fit: direct
review_id: rev-promise
figure_number: Fig. 6.01
figure_caption: The caller gets a handle at once and the result later.
diagram: promise.svg
analogy_title: The buzzer at a food court
---
## Gist

Give back a placeholder for a result that will arrive later, so the caller keeps working instead of waiting.

## Everyday comparison

### The buzzer at a food court

You order, pay, and get a plastic buzzer. You do not stand at the counter. You find a seat and talk. When the food is ready, the buzzer goes off and you collect it. If the kitchen runs out, the buzzer flashes a different light. Then you go back to sort it out.

## Classic meaning

A promise is an object that stands for the future result of work running in the background (asynchronous work). The caller can wait for it or attach next steps to it.

## In the agent system

The main agent can launch a subagent (a helper agent that does one task) to run in the background. When it does, the harness at once returns a handle, which is an agent id, not the finished report. The orchestrator (the main agent that hands out work) keeps planning or answering the user. When the subagent finishes, the harness resolves the handle, which means it fills the handle with the result. It then adds a notice into the conversation. If the subagent fails, the harness rejects the handle with an error. The orchestrator can then deal with that error.

## In a large company

In an enterprise harness, long subagents and batch jobs return a durable job id. This id survives process restarts. It is stored in a database or in a durable execution engine such as Temporal (a system that keeps long tasks running through crashes). It is not kept as an in-memory future, which a restart would lose. The handle carries the tenant (one customer company sharing the platform) and the user's identity. So only the owner can check on it or cancel it. Every handle needs a deadline and a cost limit. Then abandoned work does not keep spending tokens (the units that model use is measured and billed in). Pass the OpenTelemetry trace context into the subagent. OpenTelemetry is a standard for tracing requests across systems. This links the final result back to the request that started it.

## Step by step

1. The orchestrator calls spawn_agent and at once gets a pending handle.
1. It keeps doing other work while the subagent runs.
1. The subagent finishes, and the harness resolves the handle.
1. A completion notice arrives, and the orchestrator reads the result.

## Code sketch

```python
# returns at once with a pending handle
h = harness.spawn('researcher', task=q)
plan_next_steps()

# resolves when the subagent finishes
try:
    report = await h
except SubagentError as e:
    log.warn(e)
    report = None
```

## Be careful

Never invent or guess the value of a promise that has not resolved yet. If the user asks early, say the work is still running.

## Diagram

![Fig. 6.01: The caller gets a handle at once and the result later.](/diagrams/promise.svg)

---

---
id: async-method-invocation
number: "6.02"
title: Async Method Invocation
chapter: async
fit: direct
review_id: rev-async-method-invocation
figure_number: Fig. 6.02
figure_caption: "The invoker returns a task id now and delivers the result later, by polling or by callback."
diagram: async-method-invocation.svg
analogy_title: Dropping film at the photo lab
---
## Gist

Start a slow job, like a background subagent, get a future (a claim ticket for the result) at once, and collect the result later.

## Everyday comparison

### Dropping film at the photo lab

You hand your roll of film over the counter. You get a numbered claim stub. You do not stand there while the prints develop. You go and do your shopping. Later you come back with the stub and ask if they are ready. Or the lab phones the number on the stub. The stub is the only link between you and the job.

## Classic meaning

A method runs on another thread (a separate line of work). The caller gets a future or a callback hook right away while the work goes on.

## In the agent system

A subagent is a helper agent that the main agent starts for a task. Say the model calls a tool like run_in_background, or starts a background subagent. The harness hands the job to an executor (the part that runs jobs). It puts a task id in the tool_result straight away. A tool_result is the message that carries a tool's answer back to the model. The model reads that result on its next step. It then goes on with other tool calls while the job runs. Later it has three ways to get the result. It can poll (ask again and again) a status tool with the id. It can await the future, which means wait for it to finish. Or a completion callback can add the result to the transcript as a new message. The transcript is the saved record of the conversation. The invoker (the part that started the job) owns the job and records it against the session. So it can cancel the job and enforce a timeout. It can also refuse status requests for task ids that belong to another session.

## In a large company

Enterprise platforms run background agent jobs on a durable engine, one that survives crashes and restarts. Examples are Temporal or a fleet of workers fed by a queue. They do this because an in-process future dies with the pod (the small server unit that runs the code) during a deploy. The task id acts as a capability, a token that grants access by itself. So status and cancel calls must check that the caller's tenant (customer company) and session own it. Otherwise one user can read another user's results. Every job carries a deadline and a token budget charged to the tenant. It also carries trace context, so the background span (one timed step in a trace) links to the turn that started it.

## Step by step

1. The model calls run_in_background with a task description.
1. The invoker hands the job to an executor and returns a task id at once.
1. The model makes other tool calls while the job runs.
1. It polls the status tool, or a done-callback adds the result to the transcript.

## Code sketch

```python
fut = executor.submit(run_subagent, task)
jobs[(session.id, fut.id)] = fut
return {'task_id': fut.id}

# later: look up by id within this session
fut = jobs[(session.id, task_id)]
if fut.done():
    report = fut.result()
else:
    fut.add_done_callback(inject_result)
```

## Be careful

A background job that nobody waits for or cancels leaks, which means it keeps using resources. Track every future per session. When the session ends, cancel or report any jobs still running.

## Diagram

![Fig. 6.02: The invoker returns a task id now and delivers the result later, by polling or by callback.](/diagrams/async-method-invocation.svg)

---

---
id: event-based-asynchronous
number: "6.03"
title: Event-Based Asynchronous
chapter: async
fit: adapted
review_id: rev-event-based-asynchronous
figure_number: Fig. 6.03
figure_caption: One running job raises separate events that different subscribers act on.
diagram: event-based-asynchronous.svg
analogy_title: The pharmacy text alerts
---
## Gist

Show a long job as events (start, progress, completed, failed, cancel), so the UI and agent loop react as things happen.

## Everyday comparison

### The pharmacy text alerts

You drop off a prescription and leave your phone number. A text comes when they start making it up. Another comes if an item is out of stock. A last one comes when it is ready to collect. If you no longer need it, you reply STOP. You never stand at the counter asking if it is done yet.

## Classic meaning

A MethodAsync call returns at once. It then raises ProgressChanged and Completed events on the caller's own thread or loop. It can also support cancelling.

## In the agent system

Some jobs run a long time, like a background subagent, a long build or a scheduled task. Each one publishes lifecycle events: started, progress, completed, failed, cancelled. An event is a short message that says something happened. The chat UI subscribes to (signs up for) progress events to update a task card. The agent loop is the cycle that calls the model and runs its tools. It subscribes to completed and failed events. Then it can add a task-notification message to the conversation. Cancelling goes the other way, as a cancel request on the same task id. The runner raises events back on the session's own event loop. That is the single loop that handles the session's work. So handlers never touch session state from a worker thread.

## In a large company

In production, the lifecycle events go onto a durable stream such as Kafka or EventBridge. A durable stream is a stored log of messages that survives crashes. Each event is keyed by task id. So a client that reconnects can replay the latest state instead of missing it. Failed events often carry stack traces or raw tool output. So remove secrets and PII (personal data such as names and emails) before an error message enters the transcript or a notification. Cancelling is cooperative, which means the job must notice the request and stop itself. Record each cancel in the audit log. Side effects already in flight must either finish idempotently (safe to run twice with the same result) or be compensated (undone by a reversing action).

## Step by step

1. The caller registers its handlers, then starts the job with run_async and gets a task id.
1. The worker raises progress events as it goes.
1. When it finishes, it raises completed with the result, or failed with the error.
1. Handlers on the session loop update the task card and tell the model.

## Code sketch

```python
task = runner.create(job, task_id='t42')
task.on('progress', ui.update_card)
task.on('completed', lambda r:
        transcript.notify(f'done: {r}'))
task.on('failed', lambda e:
        transcript.notify(f'failed: {e}'))
task.run_async()     # subscribe first

# user presses Stop on the task card
task.cancel_async()
```

## Be careful

Each event fires only once. A handler registered after completed has fired misses the result. So subscribe before you start the job, or let late subscribers read the last state.

## Diagram

![Fig. 6.03: One running job raises separate events that different subscribers act on.](/diagrams/event-based-asynchronous.svg)

---

---
id: producer-consumer
number: "6.04"
title: Producer-Consumer
chapter: async
fit: direct
review_id: rev-producer-consumer
figure_number: Fig. 6.04
figure_caption: "Producers and consumers never meet, and the bounded buffer sets the pace for both."
diagram: producer-consumer.svg
analogy_title: The bakery cooling rack
---
## Gist

Many sources put agent jobs into a bounded (size-limited) buffer, and a separate set of workers takes them off at its own pace.

## Everyday comparison

### The bakery cooling rack

Bakers slide fresh trays onto a tall cooling rack. Shop staff lift trays off the other side to stock the counter. Nobody hands bread from person to person. When every shelf is full, the bakers wait. When the rack is empty, the staff wait. The number of shelves decides how far ahead the ovens can run.

## Classic meaning

Producers and consumers share a bounded buffer instead of talking directly. Producers wait when it is full, and consumers wait when it is empty.

## In the agent system

Agent jobs come from many places. Webhook handlers produce them. A webhook handler is code that runs when another service sends an event. Scheduled tasks fired by cron (a timer) produce them. So do user messages from many sessions. These producers do not call the agent loop directly. Instead they put jobs on a bounded asyncio.Queue or a broker list. A bounded queue has a fixed maximum size. A broker is a separate service that holds messages. A fixed set of consumer workers take jobs off. Each one runs the model and tool calls, and stores the results. When the queue is full, producers wait or answer 429 (the HTTP code for 'too many requests'). This protects model rate limits and token budgets from sudden bursts.

## In a large company

Enterprise harnesses replace the in-memory queue with a durable broker such as Kafka, SQS or Pub/Sub. A durable broker keeps messages safe even if a server crashes. The worker acknowledges a job only after the turn is recorded. So if a worker crashes, the broker delivers its job again. A single shared queue lets one tenant's (customer company's) burst starve everyone else. So platforms use per-tenant queues or weighted fair scheduling. Each tenant also gets a concurrency cap, a limit on jobs running at once. The cap is tied to the tenant's model quota. Two numbers drive autoscaling and SLO alerts (alerts on reliability targets). They are the queue depth and the age of the oldest job.

## Step by step

1. Producers wrap incoming work as job messages.
1. They put jobs on a bounded queue, and wait if it is full.
1. Consumers take one job at a time, and wait if it is empty.
1. Each consumer runs the agent turn and records the result.

## Code sketch

```python
jobs = asyncio.Queue(maxsize=100)

async def on_webhook(evt):     # producer
    try:
        jobs.put_nowait(Job.from_event(evt))
    except asyncio.QueueFull:
        return 429             # shed load

async def worker():            # consumer
    while True:
        job = await jobs.get()
        try: await run_agent(job)
        finally: jobs.task_done()
```

## Be careful

An unbounded queue (one with no size limit) hides overload until memory runs out. Always set a size. Then decide whether producers wait, drop the job or reject it.

## Diagram

![Fig. 6.04: Producers and consumers never meet, and the bounded buffer sets the pace for both.](/diagrams/producer-consumer.svg)

---

---
id: event-queue
number: "6.05"
title: Event Queue
chapter: async
fit: direct
figure_number: Fig. 6.05
figure_caption: Events wait in the inbox until the loop reaches a turn boundary.
diagram: event-queue.svg
analogy_title: The radio request line
---
## Gist

Hold events that arrive mid-turn in a queue, so the agent loop handles them in order at a safe point.

## Everyday comparison

### The radio request line

Listeners phone in song requests while a track is playing. The producer writes each one on a card. The card goes to the back of a pile in the booth. The DJ never cuts a song off halfway. Between tracks, the DJ takes the next card from the front of the pile and plays it.

## Classic meaning

Sending an event and handling it happen at different times. The sender puts it in a queue, and the receiver empties the queue when it is ready.

## In the agent system

While the model streams a reply or a tool runs, other things keep happening. The user types a follow-up. A background subagent finishes. A file watcher fires. A scheduled trigger arrives. Handling each one at once would push it into the middle of the current turn. A turn is one round of model reply plus tool calls. That would corrupt the transcript (the saved record of the conversation). So the harness adds each event to a per-session event queue and returns. At the turn boundary, the agent loop drains (empties) the queue in arrival order. It turns the events into messages before the next model call.

## In a large company

Sometimes sessions can move between pods (the small server units that run the code). Then the per-session inbox lives in a durable store, or in a stream partition keyed by session id. A partition is one ordered slice of a stream. So events survive failover (a switch to a backup server) and stay in order. Events from webhooks, file watchers or other agents are untrusted input. So the loop should add them as clearly labelled notifications that say where they came from. It must never add them as if the user had typed them. Cap and merge events per session. Log dropped or merged events for audit.

## Step by step

1. A sender posts an event to the session queue and returns at once.
1. The current model call or tool call goes on undisturbed.
1. At the turn boundary, the loop drains queued events in arrival order.
1. Each event becomes a message in the context for the next model call.

## Code sketch

```python
inbox = collections.deque()

def post(event):        # any hook or thread
    inbox.append(event)

def at_turn_boundary(ctx):
    while inbox:
        ev = inbox.popleft()
        ctx.messages.append(ev.to_message())
```

## Be careful

Events may arrive faster than turns finish. Then merge or cap them, or the next prompt fills up with old notices.

## Diagram

![Fig. 6.05: Events wait in the inbox until the loop reaches a turn boundary.](/diagrams/event-queue.svg)

---

---
id: active-object
number: "6.06"
title: Active Object
chapter: async
fit: direct
figure_number: Fig. 6.06
figure_caption: "Callers only add requests, and the task's own thread does all the work."
diagram: active-object.svg
analogy_title: "The assistant's in-tray"
---
## Gist

Give a scheduled task its own thread and request queue, so callers add requests and get futures back.

## Everyday comparison

### The assistant's in-tray

You do not interrupt the executive assistant in the middle of a task. You drop a note in their in-tray and keep a carbon copy as your receipt. They take notes from the tray one at a time. They put each answer in the sender's pigeonhole. Their work always happens at their own desk, never at yours.

## Classic meaning

Calling a method and running it are kept apart. A proxy (a stand-in object) turns each call into a request on an activation queue. A scheduler runs each request on the object's own thread and fills in its future (a placeholder for the result).

## In the agent system

Take a scheduled task such as a daily inbox triage (sorting the inbox). It runs as an active object. It owns a session, a transcript and a single worker thread or asyncio task. Callers never touch that session directly. A caller may be the cron trigger (a timer), a Run now button or another agent. Each one calls a proxy method, run(prompt). The proxy wraps the call as a request and puts it on the task's activation queue. Then it returns a future, a placeholder for the result that fills in later. The task's scheduler takes requests in order. It runs each turn against the task's own session. Then it resolves (fills in) the matching future.

## In a large company

At platform scale, the active object becomes a durable single writer per session. Durable means it survives crashes. Single writer means only one owner changes the session. One example is a Temporal workflow per scheduled task. It receives Run now requests as signals (messages to a running workflow). It handles them one at a time. Each session is pinned to one owner by a lease (a time-limited lock) or a partition key. This stops two pods (server units) from running turns against the same transcript. The scheduled task runs under a service identity, an account for software rather than a person. That identity is limited to what its owner approved. The harness records who sent each request, for audit.

## Step by step

1. A caller calls proxy.run(prompt) and gets a future.
1. The proxy puts a method request on the activation queue.
1. The scheduler on the task's thread takes the next request.
1. The servant (the object that does the real work) runs the turn in its own session and resolves the future.

## Code sketch

```python
class ScheduledTask:          # proxy side
    def run(self, prompt):
        fut = Future()
        self.q.put((prompt, fut))
        return fut

    def _loop(self):          # own thread
        while True:
            prompt, fut = self.q.get()
            out = self.session.turn(prompt)
            fut.set_result(out)
```

## Be careful

Code running on the task's own thread must never call the task's proxy and wait on the future. It deadlocks (gets stuck forever), because the request waits in line behind itself.

## Diagram

![Fig. 6.06: Callers only add requests, and the task's own thread does all the work.](/diagrams/active-object.svg)

---

---
id: reactor
number: "6.07"
title: Reactor
chapter: async
fit: direct
figure_number: Fig. 6.07
figure_caption: "One wait covers every connection, and ready ones go to their handlers."
diagram: reactor.svg
analogy_title: The switchboard operator
---
## Gist

Run one event loop that waits on many streaming connections at once and sends each ready event to its handler.

## Everyday comparison

### The switchboard operator

One operator sits in front of a panel of sockets. They do not watch any single line. They wait for a lamp to light. When one does, they plug in the cord for that caller. They deal with it in seconds and turn back to the panel. Hundreds of lines share one pair of hands, because each job is short.

## Classic meaning

A single wait watches many handles (open connections or files) at once. Each event that arrives goes to a registered handler that must not block.

## In the agent system

A harness server holds thousands of open connections. Some are SSE streams from the model provider. SSE (Server-Sent Events) is a way to stream text over HTTP. Some are WebSocket links (two-way live connections) to chat clients. Some are stdio pipes (standard input and output) to local MCP servers. MCP is a standard way to connect tools to an AI model. A single asyncio event loop registers them all with the OS selector, such as epoll or kqueue. The selector is the operating system feature that reports which sockets have data. When a socket has bytes, the loop calls that connection's handler. The handler adds a token delta (a small piece of new text). Or it forwards text to the right client, or reads a JSON-RPC reply. JSON-RPC is the message format MCP uses. Handlers must return quickly. So CPU-heavy work, such as tokenising a large file, goes to a thread pool.

## In a large company

Enterprise harness gateways run several event-loop processes per host behind a load balancer. They use sticky routing for WebSocket and SSE sessions, which keeps each session on the same process. During deploys they drain connections gracefully, letting them finish before shutdown. Event-loop lag is a key health metric. It measures how late the loop is in handling events. It is exported through OpenTelemetry, a standard for traces and metrics. It matters because one blocking handler slows every tenant (customer company) on that loop. Per-tenant connection limits and idle timeouts protect shared hosts. They stop one customer's clients from using up all the file descriptors (the limited slots for open connections).

## Step by step

1. Each connection registers a handler with the event loop.
1. The loop blocks once in select or epoll across all handles.
1. For each ready handle, it calls the registered handler.
1. Handlers do one small non-blocking step and return to the loop.

## Code sketch

```python
sel = selectors.DefaultSelector()
sel.register(model_sse, READ, on_token)
sel.register(client_ws, READ, on_user_msg)
sel.register(mcp_pipe, READ, on_rpc_reply)

while running:
    for key, _ in sel.select():
        key.data(key.fileobj)   # dispatch
```

## Be careful

One blocking call inside a handler freezes every stream on the loop. A synchronous HTTP request, one that waits for its answer, is an example.

## Diagram

![Fig. 6.07: One wait covers every connection, and ready ones go to their handlers.](/diagrams/reactor.svg)

id: thread-pool-executor
number: "6.08"
title: Thread-Pool Executor
chapter: async
fit: direct
review_id: rev-thread-pool-executor
figure_number: Fig. 6.08
figure_caption: Work waits in a queue for a fixed set of reused workers instead of creating more threads.
diagram: thread-pool-executor.svg
analogy_title: The taxi rank
---
## Gist

Run tool calls or whole sessions on a fixed set of reusable workers, so extra load waits in a queue instead of creating endless threads.

## Everyday comparison

### The taxi rank

A rank has a fixed number of licensed cabs. Passengers join one queue at the stand. Each cab that pulls in takes whoever is at the front. On a busy night the queue grows. But the town never gets a hundred extra taxis clogging the streets. And no cab is built for one ride and then scrapped.

## Classic meaning

A pool of worker threads takes tasks from a shared queue. The threads are reused, and the pool caps how many tasks run at once.

## In the agent system

Sometimes the model returns several tool_use blocks in one turn. A tool_use block is the model's request to run one tool. The harness sends the independent, read-only ones to a ThreadPoolExecutor, with say max_workers=8. It runs calls that change shared state one at a time. Then it returns every result in the next user message as tool_result blocks. Each result is matched to its call by tool_use_id. A tool that fails becomes a tool_result with is_error set. is_error is a flag that marks the result as an error. So one bad call does not lose the results of the other calls. A server hosting many sessions uses the same idea at a larger scale. It runs N worker processes, each running one agent session at a time. Model request concurrency and sandbox count have their own separate limits. A sandbox is an isolated space where tools run.

## In a large company

Enterprise platforms size worker pools per tenant tier and per tool class. A tenant tier is a level of customer plan. They enforce caps again at the LLM gateway, the shared entry point for model calls. There the caps cover model concurrency and tokens per minute. Parallel tool runs are limited to independent read-only calls. Anything with side effects runs one at a time, behind the approval and audit path. Pool saturation (how full the pool is) and queue wait time are exported as metrics. They drive autoscaling. One example is a Kubernetes HorizontalPodAutoscaler on a custom metric. That is the Kubernetes feature that adds or removes servers based on load.

## Step by step

1. The harness creates a pool with a fixed number of workers.
1. Each tool_use block goes into the pool's queue as a task.
1. Free workers take tasks, and the rest wait in the queue.
1. The harness collects results by call id and builds the tool_result message.

## Code sketch

```python
pool = ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=8)

safe = [b for b in blocks if b.read_only]
futs = {pool.submit(run_tool, b): b.id
        for b in safe}
results = {}
for f in as_completed(futs):
    try: results[futs[f]] = f.result()
    except Exception as e:
        results[futs[f]] = tool_error(e)
for b in blocks:          # writes: one by one
    if not b.read_only:
        results[b.id] = run_tool(b)
reply = [results[b.id] for b in blocks]
```

## Be careful

Tasks that wait on each other inside one small pool can deadlock it, so all of them get stuck. Keep dependent steps out of the pool, or size the pool with care.

## Diagram

![Fig. 6.08: Work waits in a queue for a fixed set of reused workers instead of creating more threads.](/diagrams/thread-pool-executor.svg)

---

---
id: thread-specific-storage
number: "6.09"
title: Thread-Specific Storage
chapter: async
fit: adapted
review_id: rev-thread-specific-storage
figure_number: Fig. 6.09
figure_caption: "The same shared code reads a different slot, depending on which task runs it."
diagram: thread-specific-storage.svg
analogy_title: "Each cashier's own till drawer"
---
## Gist

Give each session its own slot for user id, budget and trace id, which shared code can read without passing it everywhere.

## Everyday comparison

### Each cashier's own till drawer

Six cashiers share one shop, one price list and one row of tills. Each logs in with their own key. The drawer that springs open is always theirs, with their own cash and takings. The screen in front of each cashier looks the same. The money is never mixed.

## Classic meaning

Code reads what looks like one global variable. But its value is private to the current thread or task.

## In the agent system

A harness server runs many sessions on one asyncio loop and a shared thread pool. Deep inside, a tool wrapper needs to know which session it serves. It needs the user id for permission checks. It also needs the token budget, the trace id and the sandbox path. A trace id is a label that links all the logs from one request. Passing all of these through every function would be messy. So the harness sets a contextvars.ContextVar at the start of each session task. A ContextVar is a Python variable whose value belongs to the current task. Any code running in that task can call session.get() and see its own values. This includes logging and the MCP client. It works even while another session's task takes turns on the same thread.

## In a large company

Enterprise harnesses keep tenant id, principal, roles and trace context in context variables. A tenant is one customer company. A principal is the user or service the action is for. OpenTelemetry's Python SDK also uses contextvars this way. OpenTelemetry is a standard for traces and metrics. So spans (timed steps) from shared code land under the right trace. Security decisions should fail closed when no context is set. Fail closed means deny when unsure. They must never fall back to a default tenant. Some context crosses a thread pool, process or queue boundary. That context must be passed explicitly. For example, put signed claims and W3C trace context on the job message. W3C trace context is a standard format for passing trace ids.

## Step by step

1. The server declares a ContextVar for session state.
1. Each session task sets it at the start with its own values.
1. Shared tool and logging code calls get() to read the current session.
1. The value goes away with the task, so nothing leaks to the next session.

## Code sketch

```python
session = ContextVar('session')

async def handle(req):
    session.set(Session(req.user, budget=5e4))
    await agent_loop(req)

def write_file(path, text):   # shared code
    s = session.get()
    s.sandbox.check(path)
```

## Be careful

The context follows asyncio tasks and asyncio.to_thread. It does not follow loop.run_in_executor or raw threads. Wrap those in copy_context().run. Otherwise the worker sees no session, or an old one.

## Diagram

![Fig. 6.09: The same shared code reads a different slot, depending on which task runs it.](/diagrams/thread-specific-storage.svg)

id: guarded-suspension
number: "6.10"
title: Guarded Suspension
chapter: async
fit: direct
review_id: rev-guarded-suspension
figure_number: Fig. 6.10
figure_caption: The tool call sleeps at the gate until the guard turns true.
diagram: guarded-suspension.svg
analogy_title: A train held at a red signal
---
## Gist

Pause an action until its condition is true, such as waiting for the user's approval before running a risky tool.

## Everyday comparison

### A train held at a red signal

A driver reaches a red signal and stops. They do not creep forward or guess. They wait. When the signaller clears the track ahead, the light turns green and the train moves off. If the light flickers, the driver checks it again before releasing the brake.

## Classic meaning

A method call is blocked until a guard condition becomes true. It waits on a condition variable (a signal that threads can wait for). It checks the condition again after each wake-up.

## In the agent system

Some tools need permission, such as sending an email or deleting files. When the model calls one, the harness records a pending approval. It then suspends (pauses) that tool call on a condition. The chat UI shows an approval card. The user clicks Allow or Deny. The UI handler sets the decision and notifies the waiting coroutine. A coroutine is a function that can pause and resume. It checks the guard again. Then it either runs the tool or returns a denial as the tool_result (the answer sent back to the model). A timeout turns a long silence into a denial. So the call never hangs forever.

## In a large company

In an enterprise platform, an approval can wait for hours. So the harness saves the pending call and frees the worker and the sandbox (the isolated space where tools run). It resumes when the decision comes in, through a durable mechanism that survives restarts. Examples are a Temporal signal or a Step Functions task token. The approval is tied to a hash (a fingerprint) of the exact tool name and arguments. So the agent cannot change the email after it was approved. The approver's identity is checked against RBAC (role-based access control: permissions given by job role). Separation of duties applies to high-risk actions, so the person who asks is not the one who approves. Every decision goes to the audit log, including timeouts.

## Step by step

1. The tool call reaches the gate while its decision is still unset.
1. The harness posts an approval card and waits on a condition.
1. The user's click sets the decision and wakes the waiter.
1. The call wakes, checks the guard again, and runs or returns a denial.

## Code sketch

```python
async def guarded_run(call, ttl=300):
    try:
        async with asyncio.timeout(ttl), cond:
            await cond.wait_for(
                lambda: call.decision)
    except TimeoutError:
        call.decision = 'deny'  # default deny
    if call.decision != 'allow':
        return denied(call)
    return await call.tool.run(call.args)
async def on_click(call, choice):   # UI
    async with cond:
        call.decision = choice
        cond.notify_all()
```

## Be careful

Always pair the wait with a timeout that denies by default. Otherwise a forgotten approval card holds a worker and a sandbox forever.

## Diagram

![Fig. 6.10: The tool call sleeps at the gate until the guard turns true.](/diagrams/guarded-suspension.svg)

---
id: balking
number: "6.11"
title: Balking
chapter: async
fit: direct
figure_number: Fig. 6.11
figure_caption: "A request that arrives mid-run is refused on the spot, not queued."
diagram: balking.svg
analogy_title: The lit lift button
---
## Gist

If an object is not in the right state, return at once instead of waiting, such as skipping a run already in progress.

## Everyday comparison

### The lit lift button

You reach the lift. The call button is already glowing, because someone pressed it a moment ago. Pressing it again changes nothing. The lift is already on its way. The button does not call a second lift or make you wait at the panel. It just ignores the extra press.

## Classic meaning

An action runs only if the object is in a suitable state. Otherwise the call returns at once and does nothing.

## In the agent system

A scheduled task fires every 15 minutes, but one run sometimes takes 20. Without care, the scheduler starts a second run on the same session while the first is still going. That doubles model spend. It also races on the transcript, with two runs writing at once. With balking, the trigger handler checks a running flag under a lock. If a run is in progress, it logs 'skipped: already running' and returns. The same check stops a double-click on Send from starting two turns. It also stops a second compaction while one is underway. Compaction is shrinking the conversation history by summarising it.

## In a large company

A harness may run as several replicas (copies on different hosts). Then an in-process flag only stops overlaps on one host. So scheduled runs take a distributed lease before starting. A lease is a lock that expires after a set time. Examples are a Postgres advisory lock or a database row with an expiry. Each skipped run is logged and counted as a metric. A job that balks every time is stuck, not busy. For user actions such as a double-clicked Send, use an idempotency key on the request. An idempotency key is a label that makes a repeat safe. It gives the same protection across retries and reconnects.

## Step by step

1. The trigger fires and calls start_run.
1. Under a lock, the handler checks whether a run is already active.
1. If one is, it logs a skip and returns at once.
1. Otherwise it marks the run active, starts it, and clears the flag when done.

## Code sketch

```python
def start_run(task):
    with task.lock:
        if task.running:
            log.info('balk: run in flight')
            return 'skipped'
        task.running = True
    try:
        execute(task)
    finally:
        task.running = False
```

## Be careful

Balking drops requests silently. So use it only when the skipped request is truly not needed. If every request matters, queue it instead.

## Diagram

![Fig. 6.11: A request that arrives mid-run is refused on the spot, not queued.](/diagrams/balking.svg)

id: poison-pill
number: "6.12"
title: Poison Pill
chapter: async
fit: direct
figure_number: Fig. 6.12
figure_caption: The stop signal travels through the queue behind the real work.
diagram: poison-pill.svg
analogy_title: The marathon sweep bus
---
## Gist

Shut down queue workers cleanly by sending a special stop message that each worker recognises and exits on.

## Everyday comparison

### The marathon sweep bus

Behind the last runner of a marathon drives the sweep bus. Volunteers at each water station keep handing out cups until it passes. When they see it, they know nobody else is coming. So they pack up the tables. Nobody phones the stations. The signal travels along the course in the same stream as the runners.

## Classic meaning

A sentinel (a special marker message) goes into a queue. Each consumer that reaches it finishes its current work and stops.

## In the agent system

Sometimes a harness host deploys a new version, or a batch eval (a large automated test run) finishes. It must then stop its agent workers without leaving turns half-done. The supervisor is the process that manages the workers. It stops taking new jobs. It then puts one STOP sentinel per worker on the job queue. Each worker finishes the job it holds. It also finishes the jobs ahead of the pill, in FIFO order (first in, first out). Then it leaves its loop when it takes STOP. The supervisor joins the workers, which means it waits for each to finish. Then it saves transcripts and closes MCP connections (links to tool servers).

## In a large company

Pills only work on an in-process queue. On a shared broker such as Kafka or SQS, another replica's worker would take the pill. A broker is a separate service that holds messages. So hosts do something else instead. They stop polling for jobs when they get SIGTERM, the signal that tells a process to shut down. They finish or checkpoint (save progress on) the current turn. Then the broker delivers anything not yet acknowledged again. Agent turns can last longer than a Kubernetes termination grace period, the time a pod gets to shut down. So long work should checkpoint into durable execution and resume on another host. Durable execution keeps work going through crashes and restarts. Do not confuse a poison pill with a poison message. A poison message is a malformed job that crashes consumers again and again. It belongs in a dead-letter queue, a holding place for messages that cannot be handled.

## Step by step

1. The supervisor stops taking new jobs.
1. It adds one STOP sentinel per worker behind the remaining jobs.
1. Workers handle the jobs ahead of the pill as usual.
1. Each worker that takes STOP exits, and the supervisor joins them and cleans up.

## Code sketch

```python
STOP = object()

def shutdown(q, workers):
    for _ in workers:
        q.put(STOP)       # one pill each
    for w in workers:
        w.join()

def worker(q):
    while (job := q.get()) is not STOP:
        run_agent_turn(job)
```

## Be careful

Send exactly one pill per consumer, and never let a worker put it back on the queue. A missing pill leaves a worker stuck on get() forever.

## Diagram

![Fig. 6.12: The stop signal travels through the queue behind the real work.](/diagrams/poison-pill.svg)

---
id: half-sync-half-async
number: "6.13"
title: Half-Sync/Half-Async
chapter: async
fit: adapted
review_id: rev-half-sync-half-async
figure_number: Fig. 6.13
figure_caption: "Blocking code above, non-blocking code below, and a queue in between."
diagram: half-sync-half-async.svg
analogy_title: The clinic desk and the lab
---
## Gist

Let clients use simple blocking calls while the backend runs model streams and tool calls asynchronously, joined by a queue.

## Everyday comparison

### The clinic desk and the lab

At the clinic desk you hand over a blood sample and fill in a form. Patients are seen one at a time, in plain step-by-step order. The sample goes into a rack. Behind the wall, machines test hundreds of samples at once, in whatever order suits them. Results come back through the rack to the desk. The desk reads yours out to you.

## Classic meaning

Concurrent work is split into three layers. A synchronous layer keeps code simple. An asynchronous layer handles I/O (input and output) efficiently. A queue sits between them.

## In the agent system

An SDK or CLI offers a blocking call: result = agent.run(prompt). A blocking call waits until the answer is ready. It is easy to script and test. Underneath, the harness runs an asyncio backend. It is asynchronous, meaning it handles many things at once without waiting on each one. It streams from the model, starts many tool calls at once and juggles many sessions. A thread-safe bridge sits between the two sides. The sync side schedules a request on the event loop. Then it waits on a reply future (a placeholder for the answer). The async side picks up the request, does the concurrent work and fills in the future. Neither side has to adopt the other's style of programming.

## In a large company

Enterprise deployments usually put an async gateway in front. It accepts WebSocket, webhook and SSE traffic on an event loop. These are kinds of live or pushed web connections. It hands jobs through a queue to synchronous worker processes. These run tools and sandboxes with plain blocking code. The queue in the middle is where the platform enforces backpressure, per-tenant quotas and deadlines. Backpressure means slowing down senders when the system is full. A tenant is one customer company sharing the platform. Timeouts on the sync side must cancel the async work. Otherwise abandoned requests keep spending the tenant's token budget.

## Step by step

1. The sync layer gets a call and places a request on the bridge.
1. It blocks on the reply future for that request.
1. The event loop takes the request and runs model streams and tool calls at the same time.
1. It fills in the future, and the sync caller wakes with a plain return value.

## Code sketch

```python
# sync half: simple and blocking
def run(prompt):
    fut = asyncio.run_coroutine_threadsafe(
        backend_run(prompt), loop)
    try: return fut.result(timeout=600)
    finally: fut.cancel()   # no-op if done

# async half: one loop, many sessions
async def backend_run(prompt):
    async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:
        async for ev in model.stream(prompt):
            if ev.tool_use:
                tg.create_task(run_tool(ev))
```

## Be careful

Never call the blocking API from inside the async layer. It would block the event loop while waiting for work that only that same loop can do.

## Diagram

![Fig. 6.13: Blocking code above, non-blocking code below, and a queue in between.](/diagrams/half-sync-half-async.svg)

id: monitor
number: "6.14"
title: Monitor
chapter: async
fit: direct
figure_number: Fig. 6.14
figure_caption: "One caller is inside at a time, and waiters park in the wait set until notified."
diagram: monitor.svg
analogy_title: The rare-books reading room
---
## Gist

Wrap shared session state in an object whose methods run one at a time, with wait and notify for conditions.

## Everyday comparison

### The rare-books reading room

Only one reader may be in the rare-books room at a time. The attendant at the door makes sure of it. Say you go in, but the book you need is still away being repaired. You step out to the bench and wait. When the book comes back, the attendant calls the waiting readers. One goes back in to check again.

## Classic meaning

An object lets only one thread run its methods at a time, which is called mutual exclusion. It also has condition variables, so threads can wait inside it for the state to change.

## In the agent system

A session has shared state: the message list, the token count and pending tool calls. Several parts touch it, such as the stream reader, tool workers and the UI handler. Making it a monitor means every method takes the same lock. The methods include append, add_tokens and end_turn. So no caller ever sees half an update. Some methods need a condition to be true first. One is wait_idle, used before compaction (shrinking the history by summarising it). It waits on a condition variable inside the monitor. A notify call wakes it when the turn ends.

## In a large company

A monitor guards state inside one process. But several replicas (copies on different hosts) may touch a session. Then the same rule moves to the database as optimistic concurrency. With optimistic concurrency, each write checks a version column or ETag. The write fails if someone changed the record first. Another option is a single-writer owner per session. It is worth exporting lock wait and hold times as metrics. When callers fight over a session object's lock, users see a slow UI. Never make network calls, remote policy checks or model calls while holding the monitor.

## Step by step

1. Callers call methods on the SessionState monitor.
1. Each method enters by taking the monitor's single lock.
1. A method whose condition is false waits and lets go of the lock.
1. A state change calls notify, and a waiter enters again and re-checks.

## Code sketch

```python
class SessionState:            # a monitor
    def append(self, m):
        with self.cv:
            self.msgs.append(m)
    def end_turn(self):
        with self.cv:
            self.busy = False
            self.cv.notify_all()
    def wait_idle(self):
        with self.cv:
            self.cv.wait_for(self.idle)
```

## Be careful

Keep monitor methods short. Never call the model or a tool while holding the lock. Otherwise every other caller stalls behind the network.

## Diagram

![Fig. 6.14: One caller is inside at a time, and waiters park in the wait set until notified.](/diagrams/monitor.svg)

---

---
id: lockable-object
number: "6.15"
title: Lockable Object
chapter: async
fit: direct
review_id: rev-lockable-object
figure_number: Fig. 6.15
figure_caption: The holder keeps the lock across several steps while others are turned away.
diagram: lockable-object.svg
analogy_title: The community hall key
---
## Gist

Let a caller lock a session object across a change of several steps, so other writers wait or back off until it is released.

## Everyday comparison

### The community hall key

A group that books the village hall signs out its single key at the shop. They keep it all evening while they set up, use and tidy the hall. Anyone else who turns up sees the group's name next to the key in the book. They either wait or come back tomorrow. Whoever holds the key owns the hall until it is handed back.

## Classic meaning

An object has explicit lock and unlock operations and records who holds it. A caller can hold it across several operations.

## In the agent system

Compaction shrinks a session's transcript by summarising it. It rewrites the transcript in several steps. First it takes a snapshot. Then it summarises with the model, replaces old turns and updates token counts. Locking each method on its own is not enough. Messages that arrive between steps would be lost. So the session is a lockable object. The compactor calls lock(owner='compactor') and holds it across all steps. Meanwhile the UI's append calls try_lock. It sees who holds the lock and saves the message for later. The lock records its owner and an expiry time. So a crashed holder cannot keep it forever.

## In a large company

Across replicas (copies on different hosts), the lock is a lease in a shared store. Examples are a Postgres row with an expiry or an etcd lease. Every write the lock protects carries a fencing token. The token is a number that only ever goes up, and the store checks it. The harness records the holder's identity, lease time and renewals. So operators can see who holds a session. They can break a stale hold through an audited admin action. Holders should be service identities (accounts for software), not browser connections. Then a client that disconnects cannot pin a tenant's session, which would keep a customer's session locked.

## Step by step

1. A caller locks the session with its owner id and becomes the holder.
1. It does several operations while holding the lock.
1. Other callers' try_lock reports the holder, so they wait or put off their work.
1. The holder unlocks, or the lease runs out, and the next caller goes ahead.

## Code sketch

```python
lease = session.try_lock('compactor', ttl=60)
if lease:
    try:
        snap = session.snapshot()
        summary = model.summarise(snap)
        # refused if the lease has expired
        session.replace_old_turns(
            summary, fence=lease.token)
    finally:
        session.unlock(lease)
else:
    log.info(f'held by {session.holder}')
```

## Be careful

A lock held across a model call can outlive its lease (its time limit). So renew the lease while working. Also have the store reject writes that carry a stale fencing token. A fencing token is a number that goes up with each new lease. Without these, an expired holder can overwrite newer messages.

## Diagram

![Fig. 6.15: The holder keeps the lock across several steps while others are turned away.](/diagrams/lockable-object.svg)

---

---
id: double-checked-locking
number: "6.16"
title: Double-Checked Locking
chapter: async
fit: direct
review_id: rev-double-checked-locking
figure_number: Fig. 6.16
figure_caption: "The second check, made under the lock, stops a racing thread from building twice."
diagram: double-checked-locking.svg
analogy_title: Lighting the stage before the show
---
## Gist

Create a shared client only when first needed, checking once without the lock and again under it, so only one thread builds it.

## Everyday comparison

### Lighting the stage before the show

Any stagehand who sees the stage is dark heads for the lighting booth. Only one person fits in the booth, so the others queue at its door. The first one in turns the lights up. The next one in looks at the board. The lights are already on, so they leave without touching anything.

## Classic meaning

Lazy initialisation builds something only on first use. To cut locking cost, code checks the condition before taking the lock and checks again after.

## In the agent system

Some things are costly to build: model provider clients, MCP connections and tokenizer tables. A client is the object that talks to a service. MCP is a standard way to connect tools to an AI model. Building these opens connection pools, fetches tool lists and loads vocabularies. A harness creates them on first use. But many sessions may reach first use at the same moment. The getter first checks for the client without locking. Every later call takes this fast path. If the client is missing, the getter takes a lock and checks again before building. So a thread that lost the race reuses the new client. It does not open a second pool. Some things carry credentials, such as an MCP connection authorised as one user. These are cached per tenant and principal, never as one global instance. A tenant is one customer company. A principal is the user or service the access belongs to.

## In a large company

In an enterprise harness, lazily built clients are usually per tenant (customer company) or per principal (user or service). That is because they carry API keys, OAuth tokens or a region-specific endpoint. The regional endpoint is for data residency, which means keeping data in a certain region. So the cache key must include whichever of those vary. A singleton is one shared instance for the whole process. A global singleton holding one user's MCP authorisation is a cross-tenant data leak. Cached clients also need a way to refresh when credentials rotate (get replaced). Credentials may rotate in Vault or in a KMS-backed secret store, which is protected by a key management service. Clients should not live for the life of the process.

## Step by step

1. A caller checks whether the shared client exists, and returns it if so.
1. If not, it takes the init lock.
1. It checks again, since another caller may have built it meanwhile.
1. Only if it is still missing does it build and publish the client.

## Code sketch

```python
_clients, _lock = {}, threading.Lock()

def get_client(tid):         # per tenant
    c = _clients.get(tid)          # check 1
    if c is None:
        with _lock:
            c = _clients.get(tid)  # check 2
            if c is None:
                c = ModelClient(creds(tid))
                _clients[tid] = c
    return c
```

## Be careful

Publishing the built object must be one atomic step (it happens all at once) after construction. A CPython name binding gives that. Java needs a volatile field and C++ needs an atomic. Otherwise a reader can see a half-built client.

## Diagram

![Fig. 6.16: The second check, made under the lock, stops a racing thread from building twice.](/diagrams/double-checked-locking.svg)

id: double-buffer
number: "6.17"
title: Double Buffer
chapter: async
fit: adapted
figure_number: Fig. 6.17
figure_caption: "Writers fill the back buffer, readers see only the front, and a swap exchanges them."
diagram: double-buffer.svg
analogy_title: "The lecture hall's sliding boards"
---
## Gist

Keep two buffers: the UI shows the finished one while the stream fills the other, then they swap in one step.

## Everyday comparison

### The lecture hall's sliding boards

A lecture hall has two chalkboards on rails. The lecturer writes the next proof on the back board. Meanwhile students copy the finished one at the front. When the proof is complete, the boards slide past each other in one motion. Students never see half-written lines. The lecturer never waits for slow copiers.

## Classic meaning

Readers see a current buffer while writers fill a next buffer. The two swap atomically, in one step, so readers never see a half-done state.

## In the agent system

The model streams its reply as token deltas (small pieces of new text). Pushing each one straight into the chat DOM causes flicker and broken markdown. The DOM is the page structure the browser draws. You might see half a code fence, or a table missing its last row. So a harness frontend keeps two buffers. The back buffer collects deltas and re-reads the markdown. The front buffer is the one the renderer paints. On each animation frame, the code checks the back buffer. If it sits at a safe boundary, such as the end of a block, the two references swap. The same idea works on the server for artifacts. Write the new version to a temp file. Then atomically rename it over the live one.

## In a large company

Enterprise chat clients can use the safe-boundary buffer as a checkpoint. There, streamed output passes DLP and secret scanning before it is painted. DLP (data loss prevention) is tooling that stops sensitive data from leaking. This matters because text already on screen cannot be taken back. The same swap-a-reference idea appears on the server when new versions are published. This covers policy bundles, prompt configs and artifact versions. Build and check the new version completely. Switch the active pointer in one step. Keep the old one for rollback. Record which version each session used, so an audit can rebuild what a user saw.

## Step by step

1. Token deltas are added to the back buffer.
1. The renderer paints only the front buffer.
1. At a frame tick, if the back buffer is at a safe boundary, the references swap.
1. The new back buffer is brought up to date and keeps filling for the next round.

## Code sketch

```python
front, back = Doc(), Doc()

def on_delta(text):
    back.append(text)          # writer side

def on_frame():
    global front, back
    if back.at_safe_boundary():
        front, back = back, front
        back.sync_from(front)
    render(front)              # reader side
```

## Be careful

Swapping only at safe boundaries can fall behind a fast stream. Cap the delay, so a long code block still shows progress.

## Diagram

![Fig. 6.17: Writers fill the back buffer, readers see only the front, and a swap exchanges them.](/diagrams/double-buffer.svg)

---
id: intercepting-filter
number: "7.01"
title: Intercepting Filter
chapter: safety
fit: direct
review_id: rev-intercepting-filter
figure_number: Fig. 7.01
figure_caption: "Traffic in both directions passes a chain of separate filters, and any of them can stop it."
diagram: intercepting-filter.svg
analogy_title: Airport security lanes
---
## Gist

Pass every prompt and response through a chain of guardrail filters, each able to inspect, rewrite or block it.

## Everyday comparison

### Airport security lanes

Before you board, you pass a chain of checks. There is the boarding pass scan, the bag x-ray, the metal detector and the passport desk. Each looks for one kind of problem and can turn you back. The airline does not run these checks itself. The airport can add a new scanner without changing anything about the plane.

## Classic meaning

Filters run in a chain before and after a request handler. They can be configured, and the handler does not need to know they exist.

## In the agent system

Some inputs reach the model, such as a user message or a fetched web page. First they pass through input filters. One is a prompt-injection scan on tool results. Prompt injection is hidden text that tries to give the model new orders. Others are a PII redactor and a size cap. A PII redactor removes personal data such as names and emails. After the model replies, output filters run. These include moderation, secret scanning, and a check that no tool call targets a blocked domain. That output check is only an early warning. The real block on domains happens where the tool runs, or in the egress proxy (the gate for outgoing network traffic). A filter manager builds the chains from config. So a team can add a new detector without touching the agent loop. Any filter can stop the chain early with a refusal. Or it can pass on a redacted payload.

## In a large company

Enterprise platforms usually build this chain into an LLM gateway or harness middleware. An LLM gateway is a shared entry point for all model calls. The chain applies PII redaction and DLP (data loss prevention), injection classifiers, moderation and secret scanning. Each tenant (customer company) gets its own settings from versioned configuration. Filters fail closed. They log each decision with a redacted payload for audit. Cheap rules run before model-based classifiers, to protect latency SLOs (targets for response speed). Streaming responses need the output chain applied to buffered chunks. The controls that truly decide, such as egress allow-lists, still sit in the tool executor and the network layer.

## Step by step

1. The filter manager builds the input and output chains from config.
1. An incoming message runs through each input filter in order.
1. If nothing blocks it, the agent loop calls the model with the cleaned input.
1. The reply runs through the output filters before it reaches the user or a tool.

## Code sketch

```python
pre = FilterChain([
    InjectionScan(), RedactPII(),
    TokenCap(50_000),
])
post = FilterChain([Moderation(),
                    SecretScan()])

def handle(msg):
    msg = pre.run(msg)   # may raise Block
    reply = agent.turn(msg)
    return post.run(reply)
```

## Be careful

Classifier filters are probabilistic, which means they guess and can be wrong. So treat the chain as defence in depth, one layer among several. It is not a security boundary. Fail closed when a filter errors, which means block when unsure. Keep hard limits, such as tool permissions and egress allow-lists, in the executor. An egress allow-list is the list of outside addresses the tools may reach.

## Diagram

![Fig. 7.01: Traffic in both directions passes a chain of separate filters, and any of them can stop it.](/diagrams/intercepting-filter.svg)

id: specification
number: "7.02"
title: Specification
chapter: safety
fit: direct
review_id: rev-specification
figure_number: Fig. 7.02
figure_caption: Small reusable rules combine into a tree that judges each proposed action.
diagram: specification.svg
analogy_title: The casting call notice
---
## Gist

Write permission rules as small predicates (yes-or-no tests) combined with and, or and not, then test each action against them.

## Everyday comparison

### The casting call notice

A casting call says: over 18, AND able to sing, AND either dances or plays guitar, AND NOT under contract elsewhere. Each line is a separate test. The director can reuse it for the next show. Putting the lines together makes the brief. Checking an applicant means going down the list.

## Classic meaning

A business rule becomes an object with an is_satisfied_by(candidate) method. Rules can be combined with boolean operators: and, or, not.

## In the agent system

Here is a policy for browser actions. Allow a form submission if the URL is localhost AND the credentials are test credentials AND the user asked for it. OR allow it if the user approved this exact action. Each clause is a Specification object: IsLocalhost, TestCreds, UserRequested, Approved. Each has is_satisfied_by(action). Each leaf (a single basic rule) reads facts the harness itself holds. These are the parsed URL, the credential's source, the recorded user turns and the approval record. A leaf never trusts claims the model puts in the tool arguments. The policy is built with &, | and ~ (and, or, not). It is unit-tested clause by clause. It can also explain itself. So the harness can tell the model which clause failed, in the denial tool_result.

## In a large company

Enterprise platforms usually move these rules into a policy engine. Examples are OPA with its Rego language, or Cedar. There, policies are versioned, code-reviewed and tested in CI (automatic checks on every change). Each check writes a decision log for audit. Cedar has a rule that a matching forbid overrides any permit. This gives explicit deny, which plain OR combining lacks. Every attribute fed to the policy must come from the identity provider and harness records, never from model output. Attributes include the tenant (customer company), the principal (the acting user), the resource and the approval state.

## Step by step

1. Write each rule as a small spec with is_satisfied_by(action).
1. Combine specs with and, or and not into a policy.
1. At the permission gate, check the policy against the proposed tool call.
1. If it fails, report which clause failed so the model can adjust.

## Code sketch

```python
class Spec:
    def __and__(s, o): return And(s, o)
    def __or__(s, o):  return Or(s, o)
    def __invert__(s): return Not(s)

policy = (IsLocalhost() & TestCreds()
          & UserRequested()) | Approved()

if not policy.is_satisfied_by(action):
    return deny(policy.explain(action))
```

## Be careful

Deeply nested specs get hard to read. Name the middle-level policies, such as safe_local_submit, and test each leaf on its own.

## Diagram

![Fig. 7.02: Small reusable rules combine into a tree that judges each proposed action.](/diagrams/specification.svg)

---

---
id: filterer
number: "7.03"
title: Filterer
chapter: safety
fit: direct
figure_number: Fig. 7.03
figure_caption: "Each filtered() call returns the same type, so the narrowing can go on."
diagram: filterer.svg
analogy_title: Stacked sieves in a soil lab
---
## Gist

Give a tool or content collection a filtered() method that returns a smaller collection of the same type, chained per session.

## Everyday comparison

### Stacked sieves in a soil lab

A soil technician pours a sample into a stack of sieves. Coarse mesh is on top and fine mesh below. Each tray catches what passed the one above. What it holds is still soil that could go through another sieve. The sample never changes kind. It only gets smaller at each level, until just what the test needs is left.

## Classic meaning

A container returns filtered copies of itself through filtered(predicate). A predicate is a yes-or-no test. Filters can chain without showing the container's insides.

## In the agent system

The harness loads a full ToolRegistry, the list of all tools it knows. It holds every built-in tool plus every tool from each connected MCP server. MCP is a standard way to connect tools to an AI model. A given session should only see some of them. So the harness calls registry.filtered(by_role).filtered(by_project).filtered(not_deferred). Each step returns a new ToolRegistry. So the result still supports lookup, schema export and more filtering. The final registry is serialised (turned into text) into the tools parameter of the model request. The same shape works for memory entries, or for search results filtered by the user's access.

## In a large company

In enterprise harnesses, the first filters come from entitlements, the access the customer has bought and allowed. First comes the tenant admin's allow-list of MCP servers and tools. Then come RBAC or ABAC rules mapped from identity provider groups through SSO (single sign-on). RBAC gives permissions by job role. ABAC gives permissions based on attributes such as team or region. The same shape applies to retrieval, which means looking up documents for the model. There, document ACLs (access control lists) should be applied as a filter inside the vector store query. A vector store is a database that finds similar text. Trimming a top-k list afterwards can return too few results, and it is easy to forget. Visibility filters are a usability layer. So the executor checks authorisation again and logs every call.

## Step by step

1. Load the full registry of built-in and MCP tools.
1. Apply filtered() with the session's role test.
1. Chain more filtered() calls for project scope and loaded state.
1. Send the final registry's schemas as the request's tools list.

## Code sketch

```python
class ToolRegistry:
    def filtered(self, pred):
        return ToolRegistry(
            t for t in self.tools if pred(t))

visible = (registry
    .filtered(lambda t: t.risk <= role.cap)
    .filtered(lambda t: t.server in project)
    .filtered(lambda t: not t.deferred))
request.tools = visible.schemas()
```

## Be careful

A filtered list hides tools from the model, but it does not stop a crafted call. Hiding a tool is not the same as blocking it. Enforce the same rule again when the tool runs.

## Diagram

![Fig. 7.03: Each filtered() call returns the same type, so the narrowing can go on.](/diagrams/filterer.svg)

id: role-object
number: "7.04"
title: Role Object
chapter: safety
fit: adapted
review_id: rev-role-object
figure_number: Fig. 7.04
figure_caption: The session stays the same object while roles come and go around it.
diagram: role-object.svg
analogy_title: Festival volunteer vests
---
## Gist

Attach role objects such as editor or operator to a session while it runs, each carrying the permissions it grants.

## Everyday comparison

### Festival volunteer vests

At a music festival, one volunteer might wear a yellow steward vest in the morning. After lunch they wear a green first-aid vest. The person stays the same. The vest decides which gates they pass, which radio channel they use and which tent they may enter. A volunteer can hold two vests. The coordinator can take one back at any time.

## Classic meaning

A core object gets different views for different contexts. Each view is a separate role object that can be added or removed while the program runs.

## In the agent system

A Session core holds identity, transcript and settings. Roles attach as separate objects. Viewer can read files. Editor can write inside the workspace. Operator can run shell commands and send messages. Reviewer can approve other agents' tool calls. The permission gate asks the session for its roles. It lets each role decide with allows(call). Access may be added mid-session, from the user's entitlements or an audited admin grant. Entitlements are the access the user really holds. Then the harness attaches a role. When access is revoked, it removes one. It does not change a permissions blob or create a subclass of Session. A session never gains a role its user does not hold.

## In a large company

In an enterprise platform, a session's roles come from the user's identity provider groups and the tenant's policy. A tenant is one customer company. An agent never holds a role its user lacks. This avoids the confused-deputy problem, where a trusted helper is tricked into using power its requester should not have. Granting a role mid-session is an audited event. It has an approver, a scope and an expiry. This follows the style of just-in-time access, where access is given only when needed and for a short time. 'Any role allows' logic cannot express explicit deny. So high-risk restrictions belong in a policy engine such as Cedar or OPA. The gate asks that engine as well as the roles.

## Step by step

1. Create the session core with identity and transcript.
1. Attach role objects based on the user's grants or the workspace policy.
1. At each tool call, the gate asks the session's roles whether any allows it.
1. Add or remove roles mid-session as access is granted or revoked.

## Code sketch

```python
s = Session(user='ana')
s.add_role(Editor(paths=['/repo']))
s.add_role(Operator(shell=True, net=False))
s.add_role(Reviewer())

def allowed(s, c):     # any role may allow
    return any(r.allows(c) for r in s.roles)

s.remove_role(Reviewer)    # access revoked
```

## Be careful

Role checks spread across the codebase drift apart over time. Send every permission question through one gate that asks the roles.

## Diagram

![Fig. 7.04: The session stays the same object while roles come and go around it.](/diagrams/role-object.svg)

---
id: bulkhead
number: "7.05"
title: Bulkhead
chapter: safety
fit: direct
review_id: rev-bulkhead
figure_number: Fig. 7.05
figure_caption: "A flooded compartment stays flooded alone, and its neighbours keep serving."
diagram: bulkhead.svg
analogy_title: Watertight compartments in a hull
---
## Gist

Split sandboxes, worker pools and quotas per session or tenant (customer), so one runaway agent cannot sink the others.

## Everyday comparison

### Watertight compartments in a hull

A ship's hull is split into sealed compartments. Say the front hits ice and one compartment floods. The doors stay shut and the water stays there. The ship tilts but floats. Without the walls, one hole would fill the whole hull.

## Classic meaning

Parts of a system are kept in separate pools. If one fails or is overloaded, the others keep working.

## In the agent system

Each session runs tools in its own container. A container is an isolated box for running code. It has limits on CPU, memory, disk and processes. So a fork bomb or a 50 GB download fills only that box. A fork bomb is a program that copies itself until the machine chokes. Above that, the harness gives each tenant (customer company) its own worker pool and model concurrency quota. It also gives each slow MCP server (a tool server) its own connection pool. So a hung connector uses up its own slots, not the shared ones. Interactive chat and batch evals (large automated test runs) run in separate pools. So a large eval sweep never starves a user who is waiting for a reply.

## In a large company

Enterprise platforms build bulkheads along tenant lines. They set per-tenant token and concurrency quotas at the LLM gateway, the shared entry point for model calls. They use Kubernetes namespaces with ResourceQuota, which caps what each group can use. They run untrusted code on separate node pools (separate groups of machines). Some use cell-based deployments, so a bad tenant or release affects only one cell. A cell is a full, separate copy of the system. Sandboxes for different tenants should not share a kernel (the core of the operating system) without a stronger isolation layer. Examples are gVisor or Firecracker microVMs. Saturation metrics for each compartment feed both alerting and chargeback, which means billing each tenant for what it used.

## Step by step

1. Group workloads by tenant, session or dependency.
1. Give each group its own pool, container and quota.
1. Send each request only to its own group's compartment.
1. When one compartment fails or fills, reject its requests while the others run normally.

## Code sketch

```python
pools = {
    'chat':    Semaphore(64),
    'evals':   Semaphore(8),
    'mcp:crm': Semaphore(4),
}

async def run(kind, job):
    if pools[kind].locked():   # full: reject
        raise Rejected(kind)
    async with pools[kind]:
        async with Container(cpus=2, mem='4g',
                             pids=256) as box:
            return await box.exec(job)
```

## Be careful

Many tiny compartments leave capacity unused. Size pools from real load. Let interactive traffic borrow spare slots, but only within set limits.

## Diagram

![Fig. 7.05: A flooded compartment stays flooded alone, and its neighbours keep serving.](/diagrams/bulkhead.svg)
