id: service-layer
number: "8.16"
title: Service Layer
chapter: architecture
fit: direct
review_id: rev-service-layer
figure_number: Fig. 8.16
figure_caption: "Every surface calls the same few operations, which direct everything behind them."
diagram: service-layer.svg
analogy_title: The post office counter
---
## Gist

Offer the harness through a few app operations, such as create_session and send_turn, that every surface calls the same way.

## Everyday comparison

### The post office counter

At the counter you ask for a few things: send this parcel, collect that one, buy stamps. Behind the counter, the clerk weighs, prices and prints a label. The clerk takes payment and drops the parcel in the right sack. You never touch the scales or the sorting bins. The same counter serves walk-ins, businesses and phone bookings.

## Classic meaning

Mark the edge of an app with a layer of services. For each thing a client can do, a service directs the domain objects (the core business objects) and the database transaction.

## In the agent system

A SessionService offers create_session, send_turn, approve_tool_call, cancel_turn and fork_session. Each operation checks that the caller is allowed and loads the session. Then it runs the agent loop or the permission policy. It saves state in one transaction (a group of database changes that succeed or fail together). It returns a result or a stream of events. The web API, the CLI (command-line tool), scheduled tasks and the SDK all call these same operations. So rules like "only one running turn per session" are enforced in one place. Domain objects such as Conversation and PermissionPolicy stay free of web and login code.

## In a large company

In large platforms the service layer applies several controls to every operation, whichever surface called it. It asks a policy engine such as OPA or Cedar whether the action is allowed. It writes audit records and checks each tenant's budget. (A tenant is one customer company.) It also uses idempotency keys (tags that make a repeated request safe to run twice). Linking each operation to a named permission makes RBAC easy to review. RBAC is role-based access control: permissions given by job role. It also gives auditors one place to inspect for SOC 2 (a security audit standard). Long turns usually pass to a durable workflow, such as Temporal, once the operation saves. (A durable workflow survives crashes and restarts.) So the service returns a handle instead of keeping a request open. The risk is surfaces that call repositories directly and skip these controls. Internal batch jobs count too.

## Step by step

1. A surface calls an operation such as send_turn(session_id, text).
1. The service checks the caller is allowed and loads the session from its repository (its storage class).
1. It directs the domain objects: the loop, the permission policy, the budget.
1. It saves the changes and returns a stream or result to the caller.

## Code sketch

```python
class SessionService:
    def send_turn(self, user, sid, text):
        with self.uow:
            s = self.repo.load_for_update(sid)
            self.authz.require(user, s, 'w')
            if s.has_running_turn():
                raise Busy(sid)
            s.mark_turn_running()
            self.repo.save(s)
        # model call starts after commit
        return self.loop.start(s, text)
```

## Be careful

A surface might skip the service and call the loop or repository directly. Then the shared rules quietly stop applying to it.

## Diagram

![Fig. 8.16: Every surface calls the same few operations, which direct everything behind them.](/diagrams/service-layer.svg)

---
id: business-delegate
number: "8.17"
title: Business Delegate
chapter: architecture
fit: direct
review_id: rev-business-delegate
figure_number: Fig. 8.17
figure_caption: "App code makes one local call. The delegate handles lookup, retries and error shapes."
diagram: business-delegate.svg
analogy_title: The wedding planner
---
## Gist

Give app code a local client that hides how the remote harness is found, called and retried, and how it fails.

## Everyday comparison

### The wedding planner

The couple says: book us a venue for June. The planner knows which venues to call. The planner redials when the line is busy and tries the second choice when the first is full. Then the planner comes back with a simple answer: booked, with a date and a deposit. The couple never learns any venue's booking system or its jargon.

## Classic meaning

An object on the client side that hides the details of finding and calling remote business services. It also handles retries and turns errors into simpler ones.

## In the agent system

App code that wants an agent to do some work calls TaskClient.run(prompt). The delegate does the rest. It picks which regional endpoint (server address) to use and attaches credentials. It opens the session. It retries 429 and 529 replies ("too many requests" and "overloaded") with backoff (waiting longer each time). It honours the Retry-After header and resends the same idempotency key. (That key makes a repeated request safe to run twice.) If the event stream drops, it resumes from the last event id. It turns network errors into a few business errors, such as TaskRejected or TaskTimedOut. The calling code stays the same when the harness moves regions or switches from REST to WebSocket.

## In a large company

Large companies ship business delegates as internal client libraries. Business apps use them to call the agent platform. The library handles SSO (single sign-on) token exchange, mTLS (both sides prove identity with certificates) and tenant headers inside. (A tenant is one customer company.) Endpoint lookup must respect data residency (keeping data in a certain region). So an EU tenant's delegate only finds EU endpoints. It never switches to another region unless a policy allows it. The delegate should pass along W3C trace context, a standard tracking header. Then the calling app and the harness appear in one OpenTelemetry trace (a record of one request across services). The risk is many client apps retrying at once and making an overload worse. So retries need jitter (random delay), a budget and respect for Retry-After.

## Step by step

1. The app calls a plain method on the delegate, such as run(prompt).
1. The delegate looks up the endpoint and logs in.
1. It makes the remote calls and retries short-lived failures with backoff.
1. It returns a business result, or raises one of a few business errors.

## Code sketch

```python
class TaskClient:
    def run(self, p):
        url = self.lookup.endpoint('agents')
        key = new_idempotency_key()
        for wait in backoff(tries=4):
            try:
                return self._post(url, p, key)
            except Overloaded as e:
                sleep(e.retry_after or wait)
        raise TaskUnavailable(p[:40])
```

## Be careful

A delegate might retry a call that is not idempotent (not safe to run twice), such as starting a session that sends email. Then the side effect can happen twice. Send an idempotency key with every retry.

## Diagram

![Fig. 8.17: App code makes one local call. The delegate handles lookup, retries and error shapes.](/diagrams/business-delegate.svg)

---

---
id: session-facade
number: "8.18"
title: Session Facade
chapter: architecture
fit: direct
review_id: rev-session-facade
figure_number: Fig. 8.18
figure_caption: "One remote call goes in, many local calls run behind the facade, and one handle comes out."
diagram: session-facade.svg
analogy_title: The interlibrary loan desk
---
## Gist

Offer one big remote call that does a whole job on the server, so clients do not chain many small calls.

## Everyday comparison

### The interlibrary loan desk

You fill in one slip at the library desk: this book, by Friday. The librarian searches the regional catalogue and requests it from another branch. The librarian books it onto the van, checks it out to your card and texts you when it arrives. Doing those steps yourself would mean five queues and three phone calls.

## Classic meaning

A facade (a single front door) on the server that wraps many small business objects behind a few big operations. It cuts the number of remote calls and keeps the workflow logic on the server.

## In the agent system

Without a facade, an SDK client would make five calls. It would create a session, upload files, register tools, set the system prompt and then send the first turn. That is five round trips, and any one can fail halfway. A start_task(spec) endpoint on the server does all of it in one call. It returns a session handle plus the event stream. Files and the runtime live outside the session database, so one database transaction cannot cover them. So the facade creates the session as "pending". It only turns it on when every step succeeds, and it cleans up on failure. An idempotency key on the request makes client retries safe. (That key makes a repeated request safe to run twice.) The small internal APIs for the session store, file service and runtime stay hidden and can change freely. Waiting time drops, and half-set-up sessions disappear.

## In a large company

Large platforms offer big operations like start_task to integration teams and workflow tools. This cuts chatty traffic across regions. It also keeps the order of policy checks on the server. The facade is a good place to apply tenant policy once for the whole job. (A tenant is one customer company.) That covers allowed tools, the data class of uploaded files, DLP scanning (checks that catch leaks of sensitive data) and reserving budget. For long jobs it usually starts a durable workflow in Temporal or AWS Step Functions and returns a handle. (A durable workflow survives crashes and restarts.) Then the engine handles retries and compensation (undoing steps after a failure). The risk is a facade that quietly grants every tool the request asks for. So it must only grant requested tools that the tenant and caller are both allowed to use.

## Step by step

1. The client sends one start_task request with the prompt, files and tool list.
1. The facade creates the session and stores the files.
1. It sets up tools and starts the first turn on the runtime.
1. It returns a single handle and event stream to the client.

## Code sketch

```python
@api.post('/v1/tasks')
def start_task(spec):
    with uow:
        s = sessions.create(spec.owner)
        files.attach(s.id, spec.files)
        runtime.configure(s.id, spec.tools)
    stream = runtime.run_turn(s.id, spec.prompt)
    return TaskHandle(s.id, stream)
```

## Be careful

A facade might grow a flag for every variation. Then it becomes one giant procedure. Keep a few well-named big operations, and let unusual clients use the internal APIs.

## Diagram

![Fig. 8.18: One remote call goes in, many local calls run behind the facade, and one handle comes out.](/diagrams/session-facade.svg)

---
id: separated-interface
number: "8.19"
title: Separated Interface
chapter: architecture
fit: direct
figure_number: Fig. 8.19
figure_caption: "The core and implementations both point at the interface package, never at each other."
diagram: separated-interface.svg
analogy_title: The shipping container standard
---
## Gist

Keep SDK interfaces in one package and their implementations in others, so code depends on the contract, never a provider.

## Everyday comparison

### The shipping container standard

A published standard sets a shipping container's size, corner fittings and lock rods. Ports build cranes to it, and factories build boxes to it, often without ever meeting. A crane in one port lifts a box made on another continent. This works because both depend on the standard, not on each other.

## Classic meaning

Put an interface (a list of functions with no code behind them) in a different package from the code that fills it in. Then clients only depend on the package that holds the interface.

## In the agent system

A harness-interfaces package declares ModelClient, ToolHost and TranscriptStore. It imports no outside libraries. The agent core and the plugin SDK depend only on that package. Separate packages, such as harness-anthropic, harness-mcp and harness-postgres, fill in the interfaces. They pull in the heavy libraries. A user who installs the CLI (command-line tool) with a local SQLite store never downloads the Postgres driver. And a third party can publish a new sandbox backend without any change to the core.

## In a large company

Large platforms publish the interface package as the contract for internal teams and third parties. These groups build tool hosts, model adapters or storage backends. The package uses semantic versioning (version numbers that signal breaking changes). It comes with contract tests that every implementation must pass. So a bank can plug in its own LLM gateway client (its shared front door to AI models). Or it can plug in an on-premises vector store (a database for search by meaning, run in its own building). It does not need to fork (copy and change) the core. Supply-chain controls apply to the implementation packages. These are signed artifacts, an SBOM (a list of every library inside) and dependency scanning. The risk is a breaking change to the interface package spreading through every plugin. So removals need a published warning period.

## Step by step

1. Put interface definitions and shared types in a small package with no heavy libraries.
1. Make the core and plugins import only that package.
1. Fill in each interface in its own package, which depends on the interface package.
1. Choose implementations at install time and wire them in at startup.

## Code sketch

```python
# harness_interfaces/model.py
class ModelClient(Protocol):
    def complete(self, req: Request) -> Reply:
        ...

# harness_anthropic/client.py
from harness_interfaces import ModelClient
class AnthropicClient(ModelClient):
    def complete(self, req):
        return self.sdk.messages.create(...)
```

## Be careful

Do not split every interface into its own package when there is only one implementation. That adds version-tracking pain for no gain. Split only where real alternatives exist.

## Diagram

![Fig. 8.19: The core and implementations both point at the interface package, never at each other.](/diagrams/separated-interface.svg)

---

---
id: domain-model
number: "8.20"
title: Domain Model
chapter: architecture
fit: direct
figure_number: Fig. 8.20
figure_caption: The handler calls one method. The objects enforce the rules among themselves.
diagram: domain-model.svg
analogy_title: The orchestra that knows its parts
---
## Gist

Put turn-handling rules inside rich objects like Conversation, Turn and ToolCall, so behaviour lives with the data it protects.

## Everyday comparison

### The orchestra that knows its parts

In an orchestra each player knows their own part. The oboist knows when to come in. The timpanist tunes their own drums. Each section leader keeps their section together. The conductor gives cues, not finger positions. How to play the violin lives with the violinist, not in a manual on the conductor's stand.

## Classic meaning

An object model of the business area that joins data and behaviour. Business rules are written as methods on the objects themselves.

## In the agent system

A Conversation aggregate (a group of objects saved and changed as one unit) owns its Turns. Its submit() method refuses new input while a turn is still running. A ToolCall moves through pending, approved, running and done. It rejects any step that breaks that order. A TokenBudget charges usage and reports when it runs out. (A token is a small chunk of text that models count and bill by.) The request handler just loads the Conversation, calls one method and saves it. Some rules matter a lot. For example, every tool_use (the model's request to run a tool) must get a tool_result before the next model call. Rules like this are enforced in one place. They are unit-tested without a database.

## In a large company

In large platforms, the domain model is where approval rules become code that is enforced. ToolCall.approve can require that the approver has the right role and is not the person who asked. This supports separation of duties (no one person can both ask and approve). Aggregates such as Conversation carry the tenant id (which customer company) and the data class. So the objects themselves can check rules on how long data is kept and where it is stored. Each change of state sends out domain events (records of what happened) that feed the audit trail. The risk is that permission checks drift out of the model and into handlers on some surfaces. So unit-test the invariants that compliance depends on at the model level.

## Step by step

1. The handler loads a Conversation aggregate from its repository (its storage class).
1. It calls a behaviour method such as conversation.submit(text).
1. The objects check invariants (rules that must always hold) and update each other: Turn, ToolCall, TokenBudget.
1. The repository saves the whole aggregate in one go.

## Code sketch

```python
class ToolCall:
    def approve(self, by):
        if self.state != 'pending':
            raise BadTransition(self.state)
        self.state = 'approved'
        self.approver = by

class Conversation:
    def submit(self, text):
        if self.turns and self.turns[-1].open:
            raise TurnInProgress()
        self.turns.append(Turn.start(text))
```

## Be careful

Loading the full rich model on every turn gets slow for long transcripts. Load old turns only when needed, or keep them as summaries inside the aggregate.

## Diagram

![Fig. 8.20: The handler calls one method. The objects enforce the rules among themselves.](/diagrams/domain-model.svg)

---

---
id: transaction-script
number: "8.21"
title: Transaction Script
chapter: architecture
fit: direct
review_id: rev-transaction-script
figure_number: Fig. 8.21
figure_caption: Each request has its own straight-line procedure that talks to the database directly.
diagram: transaction-script.svg
analogy_title: The flat-pack instruction sheet
---
## Gist

Handle each request with one procedure that runs top to bottom: load rows, call the model, run tools, write rows, return.

## Everyday comparison

### The flat-pack instruction sheet

Every flat-pack wardrobe comes with its own sheet. Step 1: lay out the panels. Step 2: fix the hinges. Step 14: hang the doors. The sheet does not teach carpentry. It does not share steps with the bookcase sheet. It lists what to do, in order, for this one item. Anyone can follow it, and you can find a mistake by its step number.

## Classic meaning

Organise business logic as procedures, one for each request or transaction. Each procedure talks to the database directly.

## In the agent system

An early harness often has one function per endpoint (web address). For example, handle_turn reads the session's messages and builds the prompt. It calls the model, then loops over the tool_use blocks (the model's requests to run tools) and runs each tool. It adds the new message rows and returns the reply. handle_approve and handle_cancel are separate procedures with their own SQL (database queries). There are no domain objects (core business objects). So each script is easy to read and you can debug it from start to end. As the harness grows, shared rules such as the token budget check get copied between scripts.

## In a large company

Transaction scripts are common in company proofs of concept. They are also common in internal tools built quickly on one model endpoint. They become a compliance problem as they multiply. Each script rebuilds its own tenant checks, audit logging, PII redaction and budget checks. (A tenant is one customer company. PII is personal data such as names and emails.) Sooner or later one of them skips a control. A common fix is to move shared rules into a service layer. Then put model access behind the LLM gateway (one shared front door to AI models). That makes usage tracking and logging the same everywhere. At the least, each script should limit steps and spending per request. It should also write an audit record for every tool call.

## Step by step

1. Each request goes to its own script, such as handle_turn.
1. The script reads the rows it needs straight from the database.
1. It calls the model and runs tools in a plain loop with a step limit.
1. It saves each message as it goes, so tool calls that ran are on record. Then it returns the reply.

## Code sketch

```python
def handle_turn(sid, text):
    msgs = db.messages(sid) + [user(text)]
    db.append(sid, msgs[-1])
    for _ in range(MAX_STEPS):
        r = model.complete(msgs, TOOLS)
        msgs.append(r.message)
        db.append(sid, r.message)
        if r.stop_reason != 'tool_use':
            return r.text
        res = [run(u) for u in r.tool_uses]
        msgs.append(user(res))  # one message
        db.append(sid, msgs[-1])
    raise StepLimit(sid)
```

## Be careful

Several scripts may end up repeating the same budget, permission and transcript logic. Then a fix lands in one script and not the others. That is the moment to pull out a service layer or domain model.

## Diagram

![Fig. 8.21: Each request has its own straight-line procedure that talks to the database directly.](/diagrams/transaction-script.svg)

---

---
id: table-module
number: "8.22"
title: Table Module
chapter: architecture
fit: direct
review_id: rev-table-module
figure_number: Fig. 8.22
figure_caption: "One module per table works on whole record sets, which pass from module to module."
diagram: table-module.svg
analogy_title: The school office registers
---
## Gist

Write one module per table or collection (sessions, messages, tool_calls) that holds the logic for all its rows at once.

## Everyday comparison

### The school office registers

The school office has one clerk for the attendance register and another for the lunch register. Ask the attendance clerk who missed Monday. They scan one page for the whole year group. Neither clerk keeps a folder for each pupil. Each one owns one register and the questions you can ask of it.

## Classic meaning

One object handles the business logic for every row in a database table or view. It works on sets of records, not one object per row.

## In the agent system

A MessagesModule offers for_session(sid), token_total(rows) and trim_to_budget(rows, limit). A ToolCallsModule offers pending(rows) and mark_approved(ids). The turn handler gets a record set (a batch of rows) of messages from one module. It hands that set to the next module. This suits harnesses already built on a SQL or dataframe-style store (data kept as tables). Bulk jobs come naturally. Examples are expiring every tool call older than an hour, or totalling tokens per org. (A token is a small chunk of text that models bill by.) This pattern sits between Transaction Script and Domain Model. Logic is grouped by table, but there is no object for each message.

## In a large company

Table modules suit company reporting and control jobs that work on whole sets of rows. Examples are totalling tokens per tenant for chargeback (billing each customer), expiring old approvals, or applying retention rules and legal holds across the messages table. (A tenant is one customer company. A legal hold stops data from being deleted during a legal case.) These jobs run in batches against a data warehouse or the live database. So every query must be limited to one tenant id. Ideally row-level security (rules in the database that limit which rows each user sees) enforces this. Each module should not have to remember a filter. GDPR erasure (a person's legal right to have data deleted) fits this shape too. One module call can remove every row about one person. The risk is a bulk update that crosses tenants because someone missed a filter.

## Step by step

1. The turn handler asks MessagesModule for the session's record set.
1. It passes that record set to functions such as trim_to_budget.
1. ToolCallsModule works on the waiting tool-call rows for the same session.
1. Each module writes its changes back to its own table.

## Code sketch

```python
class MessagesModule:  # one per table
    def for_session(self, sid):
        return db.select('messages', sid=sid)
    def trim_to_budget(self, rows, limit):
        # cut at turn edges so no tool_use
        # loses its tool_result
        keep, total = [], 0
        for t in reversed(turns(rows)):
            total += tokens(t)
            if total > limit: break
            keep = t + keep
        return keep
```

## Be careful

Table modules fit badly when a rule covers more than one table. One example is a tool call that changes the session's state. That logic drifts into the handler, with no clear home.

## Diagram

![Fig. 8.22: One module per table works on whole record sets, which pass from module to module.](/diagrams/table-module.svg)

id: collection-pipeline
number: "9.01"
title: Collection Pipeline
chapter: functional
fit: direct
review_id: rev-collection-pipeline
figure_number: Fig. 9.01
figure_caption: "Each operation returns a new list, smaller or cleaner than the last."
diagram: collection-pipeline.svg
analogy_title: The orchard packing house
---
## Gist

Prepare the transcript for the model as a chain of filter, map and take steps over the message list.

## Everyday comparison

### The orchard packing house

Apples come off the truck onto a sorting line. Workers pull off the bruised ones. The rest are washed and given stickers one by one. At the end, a worker fills crates until each holds exactly forty. Every station handles the whole stream and passes a smaller or tidier stream along.

## Classic meaning

Organise work as a series of operations that each take a collection and return a new one. The usual ones are filter (keep some items), map (change each item) and reduce (combine them).

## In the agent system

Turning a stored transcript into the messages for the next request is a collection task. First the harness filters out events that are only for the screen. Then it maps old tool results to a short placeholder. This way every tool_use (the model's tool request) still has its tool_result (the tool's answer). Next it maps each record into the API's message format and cuts down outputs that are too large. Then it takes messages from the newest end until the token budget is reached. Each step is a pure operation, with no side effects, over lists that never change. So each step is easy to test, and preparing a request never changes the transcript on disk. Keep the output the same from turn to turn where you can. This matters for the prompt cache (saved work the provider can reuse when a request starts the same way). The cache only reuses an unchanged prefix, the start of the request.

## In a large company

Enterprise harnesses build the request with the same kind of chain, plus extra stages. One stage does PII redaction (removing personal data such as names and emails). Another removes content that the tenant (the customer company) has marked as not to be shared with the model. A third checks residency rules before the request leaves the region. The stored transcript is the system of record for audit, meaning the official copy. So the chain must never change it. It makes a separate derived view for each request. The cost control is cache-awareness. Stable prefixes keep prompt cache hit rates high, and that shows up directly in each tenant's bill.

## Step by step

1. Start from the full list of stored transcript records.
1. Filter out records the model should not see.
1. Map each remaining record to an API message, and cut down large content.
1. Take from the newest end until the token budget is used, then send.

## Code sketch

```python
msgs = (Seq(transcript)
        .filter(lambda r: r.kind != 'ui')
        .map(stub_if_stale)  # keep pairs
        .map(to_api_message)
        .map(truncate(max_chars=8000))
        .take_last_within(tokens=60_000)
        .to_list())
```

## Be careful

Taking from the end can split a tool_use from its tool_result. A window that slides every turn also defeats the prompt cache. Drop each pair together, and trim in larger steps.

## Diagram

![Fig. 9.01: Each operation returns a new list, smaller or cleaner than the last.](/diagrams/collection-pipeline.svg)

id: function-composition
number: "9.02"
title: Function Composition
chapter: functional
fit: direct
review_id: rev-function-composition
figure_number: Fig. 9.02
figure_caption: Small functions snap together into one function that is applied once.
diagram: function-composition.svg
analogy_title: Stacked camera lens filters
---
## Gist

Build one tool-result formatter by joining small single-purpose functions, then reuse that joined function everywhere.

## Everyday comparison

### Stacked camera lens filters

A photographer screws a UV filter onto the lens, a polarising filter onto that, and a neutral density filter on top. Light passes through all three, but to the camera they are one attachment. Unscrew one and the rest still work. Buy a new one and it screws onto the stack.

## Classic meaning

Join simple functions into a new function, where each one's output becomes the next one's input. In maths, compose(f, g)(x) means f(g(x)), which runs right to left. The left-to-right form used here is often called pipe.

## In the agent system

Raw tool output needs several clean-ups before it goes back to the model. The harness strips ANSI colour codes, the hidden characters that colour terminal text. It redacts (hides) anything that looks like a credential, such as a password or key. It cuts the text to a size limit and wraps it in a tool_result block (the tool's answer to the model). Each clean-up is a small pure function, with no side effects, that takes a string and returns a string. The harness composes (joins) them once into format_result. It then uses that one function for every tool. A tool with special needs composes a slightly different chain from the same parts.

## In a large company

Enterprise platforms compose tool-output cleaners in one central place. This is often the LLM gateway (the central service all model calls pass through) or a shared harness library. So every team gets the same ANSI stripping, secret redaction, PII masking and size limits. PII is personal data such as names and emails. Regex-based secret redaction, which finds secrets by text patterns, is only an extra layer of defence. The main control is that the tool runtime injects credentials from Vault or workload identity. Vault is a secrets store, and workload identity gives each service its own login. Then credentials never appear in tool output at all. Each composed formatter should have a version number and tests that use known fake secrets. Then a reordering that weakens redaction fails CI, the automatic checks run on every change.

## Step by step

1. Write each clean-up as a small function with one input and one output.
1. Compose them in order into a single named function.
1. Apply the composed function to every raw tool output.
1. Build variants by composing a different set of the same parts.

## Code sketch

```python
def compose(*fns):
    return lambda x: reduce(
        lambda acc, f: f(acc), fns, x)

format_result = compose(strip_ansi,
                        redact_secrets,
                        truncate(16_000),
                        to_tool_result)

block = format_result(proc.stdout)
```

## Be careful

Order matters. Cutting the text before redacting can split a secret in half, so the redactor misses it.

## Diagram

![Fig. 9.02: Small functions snap together into one function that is applied once.](/diagrams/function-composition.svg)

id: combinator
number: "9.03"
title: Combinator
chapter: functional
fit: direct
review_id: rev-combinator
figure_number: Fig. 9.03
figure_caption: Operators combine checks into a bigger check of the same shape.
diagram: combinator.svg
analogy_title: The box of interlocking toy bricks
---
## Gist

Build complex permission rules or output checkers from a few basic checks and operators such as all_of, any_of and not_.

## Everyday comparison

### The box of interlocking toy bricks

A child's brick set has only a few shapes: the flat plate, the two-stud brick and the hinge. Every piece clicks onto every other. So those few shapes become a castle, a truck or a rocket. Nobody needs a special castle piece, because the connectors do the work.

## Classic meaning

Build complex functions by combining simpler ones. You use higher-order functions (functions that take and return functions) of the same type.

## In the agent system

Permission policies grow fast when written as nested if-statements. With combinators, the harness offers basic predicates over a tool call. A predicate is a check that answers true or false, such as read_only, in_workspace and matches(glob). A glob is a file name pattern, like *.env. The harness also offers the operators all_of, any_of and not_. Each one takes predicates and returns a new predicate. Take the policy all_of(not_(matches('*.env')), any_of(read_only, in_workspace)). It is itself a predicate. So it can be nested further, tested on its own, and built from configuration. The same approach builds output checkers and parsers for structured model output.

## In a large company

Enterprise policy languages such as Cedar and Rego are combinator systems at heart. They join small conditions with and, or and not into policies that can be tested and versioned. Platforms often let tenants (customer companies) build their own tool policies from approved basic checks. The platform wraps its required deny rules around the outside, so a tenant rule cannot weaken them. Each decision should carry an explanation of the deciding branch into the audit log. Reviewers and incident responders depend on it.

## Step by step

1. Define basic predicates that take a tool call and return true or false.
1. Define operators that take predicates and return a new predicate.
1. Combine them into a policy expression.
1. Call the policy on each tool call before it runs.

## Code sketch

```python
def all_of(*ps):
    return lambda c: all(p(c) for p in ps)
def any_of(*ps):
    return lambda c: any(p(c) for p in ps)
def not_(p):
    return lambda c: not p(c)

allow = all_of(not_(matches('*.env')),
               any_of(read_only,
                      in_workspace))
if not allow(call): ask_user(call)
```

## Be careful

Deeply nested combinators are hard to debug. Give each policy an explain() method that reports which branch made the decision.

## Diagram

![Fig. 9.03: Operators combine checks into a bigger check of the same shape.](/diagrams/combinator.svg)

---
id: currying
number: "9.04"
title: Currying
chapter: functional
fit: direct
figure_number: Fig. 9.04
figure_caption: Each stage fixes one argument and hands on a smaller function.
diagram: currying.svg
analogy_title: The prepaid return envelope
---
## Gist

Turn a tool runner with many inputs into a chain of one-input functions, fixing the sandbox at startup and permissions per session.

## Everyday comparison

### The prepaid return envelope

An online shop puts a return envelope in every parcel. Its address is printed and the postage is already paid. All you add is the item you are sending back. The shop fixed two of the three things long before you opened the box.

## Classic meaning

Turn a function with several arguments into a series of functions that each take one argument. This allows partial application, which means filling in some arguments early.

## In the agent system

Running a tool needs a sandbox (a locked-down area where code runs safely), a permission policy and the tool call itself. But the harness learns these at different times. It picks the sandbox when it starts. It sets the permission policy when a session begins. A tool call arrives every turn. So run_tool is written as a curried function. Startup code fills in the sandbox to make run_in_sandbox. The session fills in the policy to make session_run. The loop then just calls session_run(call). Subagents (helper agents) get their own partly filled runner, with a stricter policy and the same sandbox.

## In a large company

Enterprise harnesses use the same staging. They fix the tenant configuration when a worker (a server process) starts. They fix the authenticated principal (the verified user or service) and its policy when a session starts. The tool call comes each turn. Identity is fixed early inside a closure, a function that remembers the values it was given. This means the model can supply only the call. It can never supply the tenant, role or credentials. This removes a whole class of confused-deputy bugs, where a trusted program is tricked into using its power for someone else. Short-lived credentials captured this way must be refreshed or fixed again when they expire. They should not be kept for the whole of a long session.

## Step by step

1. Write the runner so each argument can be given separately.
1. At startup, fill in the sandbox to get a narrower function.
1. At session start, fill in the permission policy.
1. In the loop, call the resulting one-input function with each tool call.

## Code sketch

```python
def run_tool(sandbox):
    def with_perms(perms):
        def run(call):
            perms.check(call)
            return sandbox.exec(call)
        return run
    return with_perms

in_sbx = run_tool(DockerSandbox())  # boot
session_run = in_sbx(user_perms)    # session
result = session_run(call)          # turn
```

## Be careful

Curried layers hide which values were fixed where. Name each partial function after what it has captured.

## Diagram

![Fig. 9.04: Each stage fixes one argument and hands on a smaller function.](/diagrams/currying.svg)

---

---
id: monad
number: "9.05"
title: Monad
chapter: functional
fit: direct
figure_number: Fig. 9.05
figure_caption: "Steps run on the Ok track, and the first Err skips straight to the end."
diagram: monad.svg
analogy_title: The railway with two tracks
---
## Gist

Chain tool steps that return Result values (a success or an error), so the first error skips the rest and arrives as one clean failure.

## Everyday comparison

### The railway with two tracks

Picture a railway line where every station has a set of points (track switches). If the train's paperwork is in order, it goes on along the main line to the next station. If anything is wrong, the points send it onto a side track. That track runs straight to the end of the line, skipping every remaining station. No station needs to check whether the train has already failed.

## Classic meaning

A type that wraps a value with extra context, such as the chance of failure. It provides bind, which chains functions that return that type and handles the context for you.

## In the agent system

Running a tool call has several steps, and each one can fail. The harness parses the JSON arguments and checks them against the schema (the expected shape). It checks permissions, runs the tool and formats the output. Each step returns Ok(value) for success or Err(reason) for failure. bind chains the steps, so the next step runs only on Ok. The first Err passes through the rest untouched. It becomes a tool_result with is_error set, a flag that marks the tool's answer as an error. The model reads it and can correct itself. The harness never throws an exception in the middle of the chain. Every failure carries a clear message instead of a stack trace, which is a dump of the program's internal calls.

## In a large company

Enterprise harnesses use Result chains so that failures are typed (labelled by kind) and auditable. This covers failures in validation, authorization, running the tool and output filtering. Without this, they get lost in exception traces. The error kind drives policy. Denials are logged as security events. Timeouts and HTTP 429 or 5xx errors (rate limits and server failures) are retried with backoff, waiting longer each time. But this happens only when the step is idempotent (safe to run twice with the same result). Validation errors go back to the model. Error messages sent to the model should be cleaned first. Stack traces and internal hostnames are a common way for data to leak out.

## Step by step

1. Each step takes a plain value and returns Ok or Err.
1. Start the chain with Ok(raw tool_use input).
1. bind runs the next step only when the current value is Ok.
1. At the end, Ok becomes a tool_result and Err becomes an error tool_result.

## Code sketch

```python
res = (Ok(block.input)
       .bind(validate(schema))
       .bind(authorize(perms))
       .bind(execute(tool))
       .map(format_output))

if res.is_ok:
    reply = tool_result(block.id, res.value)
else:
    reply = tool_error(block.id, res.error)
```

## Be careful

Wrapping everything in Result hides which failures are worth retrying. Carry an error kind, so the loop can retry timeouts but not denials.

## Diagram

![Fig. 9.05: Steps run on the Ok track, and the first Err skips straight to the end.](/diagrams/monad.svg)

---

---
id: mvc
number: "10.01"
title: MVCModel-View-Controller
chapter: frontend
fit: direct
aka: Model-View-Controller
review_id: rev-mvc
figure_number: Fig. 10.01
figure_caption: "Input goes through the controller. The view reads the model, never the controller."
diagram: mvc.svg
analogy_title: The cricket scorer and the scoreboard
---
## Gist

Split the chat app into three parts: a model that holds the conversation, a view that shows it, and a controller that changes it.

## Everyday comparison

### The cricket scorer and the scoreboard

At a cricket ground, the umpire signals a boundary. The scorer watches only the umpire and writes four runs into the scorebook. The scoreboard crew never talk to the umpire. They read the scorebook and change the numbers on the big board. If the board breaks, the book is still right. A second board across the ground can read the same book.

## Classic meaning

MVC splits an app into three parts. The model holds the data, views show it, and controllers handle input and update the model.

## In the agent system

The Conversation model holds the messages, the tool calls (the model's requests to run tools) and the run status. It knows nothing about the screen. The transcript view (the list of messages on screen) subscribes to the model, which means it asks to be told about changes. It redraws when a message is added, or when a streamed delta (a small new piece of text arriving live) makes one longer. The input controller owns the composer, the box where the user types. On Enter, it adds the user's message to the model and asks the harness to start a turn. On Escape, it asks the harness to cancel the run. The harness then records the cancelled status in the model. Streamed events from the agent loop also go into the model. So the view has exactly one place to read from.

## In a large company

In a large company, the transcript store on the server is the system of record (the official copy). It is used for audits and for rules about how long data is kept. The Conversation model in the app is only a cache (a local copy). The app reloads it from the server after a reconnect. Controller actions such as cancel must reach the server. Only the server can stop running tools and stop token spend (the cost of model usage). Client telemetry (usage data the app sends home) that watches the model should remove PII (personal data such as names and emails) before events leave the browser.

## Step by step

1. The user types in the composer, and the input controller receives the key presses.
1. The controller adds a user message to the Conversation model and starts a turn.
1. Streamed pieces of text from the agent loop make the assistant's message in the model longer.
1. The model tells the transcript view, which reads the model and redraws.

## Code sketch

```python
class InputController:
    def __init__(self, convo, harness):
        self.convo, self.h = convo, harness
    def on_enter(self, text):
        self.convo.append('user', text)
        self.h.start_turn(self.convo.id)

convo.subscribe(transcript_view.redraw)
harness.on_delta(convo.extend_last)
```

## Be careful

Do not let the view also read the harness stream directly. Then there are two sources of truth (two places that each claim to be correct). The transcript on screen slowly stops matching the saved conversation.

## Diagram

![Fig. 10.01: Input goes through the controller. The view reads the model, never the controller.](/diagrams/mvc.svg)

---

---
id: mvp
number: "10.02"
title: MVPModel-View-Presenter
chapter: frontend
fit: direct
aka: Model-View-Presenter
figure_number: Fig. 10.02
figure_caption: The view and the model never touch. The presenter sits between them.
diagram: mvp.svg
analogy_title: The theatre prompter
---
## Gist

Make the transcript view passive. A presenter reads the conversation, decides what to show, and tells the view what to display.

## Everyday comparison

### The theatre prompter

An actor on stage never opens the script. When a line is needed, the prompter, hidden in a box below the stage, reads the script. The prompter whispers the exact words, and the actor says them. The actor signals what happened on stage, such as a dropped prop or a missed cue. The prompter decides what comes next. An understudy can step in, and neither the script nor the prompter changes.

## Classic meaning

MVP is a kind of MVC where the view is thin and passive. A presenter holds the display logic and stands between the view and the model. Unlike MVC, the view never reads the model itself.

## In the agent system

The transcript view offers a small interface (a fixed list of functions). Examples are show_messages, show_spinner, disable_composer and an on_send callback (a function the view calls when the user presses Send). The view holds no logic. The ChatPresenter receives on_send. It adds the message to the Conversation model and starts the turn. When the model changes, the presenter decides how to show it. It may fold up a long tool result, or show a retry banner after an overloaded error. It disables the composer (the typing box) while a run is active. The view is only an interface. So tests can give the presenter a fake view that records each call, with no browser needed.

## In a large company

Regulated teams (teams under strict legal rules) like MVP for approval and consent screens. With a fake view, unit tests (small automatic checks) can prove one thing. A destructive tool call never appears without its Deny option or its risk banner. The presenter also turns tenant policy into controls. A tenant is one customer company sharing the platform. The server sends policy decisions, such as which actions a role may take. The presenter turns them into enabled or disabled buttons. The server must still enforce those policies, because a hidden button is not an access control.

## Step by step

1. The view passes the user's Send event to the presenter.
1. The presenter updates the Conversation model and starts a turn.
1. As new text arrives, the model tells the presenter, not the view.
1. The presenter formats the state and calls view methods such as show_messages.

## Code sketch

```python
class ChatPresenter:
    def __init__(self, view, convo):
        self.v, self.c = view, convo
        view.on_send = self.send
        convo.on_change = self.refresh
    def send(self, text):
        self.c.append('user', text)
        self.v.disable_composer()
    def refresh(self):
        self.v.show_messages(self.c.rows())
```

## Be careful

Presenters grow too big when every small display rule goes into them. Move pure formatting into helper functions. Then the presenter only decides what to show.

## Diagram

![Fig. 10.02: The view and the model never touch. The presenter sits between them.](/diagrams/mvp.svg)

---

---
id: model-view-viewmodel
number: "10.03"
title: Model-View-ViewModel
chapter: frontend
fit: direct
review_id: rev-model-view-viewmodel
figure_number: Fig. 10.03
figure_caption: "Bindings keep widgets and view model fields in sync, with no hand-written glue."
diagram: model-view-viewmodel.svg
analogy_title: The motorised mixing desk
---
## Gist

Bind chat widgets to a view model's watched fields, so typing, streaming and busy states stay in sync without hand-written glue code.

## Everyday comparison

### The motorised mixing desk

At a concert, the sound engineer pushes a fader (a sliding volume control), and the singer gets louder. That works because the fader is bound to that channel's level. For the encore, the engineer loads a saved setting. The faders then slide by themselves to the stored positions. Nobody writes instructions linking hand to channel. The desk keeps both sides matched, in both directions.

## Classic meaning

A view model offers state and commands as bindable properties (fields a screen element can be linked to). A binding framework keeps the view and the view model in sync. The view model talks to the model. Unlike MVP, nobody calls the view's methods; the bindings copy changes automatically.

## In the agent system

A ChatViewModel holds observable fields (values that announce when they change). They are draft, messages, busy, pending_approval and token_usage. It also has commands such as send and stop. The composer's text box has a two-way binding to draft, so each side updates the other. The Send button is enabled or disabled by a computed value, can_send, which is worked out from other fields. The transcript list is bound to messages. When the harness streams a text_delta (a small new piece of text), the view model updates messages. The binding layer then redraws only that row. The view model imports no widgets (screen elements). So a unit test can simply set draft and call send.

## In a large company

Enterprise apps built on binding frameworks use the view model as the single place where server policy becomes screen state. Examples are pending approvals, remaining budget and data residency banners (notices about which country data is kept in). View models are plain objects, so they get fast unit tests in CI (the automatic build and test system). Screenshot tests catch visual mistakes separately. App analytics should never log whole bound fields that hold user text. Drafts often contain PII (personal data such as names and emails) or pasted secrets.

## Step by step

1. When the screen opens, the binding layer links widget properties to view model fields.
1. Typing updates draft through the two-way binding, and can_send is worked out again.
1. The send command calls the session service and sets busy.
1. New streamed text updates messages, and the bound widgets redraw on their own.

## Code sketch

```python
class ChatViewModel:
    draft = observable('')
    messages = observable([])
    busy = observable(False)
    @computed
    def can_send(self):
        return self.draft and not self.busy
    def send(self):
        self.busy = True
        session.start_turn(self.draft)
        self.draft = ''
```

## Be careful

If you update a bound messages field on every token (a small piece of text), it redraws on every token. So coalesce deltas per animation frame: collect the new pieces and apply them once per screen refresh. Also keep two-way bindings few. Chains of them make the order of updates hard to follow.

## Diagram

![Fig. 10.03: Bindings keep widgets and view model fields in sync, with no hand-written glue.](/diagrams/model-view-viewmodel.svg)

---

---
id: mvi
number: "10.04"
title: MVIModel-View-Intent
chapter: frontend
fit: direct
aka: Model-View-Intent
review_id: rev-mvi
figure_number: Fig. 10.04
figure_caption: "One loop: intent in, new state out, and the view redrawn from the state alone."
diagram: mvi.svg
analogy_title: Correspondence chess by post
---
## Gist

Turn every click and stream event into an intent, fold it into one fixed state, and draw the whole chat from that state.

## Everyday comparison

### Correspondence chess by post

Two players in different countries never share a board. Each one posts a card with one move. The club secretary applies the move to the official position. Then the secretary mails back a picture of the whole board. Each player resets their own board to match the picture exactly before thinking again. The pile of cards can replay every game from the first move.

## Classic meaning

In MVI, data flows in one direction only. The view sends intents (messages saying what happened). A pure function (one with no side effects) combines each intent with the current state into a new state, and the view draws that state. Unlike MVVM, there is one state value, and only this function makes new versions of it.

## In the agent system

The chat app keeps one ChatState value. It holds the messages, the run status, pending approvals and the composer draft (the text being typed). Clicks become intents, such as Send, Stop and ApproveTool. The harness event stream becomes intents too, such as TextDelta, ToolUseStarted and TurnEnded. A pure function, reduce(state, intent), returns a new state. It never changes the old one. The view redraws from the new state and uses no other input. If you record the intents, you can replay a session exactly. This helps with bug reports and eval review (checks of how well the agent behaves).

## In a large company

Recorded intent logs let support staff replay a customer's session on a new app version. This makes them strong input for debugging and evals. In a large company they are also personal data. So recording is opt-in or done for only a sample of users. PII (personal data such as names and emails) is removed at the edge, before data leaves the device. They are kept and deleted under the same rules as transcripts, following GDPR (the EU data protection law) and the tenant contract. A tenant is one customer company sharing the platform. Side-effect commands sent after a state change, such as starting a turn, should carry an idempotency key. That is an ID that makes a repeated request safe to run twice. These commands should also be switched off during replay, so a replay never triggers real work.

## Step by step

1. The view or the event stream sends an intent, such as TextDelta.
1. The reducer combines the current state and the intent into a new state.
1. The store replaces the old state with the new snapshot.
1. The view draws the whole screen from the snapshot and waits for the next intent.

## Code sketch

```python
def reduce(s, i):
    if i.kind == 'send':
        m = s.msgs + [Msg('user', i.text)]
        return s.copy(busy=True, msgs=m)
    if i.kind == 'text_delta':
        old = s.msgs[-1]
        new = old.copy(text=old.text + i.text)
        msgs = s.msgs[:-1] + [new]
        return s.copy(msgs=msgs)
    if i.kind == 'turn_end':
        return s.copy(busy=False)
    return s
```

## Be careful

Do not call the harness API from inside the reducer, because that breaks replay. Instead, return side effects (actions that change the outside world) as separate commands. They run after the state changes.

## Diagram

![Fig. 10.04: One loop: intent in, new state out, and the view redrawn from the state alone.](/diagrams/mvi.svg)

---
id: flux
number: "10.05"
title: Flux
chapter: frontend
fit: direct
figure_number: Fig. 10.05
figure_caption: One dispatcher sends each action to all stores. Every store updates only its own part.
diagram: flux.svg
analogy_title: The newsroom wire desk
---
## Gist

Send every action through one dispatcher to several stores, each updating its own part, so chat views refresh in one direction.

## Everyday comparison

### The newsroom wire desk

Every story from the news wire is printed once, and a copy lands on every desk in the newsroom. The sports desk keeps the football result. The business desk keeps the share prices. The weather desk ignores both. Each desk updates only its own pages before the next edition is printed. Nobody walks over to edit another desk's page.

## Classic meaning

Flux is an app design where data flows one way. Actions go to a single dispatcher. The dispatcher passes each action to every registered store. Stores update and tell the views. Unlike MVI's single state, Flux has several stores, each keeping its own slice of the data.

## In the agent system

Harness events and clicks become plain action objects, such as text_delta, tool_result, usage and approve. A single dispatcher hands each action to every registered store. The TranscriptStore adds text. The ToolStore tracks the cards for running tools. The UsageStore adds up token counts (tokens are the small pieces of text the model reads and writes) for the cost meter. Each store sends a change event, and the views subscribed to that store redraw. The dispatcher refuses a new action while one is still being handled. This stops chains of updates that trigger more updates.

## In a large company

Large enterprise chat apps split state into separate stores per area, such as transcript, tool runs, approvals and usage. Then separate teams can own each part. The UsageStore behind the cost meter is for display only. Per-tenant budgets and chargeback (billing each team or customer for its own usage) are measured and enforced on the server, at the LLM gateway (one shared front door to all AI models). A tenant is one customer company sharing the platform. The app's figure should be checked against that server record. Dispatcher action logs make useful client traces (records of what happened in a request). Tag them with the OpenTelemetry trace id (a standard tracing ID) that the server returns.

## Step by step

1. An SSE event (a message streamed from the server) or a click becomes an action object.
1. The dispatcher passes the action to every registered store, one at a time.
1. Each store updates its own part if the action concerns it, then announces the change.
1. Subscribed views redraw, and the next user action starts the cycle again.

## Code sketch

```python
dispatcher = Dispatcher()
dispatcher.register(transcript_store.handle)
dispatcher.register(tool_store.handle)
dispatcher.register(usage_store.handle)

def on_sse(evt):
    dispatcher.dispatch({'type': evt.type,
                         'data': evt.data})
```

## Be careful

Avoid stores that wait on each other through chains of waitFor calls. They bring back the tangle that Flux removes. Keep stores independent, or merge them.

## Diagram

![Fig. 10.05: One dispatcher sends each action to all stores. Every store updates only its own part.](/diagrams/flux.svg)

---
id: bloc
number: "10.06"
title: Bloc
chapter: frontend
fit: direct
review_id: rev-bloc
figure_number: Fig. 10.06
figure_caption: "One event goes in, and a stream of states comes out over time."
diagram: bloc.svg
analogy_title: The automatic car wash
---
## Gist

Feed screen events into a component's input and listen to the stream of states it sends back, so one Send gives many states.

## Everyday comparison

### The automatic car wash

You drive up, press one button and roll onto the conveyor belt. You cannot steer or reach the brushes. You watch the sign over the tunnel change: Soaping, Rinsing, Waxing, Drying, Done. One press at the entrance produces a whole series of signs. If the dryer jams, the sign reads Fault instead.

## Classic meaning

Bloc means Business Logic Component. It receives events through a sink (an input slot), runs logic that may wait on other work, and sends its results out as a stream of states. Widgets rebuild from each state. Unlike Flux, one event can produce a whole series of states over time.

## In the agent system

A ChatBloc accepts events such as SendPressed, StopPressed and ApprovalGiven on its sink. Its SendPressed handler is an async generator, a function that can wait and hand out several results over time. First it yields (sends out) Sending. Then it waits on the harness stream and yields Streaming, with the growing text, after each new piece. It yields AwaitingApproval when a tool needs permission. It ends with Done or Failed. Widgets only listen to the state stream and rebuild. They never call the harness. A StopPressed event cancels the running handler. It then calls the harness cancel endpoint, so the server stops the turn. Finally it sends out Cancelled.

## In a large company

Enterprise agents often have mobile apps built with Flutter (a toolkit for phone apps). There, one bloc per screen keeps streaming, approval and error states testable. CI (the automatic build and test system) feeds them recorded event sequences. Cancelling is the critical path. StopPressed must reach a cancel endpoint on the server, so tools stop and spending ends. The cancel is written to the audit trail (the permanent record of who did what). Failed states should turn server error types into clear messages, without showing internal details. Examples are 429 (too many requests) with Retry-After, and 529 (overloaded).

## Step by step

1. The widget adds SendPressed to the bloc's event sink.
1. The bloc's handler yields Sending and opens the harness stream.
1. Each new piece of streamed text yields a new Streaming state with the text so far.
1. When the turn ends, the bloc yields Done, and widgets rebuild on every state.

## Code sketch

```python
class ChatBloc(Bloc):
    async def on_send(self, ev):
        yield Sending()
        text = ''
        async for d in harness.stream(ev.msg):
            text += d.text
            yield Streaming(text)
        yield Done(text)

bloc.add(SendPressed('fix the test'))
```

## Be careful

Sending a state for every token (small piece of text) floods widgets with rebuilds. Collect the new pieces and send at most one Streaming state per frame (one screen refresh).

## Diagram

![Fig. 10.06: One event goes in, and a stream of states comes out over time.](/diagrams/bloc.svg)

---
id: presentation-model
number: "10.07"
title: Presentation Model
chapter: frontend
fit: adapted
review_id: rev-presentation-model
figure_number: Fig. 10.07
figure_caption: "One screen model class, usable on any screen, feeds several thin views and is tested on its own."
diagram: presentation-model.svg
analogy_title: The school office timetable board
---
## Gist

Keep the chat screen's state and behaviour in a plain object that several thin views copy from and tests use directly.

## Everyday comparison

### The school office timetable board

The school office keeps one master board. It says which rooms are in use, which classes are cancelled and who is covering. The corridor screens, the text alerts to parents and the sheet on the staffroom door all copy from that board. An inspector can check that every class has cover by reading the board, without walking a single corridor.

## Classic meaning

The state and behaviour of a screen live in a model that is separate from any buttons or widgets. Each view keeps itself in step with that model. It is like MVVM without a binding framework: each view copies fields by hand.

## In the agent system

A ChatScreenModel holds everything the screen shows, in terms that fit any kind of screen. It holds the rows to show and whether Stop is visible. It holds the banner text after a rate-limit error (an error saying too many requests were sent). It also holds which tool card is open and the options on the approval prompt. The same class drives the web app, the terminal app and an IDE (code editor) side panel. Each screen gets its own instance (copy) of the class. Each view is a thin adapter (connecting code). It copies fields into its widgets and passes clicks back as method calls. Unit tests (small automatic checks) call model methods directly and check the fields. They run in milliseconds, with no browser.

## In a large company

Some platforms ship web, desktop, IDE and terminal apps. They share one presentation model class per screen, often in a shared TypeScript or Kotlin Multiplatform package (code that runs on many platforms). So approval and error behaviour is the same everywhere. That matters for compliance (meeting legal and audit rules). An approval prompt that shows risk text on the web but not in the terminal is an audit finding. The model's tests give the same result every time. They run on every pull request (proposed code change). They are separate from model-graded evals, which use an AI model to score how well the agent behaves.

## Step by step

1. Harness events update the ChatScreenModel through its methods.
1. The model works out derived fields again, such as stop_visible and banner.
1. Each view catches up by copying fields into its own widgets.
1. Input in any view calls the same model method, such as approve or stop.

## Code sketch

```python
class ChatScreenModel:
    def __init__(self):
        self.rows, self.banner = [], None
        self.stop_visible = False
    def on_error(self, err):
        if err.type == 'overloaded_error':
            self.banner = 'Busy, retrying'

def test_banner():
    m = ChatScreenModel()
    m.on_error(Err('overloaded_error'))
    assert m.banner == 'Busy, retrying'
```

## Be careful

With no binding framework, each view must catch up by hand. One forgotten update call leaves a screen showing old state.

## Diagram

![Fig. 10.07: One screen model class, usable on any screen, feeds several thin views and is tested on its own.](/diagrams/presentation-model.svg)

---
id: front-controller
number: "10.08"
title: Front Controller
chapter: frontend
fit: direct
review_id: rev-front-controller
figure_number: Fig. 10.08
figure_caption: Every request passes the same checks before any handler sees it.
diagram: front-controller.svg
analogy_title: The hospital front desk
---
## Gist

Send every request to the harness server through one entry handler that checks identity, logs, and passes it to the right handler.

## Everyday comparison

### The hospital front desk

Every visitor, courier and patient enters the hospital through the same front desk. The desk checks ID, hands out a badge, writes the arrival in the log and points each person to the right ward. The wards never check badges themselves, because nobody reaches them without passing the desk.

## Classic meaning

One handler receives all requests for a web app. It does the shared work, then passes each request to a specific command or view.

## In the agent system

The harness server has one entry point that every app request hits. That includes starting a turn, listing sessions, uploading a file and answering an approval. It checks the session token (proof of who is logged in). It finds the user's tenant, the customer company they belong to. It applies the rate limit for that tenant (a cap on how many requests it may send). It adds a trace id, a label used to follow the request through the system. Only then does it look up the route table and call the matching handler. New endpoints get authentication (checking who the user is) and audit logging for free. A fix to token checking goes into one file. Handlers still check that the user may act on this specific session or file. Checking identity at the door is not object-level authorization (permission for one specific item).

## In a large company

In large company setups, the front controller's job is usually split in two. An API gateway at the edge (a shared front door for all requests) checks OIDC tokens (sign-in proof from the company login system). It also applies per-tenant rate limits and terminates TLS, meaning it decrypts the secure connection. Then an entry point inside the app finds the tenant, starts an OpenTelemetry span (one timed step in a trace) and writes the audit record. Permission for a specific item still belongs in each handler. An example is whether this user may resume this session. It can also be a shared policy check against OPA or Cedar (policy engines that answer "is this allowed?"). A route table written as plain data lets security reviewers see every open endpoint in one place.

## Step by step

1. An app request arrives at the single entry handler.
1. The handler checks the session's identity and the rate limit.
1. It tags the request with a trace id and logs it.
1. It looks up the route and passes the request to the turn, sessions or upload handler.

## Code sketch

```python
ROUTES = {'POST /turn': turn_handler,
          'GET /sessions': sessions_handler,
          'POST /upload': upload_handler}

def front_controller(req):
    user = auth.verify(req.token)
    limiter.check(user)
    req.trace_id = new_trace_id()
    key = f'{req.method} {req.path}'
    return ROUTES[key](req, user)
```

## Be careful

A front controller that collects business logic becomes the file every team edits. Keep it to shared checks and routing.

## Diagram

![Fig. 10.08: Every request passes the same checks before any handler sees it.](/diagrams/front-controller.svg)

---

---
id: page-controller
number: "10.09"
title: Page Controller
chapter: frontend
fit: adapted
review_id: rev-page-controller
figure_number: Fig. 10.09
figure_caption: Each route has its own controller and view. The router only links paths to controllers.
diagram: page-controller.svg
analogy_title: "Stalls at a farmers' market"
---
## Gist

Give each screen of the harness app, such as sessions, chat and settings, its own controller that handles its route.

## Everyday comparison

### Stalls at a farmers' market

There is no central till at a farmers' market. The cheese stall has its own seller who cuts, weighs and wraps cheese. The baker at the next stall handles bread. A shopper walks to the stall for what they want. A new honey stall can open on Saturday, and the others change nothing.

## Classic meaning

A page controller handles the requests for one page or action on a web site. There is one controller for each page.

## In the agent system

The app's router links each path (web address) to one controller. /sessions goes to a SessionsController. It loads the list of sessions and handles rename and delete. /chat/:id goes to a ChatController. It opens the event stream and handles send and stop. /settings goes to a SettingsController. It reads and saves permission modes and MCP server settings (MCP is a standard way to connect tools to an AI model). The router only links a path to a controller and does no shared work. So each controller owns its own page's data loading and actions. Adding a usage page means one new route and one new controller. The others need no edits.

## In a large company

Agent platforms have admin consoles for tenants, policies, MCP server allowlists (lists of approved servers), audit search and usage. A tenant is one customer company sharing the platform. These consoles are often built page by page. The team behind each backend owns its page. Each controller must limit every query to the right tenant and check the caller's role. Page controllers share no gate unless one is added. A common safeguard is a base controller or middleware (code that runs before every handler). It enforces the SSO session (single sign-on), RBAC (role-based access control: permissions given by job role) and audit logging. Then a new page cannot skip them.

## Step by step

1. The router matches the web address to one page controller.
1. That controller loads the data its page needs.
1. It draws its own view and handles that page's actions.
1. Other pages and their controllers stay untouched.

## Code sketch

```python
class SessionsController:
    def get(self, req):
        rows = store.list_sessions(req.user)
        return view('sessions', rows=rows)
    def post_rename(self, req):
        s = store.get(req.id, owner=req.user)
        s.rename(req.title)

router.add('/sessions', SessionsController)
router.add('/chat/:id', ChatController)
router.add('/settings', SettingsController)
```

## Be careful

Shared steps, such as checking login and loading the user, get copied into every controller. Move them into a base class (shared parent code), or put a front controller in front.

## Diagram

![Fig. 10.09: Each route has its own controller and view. The router only links paths to controllers.](/diagrams/page-controller.svg)

---

---
id: composite-view
number: "10.10"
title: Composite View
chapter: frontend
fit: direct
review_id: rev-composite-view
figure_number: Fig. 10.10
figure_caption: "Messages and blocks share one interface, so a new piece of text finds its leaf by walking the tree."
diagram: composite-view.svg
analogy_title: A toy spaceship built from sub-assemblies
---
## Gist

Build the transcript as a tree of message parts, so text, tool cards and artifact cards all draw through one shared interface.

## Everyday comparison

### A toy spaceship built from sub-assemblies

The building-brick instructions have you make the cockpit, each wing and the engine pod from separate bags. Each part is complete on its own and clicks onto the body with the same studs. Lift the ship, and everything comes with it. Pull off a wing, and you can rebuild it without touching the cockpit.

## Classic meaning

A screen is built from smaller views arranged in a tree. Each one is managed on its own, so a page is put together from reusable parts.

## In the agent system

The TranscriptView holds one MessageView per message. Each assistant MessageView holds child views, chosen by content block type (the kind of piece inside a message). TextView is for text. ThinkingView is for a folded-up thinking block. ToolCardView is for a tool_use, the model's request to run a tool. The card is later matched to its tool_result (the tool's answer) by tool_use_id. That result arrives in the next user message. If the tool call produced an artifact (a file or page the agent made), the card holds an ArtifactCardView child. Every part has the same two functions: render() to draw itself and update(delta) to take in new text. Suppose a streamed piece of text arrives for block 2 of the last message. The transcript passes it down the tree, and only that leaf (end part) redraws.

## In a large company

Enterprise transcripts can run to thousands of blocks. So the views are virtualised: only the parts visible on screen are drawn. Each part is keyed by message id and block id. Each leaf type is a natural place for policy. For example, a tool card can hide redacted fields (data removed for privacy). A citation view can show document sensitivity labels. An older app may meet block types it does not know. It should show a safe placeholder for them, so a server upgrade never breaks the whole tree.

## Step by step

1. The transcript view creates one message view per message.
1. Each message view creates a child view per content block, chosen by block type.
1. render() on the top view draws the children, in order, all the way down.
1. A streamed piece of text is passed down the tree to the one leaf it belongs to.

## Code sketch

```python
BLOCK_VIEWS = {'text': TextView,
               'thinking': ThinkingView,
               'tool_use': ToolCardView}

class MessageView(View):
    def __init__(self, msg):
        self.kids = [BLOCK_VIEWS[b.type](b)
                     for b in msg.content
                     if b.type in BLOCK_VIEWS]
    def render(self):
        return div(*(k.render()
                     for k in self.kids))
```

## Be careful

If one new piece of text makes the whole tree redraw, long transcripts get slow. Give each part a stable key (a fixed ID), so only the changed leaf redraws.

## Diagram

![Fig. 10.10: Messages and blocks share one interface, so a new piece of text finds its leaf by walking the tree.](/diagrams/composite-view.svg)

---

---
id: template-view
number: "10.11"
title: Template View
chapter: frontend
fit: direct
review_id: rev-template-view
figure_number: Fig. 10.11
figure_caption: The layout lives in the template. Each block only supplies values for its gaps.
diagram: template-view.svg
analogy_title: The wedding invitation print shop
---
## Gist

Draw tool cards and status lines from page templates with blanks, filled from the content block's fields when shown.

## Everyday comparison

### The wedding invitation print shop

The print shop keeps a few card designs with gaps in the wording. The gaps are for the couple's names, the date and the place. When a new order arrives, the clerk types the details into the gaps and runs the press. Hundreds of couples get cards in the same layout. Change the font on one design, and every future order that uses it changes too.

## Classic meaning

A template view makes a web page from a fixed page template with markers in it. When the page is made, each marker is replaced with a worked-out value.

## In the agent system

Each content block type (kind of piece in a message) has a template file. tool_card.html shows the tool name, a summary of its input, a status badge and a result you can fold up. approval.html shows the command, the reason, and Allow and Deny buttons. The renderer (the code that draws the screen) picks the template by block type. It fills the placeholders from the fields of the tool_use (the model's request to run a tool) and the tool_result (the tool's answer). It escapes every value, which means special characters are made harmless. So model output cannot inject markup (sneak page code into the screen). Designers change the layout in templates. They do not touch the code that handles the event stream.

## In a large company

Model output and tool results are untrusted input. So enterprise apps use a template engine that escapes values automatically (autoescaping). They also use a strict Content Security Policy, a browser rule that limits which scripts may run. Any markdown (formatted text) shown on screen also goes through an HTML sanitiser such as DOMPurify, which strips dangerous page code. White-labelled setups (sold under each customer's own brand) often give each tenant its own template theme. A tenant is one customer company sharing the platform. This keeps branding out of code. Security review treats any raw or unescaped filter in a template as a finding. Otherwise a tool result with prompt injection (hidden instructions planted in content) could run script in an approver's browser.

## Step by step

1. A content block arrives, such as a finished tool_use with its result.
1. The renderer picks the template for that block type.
1. It fills each placeholder from the block's fields, escaping the values.
1. The filled-in page code is added to the transcript.

## Code sketch

```python
# tool_card.html (autoescape on)
# <div class='tool'>{{ name }}: {{ status }}
#   <pre>{{ result | truncate(400) }}</pre>
# </div>

tpl = templates.get('tool_card.html')
# the engine escapes every placeholder
html = tpl.render(name=block.name,
                  status=result.status,
                  result=result.text)
```

## Be careful

Templates that call services or follow business rules become hidden code. Keep them to placeholders and simple loops. Put formatting in helpers.

## Diagram

![Fig. 10.11: The layout lives in the template. Each block only supplies values for its gaps.](/diagrams/template-view.svg)
