id: view-helper
number: "10.12"
title: View Helper
chapter: frontend
fit: direct
figure_number: Fig. 10.12
figure_caption: "Views keep only layout. Every formatting rule lives once, in a shared helper."
diagram: view-helper.svg
analogy_title: "The library's date stamp and label maker"
---
## Gist

Move markdown display, code colouring and number formatting out of views into small helpers that every view calls.

## Everyday comparison

### The library's date stamp and label maker

The librarian at the desk does not hand-write due dates or spine labels. She presses the date stamp, which always prints the date in the same style. She uses the label maker, which prints shelf numbers in the library's format. Every branch has the same two tools. So a book stamped anywhere looks the same.

## Classic meaning

Formatting logic lives in helper objects, so views stay focused on layout. Many views can reuse the same logic.

## In the agent system

Message views, tool cards and the usage meter all need the same formatting. Markdown (formatted text) must become safe HTML. Code blocks need colouring by language. 12345 tokens (small pieces of text the model reads and writes) show as 12.3k. Cost shows as $0.04. Timestamps show as 2m ago. Long file paths get shortened. All this lives in helpers such as md(), highlight(), fmt_tokens() and rel_time(). Views call them and stay as plain layout. A change to how token counts look is made once.

## In a large company

Shared helpers hold the company's display rules. They format numbers and currency for each country, for chargeback figures (billing each team for its usage). They show timestamps in the user's time zone. They also mask secrets or PII (personal data such as names and emails) in tool output. With masking in one helper, it is easy to test and audit. But masking in the browser is only cosmetic. Sensitive values should already be removed on the server. The markdown helper must sanitise HTML (strip dangerous page code). Model output and tool results can carry injected page code.

## Step by step

1. A view receives a message or usage record to show.
1. It calls a helper for each formatted piece, instead of formatting inside the view.
1. Helpers return safe strings or page pieces, ready to show.
1. The view places them into its layout.

## Code sketch

```python
def fmt_tokens(n):
    if n < 1000:
        return str(n)
    return f'{n / 1000:.1f}k'

# inside the usage meter view
label = f'{fmt_tokens(u.input)} in, '
label += f'{fmt_tokens(u.output)} out'
body = md(msg.text, highlight=highlight)
```

## Be careful

Helpers that fetch data, such as prices over the network, slow down every redraw. Pass the data in, and keep helpers pure (no side effects, same output for the same input).

## Diagram

![Fig. 10.12: Views keep only layout. Every formatting rule lives once, in a shared helper.](/diagrams/view-helper.svg)

---
id: service-to-worker
number: "10.13"
title: Service to Worker
chapter: frontend
fit: direct
figure_number: Fig. 10.13
figure_caption: The work finishes before any view is chosen or drawn.
diagram: service-to-worker.svg
analogy_title: The garage service desk
---
## Gist

Run the turn to the end first, then choose and draw a result view, so views only show results that already exist.

## Everyday comparison

### The garage service desk

You leave your car at the desk and go for a coffee. The mechanics inspect it in the workshop. Only when the work is finished does the desk print your paperwork. The form depends on the outcome: a pass certificate, a list of repairs or a quote for parts. The desk clerk never picks up a spanner.

## Classic meaning

A front controller and a dispatcher handle the request and run the business logic first. Then they hand control to a view. The view draws the prepared data, with help from view helpers.

## In the agent system

This suits an endpoint that does not stream, such as a scheduled task run or a summarise-this-session call. The controller passes the request to the agent loop. The loop calls the model and tools until the turn ends. The loop returns a TurnResult with the final text, the tool calls, the stop_reason (why the model stopped) and the usage. The dispatcher then picks the view from that result. It shows a summary page for end_turn and an error page for max_tokens (the reply hit its length limit). It shows an approval page if a tool is waiting for permission. Views get a finished result they cannot change, and they never call the model.

## In a large company

Enterprise platforms use this style for batch and scheduled agent work, such as nightly report runs. But they run the turn in a durable workflow engine like Temporal or AWS Step Functions. These tools keep long jobs going even through crashes. The server replies 202 Accepted (request received, work in progress) with a job id. The result view is drawn when the app polls (checks back) or a webhook (a call back from the server) fires. So gateway timeouts never cut a long turn in half. The stored TurnResult carries its trace id and usage. So the page shown, the audit log and the chargeback ledger (the record used for billing) all agree.

## Step by step

1. The front controller receives the request and checks who sent it.
1. The dispatcher runs the agent loop to the end and gets a TurnResult.
1. It chooses a view based on stop_reason and pending approvals.
1. The view draws the prepared result, using view helpers for formatting.

## Code sketch

```python
def handle(req):
    result = agent_loop.run(req.session,
                            req.prompt)
    if result.pending_approval:
        view = 'approval'
    elif result.stop_reason == 'end_turn':
        view = 'summary'
    else:
        view = 'error'
    return render(view, result=result)
```

## Be careful

In this style, a long agent turn keeps the response waiting. So use it for short or background work, and stream interactive chat instead.

## Diagram

![Fig. 10.13: The work finishes before any view is chosen or drawn.](/diagrams/service-to-worker.svg)

---
id: client-side-ui-composition
number: "10.14"
title: Client-Side UI Composition
chapter: frontend
fit: direct
review_id: rev-client-side-ui-composition
figure_number: Fig. 10.14
figure_caption: Each service ships its own piece. The shell only lays them out and passes messages.
diagram: client-side-ui-composition.svg
analogy_title: The trade-show hall
---
## Gist

Let the chat shell build its screen from pieces owned by separate services: the transcript, the artifact viewer and widgets.

## Everyday comparison

### The trade-show hall

The organiser rents the hall, draws the floor plan and runs the entrance and the signs. Each exhibitor designs, builds and staffs its own booth in its assigned space. Visitors walk through one show. When a booth is rebuilt overnight, the organiser and the neighbouring booths do nothing.

## Classic meaning

Each microservice team (a team owning one small, separate service) ships its own piece of the screen. A shell in the browser loads those pieces and puts them together into one page while the app runs.

## In the agent system

The chat app is a thin shell. It owns the layout, the login and an event bus (a shared channel for passing messages). The transcript pane comes from the chat service. The artifact panel comes from an artifact service. It loads into a sandboxed iframe, a walled-off frame on its own origin (its own web address). Inline widgets such as a map or chart are bundles (packed code files) from a widget service. The shell mounts (places) each piece into a slot. It passes messages between them, such as open artifact 42 from a link in the transcript. Each service releases its piece on its own schedule.

## In a large company

Large agent platforms build the app from team-owned pieces. They use module federation or web components (two ways to load separate code pieces into one page). The shell owns SSO (single sign-on), the design system and a typed message bus (one that checks the shape of each message). Untrusted pieces, such as artifacts, run in sandboxed iframes on a separate origin. A strict Content Security Policy (a browser rule limiting what may run) applies. The shell checks the origin and the schema (expected shape) of every postMessage, the browser's way of sending messages between frames. A manifest (a list of versions) pins each piece's version. So one piece can be rolled back without redeploying the shell.

## Step by step

1. The shell loads with layout slots and a shared event bus.
1. It fetches each piece's code or frame from the service that owns it.
1. Pieces mount into their slots and draw on their own.
1. Actions across pieces, such as opening an artifact from a transcript link, go through the bus.

## Code sketch

```python
shell = Shell(layout='chat')
shell.mount('main',
    remote('chat-svc/transcript.js'))
shell.mount('side',
    iframe('artifacts-svc/view/42',
           sandbox='allow-scripts'))
shell.mount('inline',
    remote('widgets-svc/map.js'))
shell.bus.on('open_artifact',
    lambda id: shell.slot('side').load(id))
```

## Be careful

If each piece packs its own copy of a UI framework, the app gets heavy and slow to load. Share core libraries through the shell.

## Diagram

![Fig. 10.14: Each service ships its own piece. The shell only lays them out and passes messages.](/diagrams/client-side-ui-composition.svg)

id: naked-objects
number: "10.15"
title: Naked Objects
chapter: frontend
fit: adapted
review_id: rev-naked-objects
figure_number: Fig. 10.15
figure_caption: The schema the model already uses becomes the form the user approves.
diagram: naked-objects.svg
analogy_title: The ballot printed from the register
---
## Gist

Build approval cards and input forms straight from each tool's JSON schema, so a new tool gets a working screen with no new screen code.

## Everyday comparison

### The ballot printed from the register

The election office does not design a new ballot for every race. Candidates go into the register with a name, party and area. The printing system lays out every ballot from those records, with the same boxes and rules. Add a candidate to the register, and they appear on the next print run, in the right place.

## Classic meaning

The screen is built automatically from the structure and behaviour of the business objects. So users act directly on those objects.

## In the agent system

Each tool already has an input_schema, written in JSON Schema (a standard way to describe the shape of data). It is there for the model, and the screen code reuses it. A string becomes a text field, an enum (fixed list of choices) becomes a dropdown, and a boolean (yes or no) becomes a checkbox. Required properties get a marker, and descriptions become help text. Some tool_use requests (the model's requests to run a tool) need approval. For those, the card is built from the schema and filled in with the model's input. So the user can read, edit and approve the exact arguments. Edited values are checked against the same schema before the tool runs. A tool newly listed by an MCP server gets an approval card at once. MCP is a standard way to connect tools to an AI model.

## In a large company

With approval cards built from schemas, a company can add new MCP tools without releasing new screen code. This matters when hundreds of internal tools are on the allowlist (the list of approved tools). Titles and descriptions in a third-party schema are untrusted text. So the card escapes them. Next to them it shows risk labels set by the platform's policy engine (the system that decides what is allowed). When a user edits arguments, the audit record keeps both the model's proposal and the approved input. The tool_result (the tool's answer) tells the model what actually ran.

## Step by step

1. The app fetches the tool list, with each tool's input_schema.
1. A tool_use that needs approval arrives with the model's input.
1. The generator builds one form field per schema property, filled in with the input.
1. The user edits or approves, the values are checked against the schema, and the tool runs.

## Code sketch

```python
WIDGETS = {'string': TextField,
           'integer': NumberField,
           'boolean': Checkbox}

def approval_card(tool, call):
    fields = []
    for k, spec in tool.input_schema[
            'properties'].items():
        w = Select if 'enum' in spec \
            else WIDGETS[spec['type']]
        fields.append(w(k, call.input.get(k)))
    return Card(tool.name, fields, ['Allow'])
```

## Be careful

Schema text from a third-party MCP server is untrusted. So escape it (make special characters harmless), and take risk labels from your own policy. When the user edits arguments, record both versions. Tell the model what actually ran.

## Diagram

![Fig. 10.15: The schema the model already uses becomes the form the user approves.](/diagrams/naked-objects.svg)

id: data-locality
number: "11.01"
title: Data Locality
chapter: performance
fit: adapted
figure_number: Fig. 11.01
figure_caption: Stable bytes at the start get reused. Only the changing end is computed fresh.
diagram: data-locality.svg
analogy_title: "The scrub nurse's instrument tray"
---
## Gist

Put stable content first in the prompt and keep a session's often-used data together, so caches hit and loads stay cheap.

## Everyday comparison

### The scrub nurse's instrument tray

Before every operation, the scrub nurse lays out the same instruments in the same order on one tray beside the surgeon. The surgeon's hand goes to the right place without looking. Nothing has to be fetched from a cupboard during the operation. Only items for today's patient go at the far end of the tray.

## Classic meaning

Data locality means storing items that are used together next to each other in memory. The CPU cache (a small fast memory) and prefetcher (which loads data ahead of time) can then serve them instead of slower main memory.

## In the agent system

Prompt caches and the provider's KV cache (the model's saved internal work for text it has already read) reuse work only for an identical prefix. The match starts from the very first token. So the harness orders every request from most stable to least stable. Tool definitions come first, then the system prompt. Next come long-lived project context and earlier turns. Only then come the new user message and fresh tool results. Timestamps, request ids and per-turn instructions go at the end, never at the top. On the storage side, a session's transcript, memory files and recent tool results live in one record or one shard (one slice of the database). So building a turn's context takes a single read.

## In a large company

In an enterprise platform, prompt layout is a governed template. The platform owns the order of tools, system policy text and tenant context. A tenant is one customer company. A template change that breaks the cached prefix is caught before release by cost and latency regression gates (checks that block a release that makes things worse). Per-tenant context goes after the shared platform prefix. This way the common part can be reused, while tenant data stays in its own section. On the storage side, keeping a session's hot (often-used) data in one record or shard also helps with data residency and erasure. Data residency means keeping data in an approved region. It is simpler because one tenant's session lives in one place.

## Step by step

1. Sort prompt sections by how often they change, most stable first.
1. Move changing items (time, ids, retrieved snippets) after the last cache breakpoint.
1. Add new turns at the end, so earlier bytes never shift.
1. Store each session's often-used data together, so one read builds the context.

## Code sketch

```python
def build_request(s, user_msg):
    return {
      'tools': TOOLS,        # never changes
      'system': [RULES, s.project_ctx],
      'messages': s.history + [  # append
          {'role': 'user', 'content': [
              user_msg, f'now: {clock()}']}],
    }
```

## Be careful

Putting a retrieved document or the current date near the top of the prompt shifts every later byte. Then the cache is lost on every turn.

## Diagram

![Fig. 11.01: Stable bytes at the start get reused. Only the changing end is computed fresh.](/diagrams/data-locality.svg)

id: spatial-partition
number: "11.02"
title: Spatial Partition
chapter: performance
fit: direct
figure_number: Fig. 11.02
figure_caption: The query visits two nearby cells and never touches the other sixty-two.
diagram: spatial-partition.svg
analogy_title: "The taxi dispatcher's district map"
---
## Gist

Split the embedding space into regions, so a memory or code search checks only the few cells nearest the query.

## Everyday comparison

### The taxi dispatcher's district map

A dispatcher with five hundred taxis does not check every driver when a call comes in from the old town. Her map is divided into districts. She radios only the cabs in that district and the two next to it. A cab across the river is never even considered.

## Classic meaning

Spatial partition organises objects by position in a structure that splits space, such as a grid, tree or clusters. A search for nearby objects then checks only the regions that matter.

## In the agent system

An agent's long-term memory, docs index or codebase can hold millions of embeddings. An embedding is a list of numbers, also called a vector, that stands for the meaning of a piece of text. A partitioned index such as IVF clustering splits these vectors into cells. Each cell has a centroid (its centre point). When a vector is written, it goes into the cell of its nearest centroid. At query time, the retrieval tool turns the question into an embedding and ranks the centroids by distance. It scans only the closest nprobe cells (nprobe is the number of cells to check). It returns the top-k chunks (the k best matches) in milliseconds. Partitions can also follow metadata. With shards per repository or per tenant (customer company), a memory search never crosses into another user's data.

## In a large company

In an enterprise platform, vector indexes use partitioning for speed. Examples are pgvector with IVFFlat, FAISS, or a managed vector database. Tenant isolation is enforced separately. It uses per-tenant indexes, namespaces or row-level security (database rules that limit which rows each user can see). It does not rely on which cells happen to be probed. Apply metadata filters for document permissions inside the index query itself. Filtering after an approximate search can return too few results. It can also tempt code to fall back to a query with no filter. Recall at a given nprobe is part of the retrieval eval suite. Teams check it again when the embedding model changes.

## Step by step

1. At write time, embed each chunk and put it in the cell of its nearest centroid.
1. At query time, embed the query and rank the centroids by distance.
1. Scan only the closest nprobe cells for candidate vectors.
1. Rerank the candidates and return the top-k chunks to the agent.

## Code sketch

```python
def add(chunk):
    v = embed(chunk.text)
    cell = nearest(centroids, v)
    cells[cell].append((v, chunk))

def search(query, k=8, nprobe=3):
    q = embed(query)
    near = closest(centroids, q, nprobe)
    cands = sum((cells[i] for i in near), [])
    return top_k(cands, q, k)
```

## Be careful

If you probe too few cells, you miss relevant memories that sit near a cell border. Tune nprobe on a recall eval (a test of how many right answers are found), not on speed alone.

## Diagram

![Fig. 11.02: The query visits two nearby cells and never touches the other sixty-two.](/diagrams/spatial-partition.svg)

id: arrange-act-assert
number: "12.01"
title: Arrange/Act/Assert
chapter: testing
fit: direct
review_id: rev-arrange-act-assert
figure_number: Fig. 12.01
figure_caption: "Setup, one run, then checks: each phase stays in its own box."
diagram: arrange-act-assert.svg
analogy_title: The car crash test
---
## Gist

Build each eval case in three steps: set up a sample conversation and fakes, run the agent, then check the transcript.

## Everyday comparison

### The car crash test

Engineers seat a dummy, strap it in, fit the sensors and set the speed. Then one thing happens: the car hits the barrier. Afterwards, they compare the sensor readings and the high-speed film with fixed limits. Nobody adjusts the dummy halfway through the crash. Each run tests one kind of impact.

## Classic meaning

Each test has three parts. Arrange sets up the starting state. Act does one thing to exercise the behaviour. Assert checks the outcome.

## In the agent system

An eval case is one test of how the agent behaves. Its arrange step sets up a starting conversation: a system prompt (standing instructions), earlier turns and a user request. It also sets up a sandbox (a walled-off workspace) with files already in it, and stubbed or recorded tools (fake tools with set answers). The act is one call: run the agent until end_turn or a turn cap (a maximum number of turns). The asserts then inspect the transcript and side effects (changes to the outside world). Fixed checks come first. Was edit_file called on the right path? Did any tool run without approval? Do the tests pass now? Then a model-graded rubric score (an AI judge scoring against a checklist) must reach a threshold. Runs vary from one to the next. So the suite repeats each case several times. It gates on the pass rate compared with the last release. Each trial still has a single act, so failures are easy to trace.

## In a large company

Enterprise eval suites keep their test cases in a versioned golden dataset (an official, tracked set of examples). Fixed cases run against recorded tool answers on every pull request (proposed code change). Cases that use the live model run several trials each. They run on a schedule and before any change of model or prompt. Regression gates in CI (automatic checks that block a change that makes things worse) compare pass rates and rubric scores with the last released baseline. A significant drop blocks the merge. Model-graded checks use a pinned judge model (a fixed version that does not change). Its rubric is calibrated against human labels. So a change of judge cannot quietly move the gate.

## Step by step

1. Arrange: load the sample conversation, fill the sandbox and register the fake tools.
1. Act: run the agent once, until it stops or hits the turn cap.
1. Assert: check tool calls, file changes and the final text in the transcript.
1. Record pass or fail, with the transcript attached for review.

## Code sketch

```python
def test_fixes_failing_test():
    # arrange
    convo = fixtures.load('bug_report.json')
    box = Sandbox(files='repo_snapshot/')
    # act
    t = agent.run(convo, box, max_turns=20)
    # assert: deterministic checks first
    assert t.called('edit_file', 'calc.py')
    assert box.run('pytest').ok
    # then a model-graded rubric score
    assert judge(t, 'explains the fix') >= 4
```

## Be careful

Checking for exact wording makes evals flaky (they pass and fail at random), because model output varies. Check tool calls, side effects and rubric scores instead.

## Diagram

![Fig. 12.01: Setup, one run, then checks: each phase stays in its own box.](/diagrams/arrange-act-assert.svg)

id: object-mother
number: "12.02"
title: Object Mother
chapter: testing
fit: direct
figure_number: Fig. 12.02
figure_caption: Evals ask for setups by name. One class knows how to build them correctly.
diagram: object-mother.svg
analogy_title: The film extras agency
---
## Gist

Give evals a factory of named, ready-made test setups, such as an angry customer or a session waiting on an approval.

## Everyday comparison

### The film extras agency

A director phones the casting agency and asks for two tired commuters and a tourist with a map. The agency sends people already dressed and briefed for those parts. So nobody explains costumes on set. When the studio changes its standard costume, the agency updates every booking at once.

## Classic meaning

An Object Mother is a class with factory methods (functions that build objects). Each one returns a ready-made test object in a named state. So tests share realistic fixtures (prepared test data) without repeating setup.

## In the agent system

Eval suites need the same starting points again and again. One is a 200-turn conversation close to the compaction threshold (the point where old messages get summarised to save space). Others are a session waiting on a tool approval and a persona (a pretend user) who writes short angry messages. Another is a sandbox (walled-off workspace) with a broken test. A FixtureMother offers methods such as long_convo(200), pending_approval(tool='bash') and angry_customer(). They build valid sessions with the correct roles and sensible defaults. Each tool_use (request to run a tool) is correctly paired by id with its tool_result (the tool's answer). When the message format changes, only the mother is updated.

## In a large company

Enterprise fixture factories build synthetic (made-up) personas and sessions. Copying real production transcripts into fixtures would move customer data into code repositories and CI logs (the logs of the automatic test system). That breaks GDPR purpose limits (the EU rule that data be used only for its stated purpose) and most customer contracts. Where real traffic is needed, it is sampled with consent and has personal data removed. It is kept in a controlled eval data store with rules on how long it is kept. The mother is also the place to describe tenant shapes. A tenant is one customer company sharing the platform. Examples are a tenant whose data must stay in the EU, or a role without approval rights. This way, policy paths get tested.

## Step by step

1. An eval asks the mother for a named setup, such as pending_approval().
1. The mother builds a valid session with defaults and paired ids.
1. The eval changes only the details it cares about.
1. Many evals share the same setups, so a format change is fixed in one place.

## Code sketch

```python
class Mother:
    @staticmethod
    def pending_approval(tool='bash'):
        s = Session(user=Mother.persona())
        s.add_user('clean up the build dir')
        s.add_tool_use(tool, cmd='rm -rf out')
        s.status = 'awaiting_approval'
        return s
    @staticmethod
    def persona(mood='neutral'):
        return Persona(name='Sam', mood=mood)
```

## Be careful

A mother with dozens of nearly identical methods gets hard to find your way around. Pair it with a builder (an object that makes small changes step by step) for small variations.

## Diagram

![Fig. 12.02: Evals ask for setups by name. One class knows how to build them correctly.](/diagrams/object-mother.svg)

id: page-object
number: "12.03"
title: Page Object
chapter: testing
fit: adapted
review_id: rev-page-object
figure_number: Fig. 12.03
figure_caption: Callers speak in user actions. Only the page object knows the selectors.
diagram: page-object.svg
analogy_title: The museum tour guide
---
## Gist

Hide a chat screen's selectors behind methods like send() and approve_tool(), so evals and browser agents speak in user actions.

## Everyday comparison

### The museum tour guide

Visitors on a tour ask to see the Dutch paintings or the dinosaur hall. They never need the floor plan. The guide knows which wing, staircase and room each request means. When the museum moves the dinosaurs to the east wing, only the guide learns the new route. Every tour still asks for the dinosaur hall.

## Classic meaning

A page object wraps a web page in an object. Its methods stand for the things a user can do on the page. So tests do not depend on how the page's HTML is built.

## In the agent system

End-to-end tests (tests that drive the whole app like a real user) use a ChatPage object. It has methods such as send(text), wait_for_turn_end(), approve_tool(name), open_artifact(n) and transcript_text(). Inside, it knows the selectors (the codes that find elements on the page) for the composer and the stop button. It also knows how to tell that streaming has finished. The same idea helps browser tools for agents. A page object for a known site gives the agent steady, high-level actions. The agent does not have to make raw clicks on fragile screen positions. A page object given to an agent leaves out approval controls. So the agent can never approve its own tool calls. When the screen is redesigned, only the page object changes.

## In a large company

Enterprise teams run page-object test suites in Playwright or Selenium (tools that drive a real browser). They run against every app build in CI, the automatic build and test system. Selectors use stable test ids, so redesigns do not break the gate. Sometimes a browser-using agent drives internal web apps. Then a page object or a narrow set of tools limits it to approved actions. Each action gets a permission check, like any other tool. The approval controls of the agent harness itself must never be reachable through such a set of tools. That would let the agent approve itself.

## Step by step

1. The test or agent calls a high-level method, such as send('hi').
1. The page object turns it into browser actions on known selectors.
1. It waits for the right signal, such as the stop button disappearing.
1. It returns plain data, such as the transcript text, for checking.

## Code sketch

```python
class ChatPage:
    def __init__(self, browser):
        self.b = browser
    def send(self, text):
        self.b.fill('#composer', text)
        self.b.press('#composer', 'Enter')
    def wait_for_turn_end(self):
        self.b.wait_hidden('[data-stop]')
    def approve_tool(self, name):
        self.b.click(f'#{name} .allow')
```

## Be careful

Putting checks inside page objects mixes checking with driving. Return data, and let the test decide what is correct.

## Diagram

![Fig. 12.03: Callers speak in user actions. Only the page object knows the selectors.](/diagrams/page-object.svg)

id: service-stub
number: "12.04"
title: Service Stub
chapter: testing
fit: direct
figure_number: Fig. 12.04
figure_caption: The real loop runs against scripted stand-ins for the model and the tools.
diagram: service-stub.svg
analogy_title: The emergency call training room
---
## Gist

Replace the model and MCP servers with fakes that give scripted answers, so agent tests run fast, free and the same every time.

## Everyday comparison

### The emergency call training room

Trainee call handlers sit at real desks. But the caller on the line is an instructor reading from a script: a kitchen fire, then a fall at a bus stop. Every trainee hears the same call, with the same pauses and the same twist at minute three. The real emergency line is never touched. A trainee who struggles can replay the exact call.

## Classic meaning

During testing, you swap a troublesome outside service for a simple stand-in that returns set answers. This removes the test's need for the real service.

## In the agent system

The agent depends on a model client interface and an MCP client. MCP is a standard way to connect tools to an AI model. In tests, a StubModel returns a fixed list of responses, in order. First comes a tool_use (request to run a tool) for read_file, then one for edit_file. Last comes a final text block with stop_reason end_turn, meaning the model has finished. A stub MCP server lists the same tools as the real one but returns set results. It can also be told to fail or time out. Everything else runs for real: the harness loop, the permission gates, compaction (summarising old messages to save space) and the transcript logic. There is no network, no token cost and no randomness.

## In a large company

Enterprise CI (the automatic build and test system) runs the harness against stubbed or recorded model and MCP answers on every pull request. Live calls are slow, costly and give different results each time. Tests with the live model are kept for scheduled and pre-release gates. Recorded fixtures (saved test data) are captured in a record mode. Secrets, tokens and PII (personal data such as names and emails) are removed from them. They are refreshed when the model version or tool schemas change. Stubs are also the cheapest way to test error handling. Examples are 429 (too many requests) with Retry-After, 529 (overloaded), MCP timeouts and badly formed tool_use input.

## Step by step

1. The test builds a StubModel with a script, and a stub MCP server with set results.
1. The harness is connected to the stubs instead of the real clients.
1. The agent loop runs as normal, taking the next scripted response on each model call.
1. The test checks the loop's behaviour and checks that the script was used up.

## Code sketch

```python
model = StubModel([
    tool_use('read_file', path='calc.py'),
    tool_use('edit_file', path='calc.py'),
    text('Fixed the off-by-one.'),
])
mcp = StubMCP(tools={'read_file': 'def add...',
                     'edit_file': 'ok'})
agent = Harness(model=model, mcp=mcp)
agent.run('fix calc.py')
assert model.exhausted()
```

## Be careful

A stub tests the harness only against answers you imagined. Refresh the scripts from recorded real transcripts, so they stay close to what the model really sends.

## Diagram

![Fig. 12.04: The real loop runs against scripted stand-ins for the model and the tools.](/diagrams/service-stub.svg)

---
id: monostate
number: "13.01"
title: Monostate
chapter: idioms
fit: direct
figure_number: Fig. 13.01
figure_caption: "Many instances, one dictionary: a change through any one is seen by all."
diagram: monostate.svg
analogy_title: Clocks on every railway platform
---
## Gist

Let code create as many config objects as it likes, while every one reads and writes the same shared state.

## Everyday comparison

### Clocks on every railway platform

A big station has a clock on every platform, in the ticket hall and over the cafe. Each looks like a separate clock, but one master signal drives them all. Hang a new clock on platform nine, and it shows the same time as the rest the moment it is plugged in.

## Classic meaning

In a monostate, all instances of a class share the same state through class-level storage. It acts like a singleton (a class with one instance) but looks like an ordinary class.

## In the agent system

Tools, hooks (code that runs at set points) and subagents often create a HarnessConfig() locally. They use it to read the model name, the sandbox root or the permission mode. No one hands them a shared object. With monostate, the class keeps its fields in one class-level dict (dictionary). So every new instance sees the current values. Suppose the session switches to plan mode or raises max_tokens. That change is visible everywhere at once. Callers keep the normal constructor syntax and do not need to know the state is shared.

## In a large company

In an enterprise platform, a multi-tenant worker serves many sessions in one process. A tenant is one customer company. A monostate holding permission mode, model or tenant settings would leak one session's choices into another. That is a security defect, not a style issue. Session and tenant settings belong in a context object or a contextvars scope (Python's way to keep values separate per request). The scope is set when the request comes in, from the logged-in identity. Monostate is acceptable only for settings that truly cover the whole process and are mostly read, such as telemetry endpoints. Changes to them go through change-managed configuration (a formal review process).

## Step by step

1. Store the configuration fields in one class-level dictionary.
1. Point each new instance's attribute storage at that dictionary.
1. When any instance changes a field, it changes for every instance.
1. Reset the shared dictionary between tests.

## Code sketch

```python
class HarnessConfig:
    _shared = {'model': 'large',
               'mode': 'default'}
    def __init__(self):
        self.__dict__ = self._shared

a = HarnessConfig()     # in a tool
b = HarnessConfig()     # in a hook
a.mode = 'plan'
assert b.mode == 'plan'  # same state
```

## Be careful

Shared state that looks local surprises readers. Two sessions in one process will also overwrite each other's settings. So scope it per session if you run more than one.

## Diagram

![Fig. 13.01: Many instances, one dictionary: a change through any one is seen by all.](/diagrams/monostate.svg)

---

---
id: mute-idiom
number: "13.02"
title: Mute Idiom
chapter: idioms
fit: direct
figure_number: Fig. 13.02
figure_caption: "One named, harmless error is ignored. Everything else still shows up."
diagram: mute-idiom.svg
analogy_title: Packing up the campsite
---
## Gist

Catch and ignore one specific, expected, harmless error, such as a failed best-effort cleanup, and explain why in the code.

## Everyday comparison

### Packing up the campsite

On the last morning, you walk around your pitch collecting tent pegs. If one is missing because a friend already pulled it, you shrug and keep packing. Nobody files a report. You do not shrug if the stove is still burning. You ignore exactly one kind of surprise, and only because you know it does not matter.

## Classic meaning

The mute idiom deliberately ignores one known, unimportant exception (an error the program raises) in a small block of code. The code also notes why it is safe to ignore.

## In the agent system

At the end of a run, the harness deletes a temporary sandbox folder or scratch file. A tool may already have removed it, so FileNotFoundError is expected there. Some other actions are best-effort (nice to have, but not required). One is sending a final 'done' event to a chat client that has already disconnected. Another is writing an optional usage metric. The harness wraps just that call in a narrow handler for the one exception type. It adds a comment explaining why, and it may log the error at debug level. Every other error still propagates (passes up to the caller). Examples are a permission error or a failed transcript write.

## In a large company

In an enterprise platform, muted exceptions are still counted, usually as a debug log line plus a metric. So if a cleanup failure becomes frequent, someone notices. They catch it before it fills disks or leaves orphaned sandboxes (sandboxes that nobody owns). Writes that feed the audit trail, billing ledger, or retention and deletion jobs are never muted. A silent failure there becomes a compliance gap (a break in legal or policy rules). Static analysis rules (automatic code checks) that flag bare except blocks are a common part of the code-review gate.

## Step by step

1. Find a call whose failure does not change the outcome of the run.
1. Name the exact exception type that is expected there.
1. Catch only that type around only that call, with a comment.
1. Let every other exception pass up as normal.

## Code sketch

```python
from contextlib import suppress

def cleanup(run):
    # the bash tool may have removed it
    with suppress(FileNotFoundError):
        shutil.rmtree(run.scratch_dir)
    # the client may already be gone
    with suppress(ConnectionClosed):
        run.ui.send({'type': 'done'})
    run.transcript.flush()   # never muted
```

## Be careful

A bare except: pass (code that catches every error and does nothing) around a tool run hides real failures from the model and the user. Mute one named exception around one line, never a whole block.

## Diagram

![Fig. 13.02: One named, harmless error is ignored. Everything else still shows up.](/diagrams/mute-idiom.svg)

---
id: crtp
number: "13.03"
title: CRTPCuriously Recurring Template Pattern
chapter: idioms
fit: adapted
aka: Curiously Recurring Template Pattern
review_id: rev-crtp
figure_number: Fig. 13.03
figure_caption: "The base is told its subclass, so shared methods hand back the specific type."
diagram: crtp.svg
analogy_title: The self-addressed return envelope
---
## Gist

Give SDK base classes the concrete subclass as a type parameter, so shared chained methods return the specific builder or client type.

## Everyday comparison

### The self-addressed return envelope

A national charity mails the same appeal leaflet to every local branch. Each branch adds a return envelope printed with its own address. A donor fills in the general form and posts it back. The reply lands at that branch, ready for the branch's own follow-up.

## Classic meaning

In CRTP, a class inherits from a generic base (a template that takes a type as input), and passes itself as that type. The base can then share behaviour that returns or calls the child type. It does this without virtual dispatch (choosing the method at run time).

## In the agent system

An agent SDK has a base RequestBuilder with shared fluent methods. Fluent methods return the object, so you can chain calls one after another. Examples are with_system, with_tools and with_max_tokens. Subclasses such as ChatRequestBuilder or BatchRequestBuilder add their own methods. Suppose with_tools says it returns the base type. Then chaining .with_custom_id() after it fails type checking. The fix is to make the base generic over its subclass, written Builder[T]. This is the same shape as C++ CRTP or Java's Builder<T extends Builder<T>>. Then every shared method returns the concrete builder. Agent code can chain freely, and the type checker catches misuse. Some languages have a self type, such as typing.Self in Python or Self in Rust traits. A self type gives the same result without the type parameter.

## In a large company

In an enterprise platform, this mostly shows up in internal SDKs and request builders that many teams share. Fluent APIs with accurate types reduce misuse of request fields such as tenant ids, budgets or data-classification tags. A tenant is one customer company. Strict type checking in CI (the automatic build and test system) is the control that makes the pattern pay off. Examples are mypy or pyright for Python, and the compiler for Java or TypeScript. Keep the class tree shallow, so platform upgrades do not break other teams' builders.

## Step by step

1. Make the base builder generic in its own subclass type.
1. Shared fluent methods update state and return self, typed as that subclass.
1. Subclasses add methods for their own kind of request.
1. Callers chain base and subclass methods in any order, with full type checking.

## Code sketch

```python
T = TypeVar('T', bound='Builder')
class Builder(Generic[T]):    # CRTP base
    def with_tools(self, tools) -> T:
        self.req['tools'] = tools
        return cast(T, self)

class BatchBuilder(Builder['BatchBuilder']):
    def with_custom_id(self, cid):
        self.req['custom_id'] = cid
        return self

b = (BatchBuilder()
     .with_tools(TOOLS)       # BatchBuilder
     .with_custom_id('run-7'))  # type-checks
```

## Be careful

In Python this helps only static type checkers (tools that check types before the code runs). So prefer typing.Self where you can. Do not build deep generic class trees for one or two methods.

## Diagram

![Fig. 13.03: The base is told its subclass, so shared methods hand back the specific type.](/diagrams/crtp.svg)

---
id: twin
number: "13.04"
title: Twin
chapter: idioms
fit: adapted
figure_number: Fig. 13.04
figure_caption: "Two halves, each with its own parent, linked to each other and to one state."
diagram: twin.svg
analogy_title: The twins who run a corner shop
---
## Gist

Pair sync and async clients as two linked objects over one shared state, instead of one class that inherits from both.

## Everyday comparison

### The twins who run a corner shop

Two siblings run one shop. One serves at the counter, where customers stand and wait for their change. The other answers the phone, takes orders and calls back when they are ready. Each is trained for their own job. But they share one order book, and either can hand a customer to the other.

## Classic meaning

Twin handles a class that would need two parents. It uses a pair of objects instead. Each extends one parent and holds a reference to the other, and together they act as one.

## In the agent system

A model SDK usually ships two clients. Client is sync (each call blocks and waits), for scripts and notebooks. AsyncClient is async (calls can wait without blocking), for the harness's event loop (the part that runs many async tasks). One class that inherits from both a blocking HTTP base and an async base would clash. Method names and event-loop assumptions would collide. As twins, each client extends its own transport base. They hold references to each other and to shared parts. These are settings, credentials, rate-limit state and the usage meter. So a sync tool in a worker thread and the async agent loop share one view of the quota. Either side can reach its twin.

## In a large company

In an enterprise platform, sync and async twins often share rate-limit state, a usage meter and credentials. The credentials are rotated from Vault or a cloud KMS (key management service). Worker threads and the event loop touch the shared part at the same time. So it must be thread-safe, using a threading lock, not an asyncio one. Keeping metering and policy in the shared state means each tenant's budget is enforced the same way, whichever twin made the call. A tenant is one customer company. Contract tests run the same scenarios through both twins, so their behaviour cannot drift.

## Step by step

1. Build the shared state once: settings, credentials and usage meter.
1. Create a SyncClient on the blocking transport and an AsyncClient on the async one.
1. Link each client to the other and to the shared state.
1. Code in either world uses its own client, or reaches the twin through .aio or .sync.

## Code sketch

```python
class SyncClient(HttpTransport):
    def create(self, **req):
        return self.post(PATH, req)

class AsyncClient(AsyncTransport):
    async def create(self, **req):
        return await self.post(PATH, req)

def make_clients(cfg):
    st = Shared(cfg)       # keys, meter
    s, a = SyncClient(st), AsyncClient(st)
    s.aio, a.sync = a, s   # the twin links
    return s, a
```

## Be careful

Keep the twins thin. If logic is copied into both instead of living in the shared part, sync and async behaviour will drift apart.

## Diagram

![Fig. 13.04: Two halves, each with its own parent, linked to each other and to one state.](/diagrams/twin.svg)
